CAN lady killers be regarded in the light of dear's talkers? THE chief symptom of a con in the head is a handkerchief. IF a man would look rosy and round he must have square meals. IT is with love as with soup—the first helping is always too hot, and the last too cold. PLENTY of sleep is conducive to youthfulness. Even a garment looks old when it looses its nap. A WOMAN'S happiness is in danger when she begins to compare her husband with other men. IN a recent issue of a contemporary appeared a question 'entitled—" How should a trunk be packed 1" The proper way to pack a trunk is to sit in an easy chair and watch your wife do it. I always turn the gas out as soon as you leave tke room."

AT A CONFECTIONER'S—" Oh, mamma I do buy me some of those lovely sweets with mottoes." "Yes, darling, if you'll divide them with your little brother?' "Certainly. I'll eat the sweets and give him the mottoes; he's awful fond of reading." "WELT a good thing it would be if men were angels?" said one young lady to another. "Well, my dear, all those who made love to me were." "How so?" eagerly asked the former. "Why, be- cause they have all flown!" FRESHLY (rising to go)—" I'm sorry to break up your hana at whist, Miss Rosalie, but really I can't stay any later." Miss Rosalie—" Oh, never mind, Mr. Freshly, I am sure we will get on with a dummy just as well." 4' I au sorry," said she, "your sister is not here, Mr. Blunt." "She didn't fell quite well." replied Mr. Blunt. "She went to the cooking school this morning, and you know after the girls get through they have to eat what they've made." IT MAXES A DIFFERENCE.—" How much did /ou say tnis was?" "Three-and-six." "That's a big price, isn't it ?" "Oh, no, I assure you: the drugs are very costly." "But lam a druggist myself." Johnny—"No, I haven't. You wouldn't believe me If I had, so what's the um of my lying ? " LEADER of Lynching Party—" Now, young man, make a full confession or up you go." VANITY is so ineradicable a quality in a woman's nature that if you were to announce to a number of them that they were about to be hung in the presence of about 20,000 people, the first thought of each of them would instinctively be, Great heavensl and I haven't a dress fit for the occasion." div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
Lord James Douglas, who committed sucide on Tuesday, married, 12 months ago. Mrs. Hennessy, of Dublin, widow of the three star brandy mer- chant. She was given away by Sir J. Pope Hen- nessy.

Whenever the Prince of Wales, by the bye, or any of his family, undertake to preside at a charity dinner or a public function of that description, they always desire the menu to be submitted to them at Marlborough House. The Prince, in particular, has some distinctive tastes, and he often " sub-edits " the menu extensively.

Lord and Lady Fgerton of Teton have come to St. James's-square for the season. Lord Egerton has purchased Air. Leader's picture in the Academy of the works on the Manchester Ship Canal. I hear that Lord Egerton was very anxious to have the picture painted for himself, but that Mr. Leader had great doubts as to its success, which doubts Lord Egerton was able to overcome success- fully.

The new member for the Stowmarket division— Baron de Stern—is a. nephew of the late Baron Stern, whose will, proved about three years ago, showed him to be the richest man in the Queen's dominious. The new M.P. is also rich, lie lives in a handsome house in Great Stanhope-street, hill of curbus and beautiful objects, and entertains exten- sively. Ile is married.

More ot the M`Callum More. A correspondent writes :--Here is another story regarding the Duke of Argyll, which was current some thirty or forty years ago. It was then reported that Lord Palmer- ston had a very mean opinion of the Duke's capa- city both as a statesman and legislator, and conver- sing one day with a friend, he contemptuously dubbed. his Grace " an aristocratic canary.' This, I presume, on account of his personal appearance and cockiness.

Mr. William Tunstill, who presided on Monday at the annual meeting of the Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society at Exeter Hall, is one of Lanca- shire's millionaires, and is the head of one of the largest firms in North-east Lancashire. His brother is a Labour Commissioner. Their mills at Nelson are constructed upon the most most modern prin- ciples, and employment is given to nearly four thousand hands. Not only is he one of the main props of Wesleyan Methodism, but he is a staunch supporter of the temperance cause, and has erected a large coffee palace opposite to his weaving sheds for the use of his workpeople.

Few persons reading in the " Times " last week I of the death in Paris of F. Howard Vyse will call to ' mind that the announcement related to one formerly well-known as "Punch Vyse," who entered "the Blues" at the age of seventeen, and rose to com- mand the "E " troop in that regiment. Many good stories are told of poor " Punch," one being that on a cntain occasion, having to go on escort duty to Buckingham Palace or somewhere, he was unable to get his men out of the courtyard,his ideas of drill being somewhat hazy, so turning to his troop, he said, "Now, men, return to barracks as I you are in the habit of doing." ,

Mr. W. Knox D'Arcy, who his bought Mr. Frank Dicksee's" Mountain of the Winds" for .E 2,000 is one of the owners of the Gold Mountain in Australia This bunk of land, called Mount Morgan, went begging .about Melbourne market some time ago for £5,000. One or two people tried it without result, but finally Mr. D'Arcy and three or four friends purchased the lot for £30,000. For five years it averaged the partners the income of .£1,000,000 a year, and has lately been turned over to a limited liability company, in which Mr. D'Arcy is a large shareholder, It is said that his income from the mine varies from .£lO,OOO to £16,000 a month, ac- cording to the output.

"The Doctor," by Luke Fildes, R.A., is likely to be a favourite picture of this year's Royal Academy. Mr. Fildes went over to Scotland on purpose to get the exact representation of a typical cottage. He had a room constructed in his large studio in Mel- bury-rd., a foe simile of the one which caught his fancy north of the Tweed. The picture was painted by lamplight, so the fogs and the continual dark- ness of the long winter months did not interfere with Mr. Fildes's work. This picture will enhance his reputation. Mr. Fildes is still in early middle life, rather good looking, and a pleasant talker. Ile is married to a sister of Mr. Wood, the well-known painter of Venetian life. Mr. Fildes has several children, and lives in a large red brick house in the Melbury-rd.

The jovial Frank Lockwood. Q.C., was caught on Monday night in a querulous mood. He had to propose the toast of the Army and Navy at the ban- quet presided over by Prince Albert Victor, and he regretted that while those professions were popular, his was the reverse. If a hero in a three-volume novel or five-act drama was wanted, a jolly tar was chosen; but if a villain was required, a lawyer was taken. He was himself once *a member of the auxiliary forces, but he was never allowed either to shoulder a rifle or to fix a bayonet. He wished bis rear rank man had never been trusted with a bayonet either. He bad never drilled with any- thing more formidable than an umbrella, he said; but so far as an umbrella made a soldier, he believed he had no equal.

Dr. Hunter, who had a hand in freeing education in Scotland up to the fifth standard, now proposes that half of Scotland's share, £200,000, in this year's surplus should also he devoted to educational purposes. Of this sum £40.000 should aid free edu- cation in the higher standards. Then there would be assistance to technical continuation, and second- ary schools, contributions towards the purchase of school bo6ks, and to improving the Universities. This would take .£lOO,OOO. Dr. Hunter proposes that the other £lOO,OOO should be utilised in nationalising the deer forests, or as a contribution to national insurance. Questioned in the House of Commons on Monday night by Mr. Bryce, Mr. Goschen declined to say what the intentions of the Government were. If Mr. Hunter's plan be adopt f d a great boon will be conferred on the people of Scotland.

With rsp,c`, to the late Archbishop of York's ' great ptech on the Irish Church Bill, there still lingers in the Commons .a story remembered and told again on Tuesday night. Amongst the mem- bers of the House of Commons who were present on that occasion was the late Sir Robert Anstruther. Ile listened entranced to the splendid peroration with which the then Bishop of Peterborough con- cluded his oration, declaring in a passage of lofty eloquence that he could not reconcile it with his hopes of life hereafter to vote for the Bill. A mem- .r meeting Sir Robert Anstruther in the lobby, a-ked who had been speaking in the Lords. Sir Robot (who, it will be rembered, stuttered), replied, `• M-m-m-ag,-.e. making splendid speech." "What did he say?" asked the interlocutor. "He said he'd d-d-d-d if he voted for the Bill."

There is one story, more or less authentic, about the late Barry Sullivan which, we believe, has not been in print before. It is, however, a " wheeze " , well known among provincial actors of the " mate" school. While Sullivan was playing in a pro- vincial town, a little boy was sent to deliver a note to him at his hotel. The lad had seen him at the theatre, and being of an observant mind, had noticed that whenever page-boys delivered letters to him on the stage. th.y invariably knelt—as for instance, in "Richard III." and "Richelieu." his favourite plays. So the lad thought this was the proper thing to do in handing notes to the great Mr. Sullivan, and promptly dropped on to his knees. The actor smiled, and, tapping the little fellow on the head, said in his deep majestic voice, "Rise, lad, rise; know that there is one above greater even than Barry Sullivan."

The receipt of fuller details of the Manipur inci- dent has deepened the indignant feeling, in which members on both sides of the house share almost equally, not only that someone has blundered fatally, but because the whole business was trans- acted in an underhand wa3 quite unworthy of Englishmen. The folly of concealing from Mr. Grimwood,the man on the spot,all the details of Mr. Quinton's mission seems almost incredible. The question of kidnapping the Manipuree chiefs after inviting them to a durbar would be described, if it were recorded in history, as an act of the blackest treachery, only justifiable, even in the view of the most cynical, if succesful. Who is responsible for this? Did the Indian Government act without the sanction of the Secretary of State? If so, why so? Did the Secretary of State for India know what was arout to be done, and not prevent it ? Both alternatives seem almost incon- ceivable. I can only hope that the full official des- patches will clear up this discreditable dilemma satisfactorily.

A legal friend assures me that—statements to the contrary notwithstanding—there is not the slightest likelihood of the O'Shea divorce ease being re-opened. The decree will be made absolute on the 17th. There is nothing in the "information said to have been laid before the Queen's Proctor beyond the frivolous personal tittle-tattle which constitutes a sort of envplope to every divorce case. Mr. Parnell does not expect the case to be re-opened; Captain O'Shea does not expect it; Mrs. O'Shea does not expect it. •
BY THE OLD FOGY.

I like writing for you, my friends, and I like to give over writing. I feel, just now, a sort of rusti- ness in beginning again. And the pen is rusty, and the ink thick. I find it more pleasing to lift my eyes from the paper and rest them, without any thought at all, upon the shade of green which the trees are at last venturing. Tam idle with the idle- nc ss of Saint Monday.

Why cannot we play us always? It was much nicer to potter about amongst those rocks as I did a week or two ago than to sit stewing over this bit of paper. (I wish the editor would take his eyes off me.) It was fine to loiter about the coast, to climb cliffs,explore chasms and caves, and to knock little bits off the rocks with an infant hammer. I was quite happy there if I could chip out the shape of a shell from the limestone, and speculate, with a fine sensation of knowing something, about the condition of the original creature, and how he came to be part of such a formation. I have some- times felt that there is a little indecency in this cool examination of the private affairs of an individual whose activities were at an end a hundred thousand years ago, who never pried into our affairs, and can- not have done us any harm.

My friends, this is a good world. I would like everybody to come to that conclusion now and then. Perhaps everybody does, each in his own way, and once in a while. It does not suit all the folks I know to go maundering about old coast villages. Perhaps only fossilized fogies can find a pleasure in fossil shells and fossil fishermen. There are those whose soul is satisfied with a concourse of people in some health resort like Blackpool or Douglas. In the latter place they attain cheerfulness only in gangs. They break forth into joy; they also sing and make a loud noise upon the instrument known 'as the skriker. I do not desire these, and they would not enjoy themselves with me. This is a good world because there is room in it for us both.

Let me tell you there is a peculiar satisfaction in the rest at one of these villages, after a good day's tramping, or climbing or rowing. I shall do it again I know. (I wish the editor would not glare.) You should reach the place not too late, or else there is nothing left but going to bed. Nor too early,or conscience is not satisfied with your day's. work. You should npt be too tired, but tired enough. You must be hungry. Ah yes! you must be huugry. It is curious, is it not, that there is no such thing as comfort except as a succession to dis- comfort? I wonder if our Socialist friends ever realise that fact. There is no pleasure except as an alternative to pain. You should have a tine hunger on you when you approach my haven. There should be anxiety. too. And one cannot always be ; sure in these out-of-the-way places. On the day of Uncle Ned's blizzard it was well with us. We had found the landlaay with good store. We had easily secured her sympathy. We had approached her and her appropriately neat and attractive wait- ing maid with the tact of long practice, and behold! —smiles and toothsome viands! A feast of fat things with rejoicing. An attendant whose deft- ness and anxiety to please were even better than her good looks An absolute certainty that in due time we should he carefully bestowed for sleep. IV hat would you have? It is a good world that con- tains these things. (Why cloth the editor frown so I much?)

You know, at a time like that, one feels the noble juices of the repast absolutely thrilling one's fibres; there is a consciousness of rectitude in one. Having done well by the body, exceeding well nourished it, the moral nature seems to settle down into its pro- per place in the midst. It makes itself at home. It concedes there is no necessity for prodding so good a frame. Conscience relaxes its rigor, agrees to let bygones be bygones, and there is great content. Standing at the door of that little inn " in such a frame as this," leisurely filling my pipe, I could let the beauties of nature have a fair chance at me. The rocks, sky, sea, the ships away on the horizon, the gulls in the air, the boats down on the shingle be- low, even the boatmen,and cottages shoved into the most picturesque and inconvenient situations, all beautiful, all lull of suggestion and interest. Aye ; and the fowls and ducks and pigs.

There were two pigs there which were a study in themselves. One was a well-favoured and fat pig, and the other was an ill-favoured and lean one. And the well-favoured pig had eaten till he had enough, and would fain have been quiet. I had sympathy with him. Perhaps he hat stolen the lean pig's share ;I do not know. But I think the ill- favoured one's leanness was of long standing. The fat piggy lay upon his fat side a picture of prosper- , ous repose. lie dreamed happy dreams and chor- tled to himself in melodious gruntlets. And as he thus lay,the ill-favoured and lean swine approached with morose look and took council with himself privily to disturb his brother's peace. Not finding other that he might do, he cast himself by the side . ot his sleeping kinsman,and forthwith malevolently thrust his sharp hoofs into the stomach of him. It was ill-done. One could see and hear that it hurt. So with squeal of fear and many a grunt of indign- ation the fat one gat him home. The lean villain also went, giving utterance to exclamations of pleasure. I fear, I greatly suspect., that, ill-favoured and lean pig was possessed of Socialistic tenden- cies. You see, he did not, by his nefarious act, increase his own comfort one whit. But he brought the other chap a fair share of what misery was knocking about. And that was his game.

BY BENET YATES. A pooacher's nobbut a spooartsmon short o' brass. They co'd him Daft Tummus, but he allus took t' prize at a gooseberry show. Everybody likes good-lookin' lasses; lasses tiler- sel's like good lookin'-glasses. T' slowest chap i' t' world con tumble us fast as onybody. Savin' an' bein' kearful's reet enough, but it's a bad plan wastin' a pinny candle i' looking for a lost hau'pny. . Tramps wodn'd need to walk so far if they'd torn to t' reight. If yo' want to see summat as yo've never seen before an'll never see ageon, stan' on a highway an' watch t' fooak as passes. Miry rooads stop mony a bootless journey. It's late to rowl one's sleeves up when t' corn's stocked. A blind chap con see as much o' t' wind as other fooak. Never grumble at a grumbler, for yo'll find him mooar to grumble at. If everybody wer successful, fooak would give o'er strivin'. Id depends heaw yo' look at things; them as is farthest fro' glory is safest when t' bugles seawnd " retreat." Everything to id use; oil ruins fiddlestrengs an' keeps engines i' order. No' corn'd suit everybody; a brewer'll co a chap as builds churches a spendthrift. If focls wer taxed, t' national debt would disap- pear if we could nobbut get a wise umpire. Puttin' cooats o' arms on coffins is like coin' th' ocean private property. mooar than o t' world can explain, but it's true, As Sally likes rooases an' Rachel likes rue. Impidence walks away on stilts, but comes back on crutches. Fooak as is gooin' to ruin think four mile an' heawr too slow. T' loyalty of a starvin' chap can be bowt for a buttercake, or sowd, oather. T' deeds of a good chap is better than t' deeds of a bad heawse. For every patent lock, another clever thief. Yo'r own last milestooan's nobbut t' beginnin' of another mon's journey. Fooak ccan be fooak beawt kings, but kings corn'tl be kings beawt fooak. Poverty's like to be bad, or fooak wodn'd shame at bein' poor. There'd be fewer fooak ill if o t' physick wer paid for wi' ready brass, an' drink's sometimes co'd phy- sick.
A beggar's suit o' clooas is good enough to be ship- wrecked in.

Diggin' deep, an' risin° soon, Brings grist to th' mill, an' looaves fro' th' oon. If packs o'fleawer were gi'en away, we could'd tell t difference between lazy fooak an' herd werkin. millers. A easy rooad meons a quick journey; it's same t' rooad o' life. A hoys wants help when it's goin' upbroo an' a chap when he's gooin' deawnbroo. A footbo player geds clapped when he meks goal, but a weyver gets 'bated. If o t' songs as is written could be turned into money, there'd be a bonny lot o' bad moats knockin' abeawt.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A LYMM FARMER
div.p: SUICIDE OF A LYMM FARMER

On Wednesday, Mr. Worsley, coroner, held an in- quest on the body of Joseph Tickle, farmer, Sta- tham, Lymm, who was found the previous morning in his calf cote, with his throat cut. Ann Tickle, the widow, an infirm old lady, said the deceased was her husband, and was 50 years of age. He got up on Tuesday morning about six o'clock, and half an hour later she found him apparently in a fit in the calf cote. She called James Sharpies, who said he had cut his throat. Latterly her husband had worried , about the farm work and had been generally low spirited. —James Sharpies spoka to finding deceased dead with a knife clenched in his hand and his throat cut. The deceased had been very low spirited.—A Juryman : Didn't he say anything about Ship Canal shares ?—Wit- ness: lie wished he had his money back.—The Coroner : That is not uncommon is it? A slate was produced bearing the following in deceased's handwriting : "Dear brother, make a home for my wife. My bank-book and Ship Canal papers in desk upstairs. What money we have in the house she will know whose it is. Get John Sharpies to look after the cows. Send for brother John. Let all be sold. All that I die possessed of I give to you. This depression night and day ; I cannot live in this state." The jury returned a verdict of suicide whilst of unsound mind.

If he had been working at the stone when the piece came out he would not have suspected there was anything dangerous.—The Government Inspector, in reply to the Coroner, said he would recommend that a printed notice should be put up in the works regulating the speed at which stones should revolve, and also that they should be examined thoroughly each morning by some competent person before being started.—Mr. Davey: I may say on behalf of the firm that that will be done.—The Coroner having briefly received the evidence. the jury had a private consultation, and returned a verdict of accidental death, coupled with recommendations that the printed notice suggested 1:37 the Government Inspec- tor should be put up in the works and that lie should -examine every stone supplied by any firm.—The Inspec- tor pointed out that it would be impossible for him to do this as he had to inspect 7,000 places,and there might be 30 or 40 stones in a place; moreover his examina- tion would be useless as he had no practical knowledge of such things.—The jury therefore altered the recommen- dation on this point to a Suggestion that the stones should be examined, at least once a week, by a competen person appointed for the purpose.

Down below me, as I stood at the door of the little pub, a little beyond the pigs, there was an object of brilliant red, and of comical shape. It was a newly- painted buoy. There is nothing redder in the world than a red buoy except it be a post pillar. And opposite the boats there was a post pillar new painted. Against the post pillar there leant a man, slowly but very deadly scratching his back against the coping thereof. The satisfaction with which that man allayed his cutaneous perplexity was worth looking at. His features beamed with heavenly joy. lie did not bless the Duke of Argyll. Ile wot not of the Duke ; but in most excellent Welsh he blessed Raikes. -4 THE MANIPUR EXPEDITION.

REUTER'S AGENCY. —SIMLA, TUESDAY, 1.30 P.M.—A despatch received here from Manipur states that a man who is declared by the villagers to be the murderer of Mr. Quinton has been caught. The man was found to be suffering from three Levere bullet wounds.

It is believed that the Regent has left the Senapati, and is coining in to surrender. MANIPUR (via Koutata), MAY I.—There is no founda- tion for the recently reported death of Surgeon Styles, of the 18th Bengal Infantry. Twenty-six of 04 elephants which belonged to he Rajah has been captured up to the present. MANIPUR (via KOHIMA), MAY 2.—One hundred men of the 43rd Goorlthas, under the command of Lieutenant Clay and Captain Dun, of the intelligence Department. left here in search of the Rajah's army. One native officer of the Rajah's army, a man of importance, was arrested to-day. Cholera is still prevalent. All the troops composing the Burnaah column have now re- turned to Tammu.

div.head: PERCIVAL GORDON;
div.p: PERCIVAL GORDON;
OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT. --- BY SYLVANUS COBB.
CHAPTER X.

WITH THE PASSING OF THE YEARS. The days—the weeks—the months—and the years rolled away into the historic past, and Richard Archer bore his high honours with becom- ing grace and dignity. If he was proud, he never put on a show of pride towards those below him. Co his servants he was a pattern of kindness and consideration; by them respected and beloved, and obeyed because it was a pleasure to obey. Upon his brother Roland he had bestowed the old family estate at Dorchester, together: with the baronetcy. Neither of these could have been his during the lifetime of the elder brother, nor yet while issue of said elder brother lived ; but Richard caused the entail to be set aside, thus opening the way to the bestowment of the estate; and the prince regent kindly gave his influence towards a transfer of the title. All this was, for a season, like coals of fire heaped upon Roland's head. The memory of his cruel, wicked treachery was present to haunt him all the time, an this brotherly kindness smote

him to the heart. At length, when three years had passed, Roland had fallen in love with a beautiful woman, who had loved him in return, and then came the crisis. He could not take to his bosom a pure and loving wife, knowing that the bodily comforts of his home were to be the creations of his brother's bounty, while that horrible crime remained unexpiated. So, one evening, visiting Richard at his home, and finding him alone in his sanctum, he entered, and closed and locked the door behind him. Then' without hesitation, he advanced, and sank upon his knees at his brother's feet, one mighty cry of anguish bursting from his bosom, followed by a sobbing that for a time choked his utterance. But, by and by, he so far controlled himself that he was able to speak, when he poured forth, in a burst of terrible agony and contrition, a full confession of the crime. "Dick," he cried, when the wretched story had been told—" 0, let me call you so once inssre I Dear old Dick! I could not tuke to my bosom a wife, and live in the enjoyment of your bounty with this awful burden on my heart. It has been ter- rible to bear,-0 1 terrible ! Only your forgiveness can open the wey to rational enjoyment in the future." Richard suffered the unhappy man to go no further. He took him in his strong embrace, and blessed him from an overflowing heart. Forgive- ness he gave with inexpressible joy; and the clouds rolled away. The brothers stood, locked in frater- nal embrace, the elder giving thanks to God for this crowning mercy; while the younger, with a glad- ness that had net been his to feel for a long, long, time, pronounced a fervent Amen! And from that time Sir Roland Archer was a better and happier man; and his neighbours and friends talked together of the marvellous effect which the young baronet's marriage had upon him. Of all in the land only the two brothers knew the whole truth, even Caroline and oleNancy, seeing the love and harmony between them, were led to believe that there had been a grave mistake about Uncle Roland's blame in the matter of the failure of the earnest lettere forwarded from the brigands' cavern in the wild Sierras. Wonderful to relate, during the passing away of all this time—or, at least, the doctors pronounced it wonderful—the Earl of Oxton did net die. He still breathed and lived, and on pleasant days, when tha,warm sun shone clearly, and the wind did not come from over the sea, his stout attendant wheeled him about over the smooth walks of the garden and over the broad carriage-way before the castle. He was very thin and very pale, looking as though a puff might blow him away. In fact, but a simple anatomy was left of the man, never strong, yet he was as much Earl of Oxton as ever earl had been. But this did not interfere with the prospects of Matthew Egerton. His right to the succession had been decided upon by the highest authorities, and the earl himself recognised the boy as his legitimate heir. Very fortunately, in his younger days, as simple Walter Buckley, he had known Rachel Tre- velyan, and had conceived a strong liking for her, and it is possible that the coming forward of Major Egerton proved a bar to her becoming Countess of Oxton. However, he never suffered any heartache on that account. It was after that—after he had married—that, in overhauling the old records of the family, he had discovered that the two families of Buckley and Trevelyan ran back to the same fount in the time of the Commonwealth, and this he had communicated to Rachel, little dre-aming then what might hinge upon the fact in the future. To the Lord of Elmdale, one day, while that in- dividual stood by the side of his trundle-cart in the garden, he said: "You will have no fear, Elmdale, in contem- plating the union of your daughter with little Matthew. Only my marriage and the birth of is- sue could remove him from the succession, and that, we know, cannot happen. Be sure your daughterevill be Countess of Oxton." This jarred upon Richard's feelings, for he was convinced that Sir Edmund had prompted the fail- ing man's speech. But he put away the unpleasant emotion as quickly as possible, and opened his heart to his daughter's affianced. With the lapse of tiene came an event which thrilled the kingdom from end to end. June, of 1815, had little more than half gone when the note of victory at Wateiloo sounded through the land, and very soon the Gazette was teeming with the wonderful story, bulletins were issued and scat- tered on every hand; and every man and woman and child who could read found means to procure a news-print, and those who could not read sat under the reading aloud of those who could. Caroline was now twelve years of age. Her floating curls, like fairy threads of silk, had taken on a tingle of deeper, richer gold; expanding in- tellect had added depth and streugth to the mar- vellous beauty of her face and figure • and in every way the added years had favoured her. She lied learned to love and to worship the Duke of Wellington, whom she had known as Sir Arthur Wellesley, and she read with keen interest all that she could find in print concerning him. On the third day after intelligence of the viCtory of Wa- terloo had reached Elmdale, her father, who knew how eager she was to read of the Duke of Welling- ton, gave to her a copy of the Gazette, and very soon she VMS by herself, lost in the thrilling inci- dents of the great battle. And here we may remark that the girl was at heart a soldier. That is—the military ardour was prominent among her aspirations. From the moment when Percival Gordon, a boy no older than herself, had shot down the savage ruffian who was bearing her away to certain death, she had been filled with admiration of true physical courage and prowess. The stories which Percival had told her, so simply yet so thrillingly told—had wrought deeply upon her feelings, and led her to honour and admire the soldier's profession. So she read of the great battle understandingly. During the Years that hed passed since those happy days with her hero, in sunny Spain, she had not once heard from him, further than the simple fact that he was alive and well, and " plod- ding along as usual, as a boy in a great fumy." This her father had told her, when he had received • a letter from Col. Maxwell. But he had not been wholly honest with his little daughter. Maxwell had written much about the heroic boy, and had told of new deeds of valour he had performed, and he had added, that Wellington wee becoming more and more attached to the little fellow. All this the earl had kept to himself. The truth was, wheu he came to compare .Matthew Egerton with the little hero of the Sierras he dared not say a word that could stir his darling's feelings in memory of Percival Gordon. Caroline sat within the arch of a deep oriel, reading the Gazette. By and by, her eyes fell upon a beadliue that startled her. "A Boy HERO I" We can judge whence her fancies directed her thought. Ever since the first note of intelligence she had been anxious to know if Per- cival had been in the battle. Now, she believed, she should know all about. With bated breath she read. The story was of an event that transpired to- wards the close of that fateful 18th of June. Wellington was anxious for the arrival of Blucher, for with the aid of the Prussian host he was sure of victory. Napoleon had made more than one serious blunder, and of the last the duke wished much to ' take advantage, but a certain important movement he dared not make until he could be assured. " 0 ! that Blucher or night would come 1" he had exclaimed, when a boy aide, who had been near enough to hear, rode to his side, and offered to speed away and discover what was co:ning from beyond the woods towards the southward and east- ward. The course lay directly through the extreme right of the French army, but the boy had no fear, and he was suffered to go.

An eye-witness had penned the article, and he told graphically the story of the little hero's brave ride through the enemy's ranks. Amid showers of shot and shell, with bullets whistling. on every hand, within reach of many a French lance and sabre, the boy made his way, speeding like the wind, thinking only of the duty he had

volunteered to do. The day was very near to its close, and Napoleon had planned a desperate charge against the English centre, led by Ney. Wellington was anxious—far more anxious than he would have his officers know —when like a flash, his horse covered with dust and foam, himself hatless, with his waving locks floating in the wind, his clothing cut and torn by bullets, the boy appeared at his chieftain's side
with the ringing report: " The Prussians are cowing! Ziethen's corps is on the field, and he bade me tell you that he would

engage instantly. The cloud was lifted from the duke's brow and the burden from his spirit ; for, from that moment victmy was assured ; and in another moment the boy was riding away, upon a fresh hmse, to carry an order to the English centre. PERCIVAL GORDON was the hero's name. And the article went on to repeat the story of his saving the transport ship when only six years of age; and also to record the fact that he was a grandson of Captain Archibald Gordon, a brave and gallant officer, well remembered by many now on the stage. Special mention would be made of the gallant youth in the duke's dispatches, and his promotion might be considered as a thing assured. Caroline read the long article through a second time, then pressed the precious paper to her lips,

crying, as she did so; - "0, my hero My own Percival! Did you think of me on that dreadful day?" Then away she sped to find Nancy; and when she had found her, she closed the doors to the outer world, after which she read aloud the story of her own brave hems; and had the story been of a son of her own flesh and blood the loyal old nurse could not have been more truly rejoiced. Some- times she told herself that she was doing wrong. in helping to keep alive in her darling's heart the affectionate remeinbcatice of their boy-deliverer ; bet she could not help it. Not for the world would she have willingly led the girl to think of Percival Gordon ; but when the little one's heart was full, and when she poured out her love-song so tenderly and so happily, she could not, with rude, unkind words, break the charm. And then the boy was her hero as well. She loved to think of the bright-faced, beautiful lad as well as did Caroline, though she thought in different mood. The girl wondered if her father would mention the name of the heroic boy. Of course he must have seen the story of Percival's gallantry in the paper; for he read carefully all the intelligence from the seat of war, having dear friends in the army. But he did not speak ; and his daughter, with more and more maidenly reserve in her character as she grew older, suffered not the name of her hero to pass her lips in her father's hearing. Matthew Egerton, who had grown to be a stout youth of eighteen, with much of his manhood's character established beyond essential change, had come to regard the Lady Caroline as his future wife, and he was really charmed by her exceeding beauty; but, as for real love, it is doubtful if he would ever deeply and truly love any one except himself. He was proud and overbearing, and very apt to be insolent to those not above him; and only one or two men of his acquaintance were, in his own estimation, to be considered above him. He had already given his step-father to understand that he should receive no instructions or directions from him. Not yet was the coronet upon his brow • but it must be his very soon. He was wise enough to be modest and gentle in the presence of the old earl; and more than once he had, with his own hands, trundled the cart in which the invalid todk his out- door exercise. And the dying man was glad that so fair and promising a youth was to uphold the honour of the grand old estate. The youth was of good figure, rather above the medium height; strongly built; with straight, dark hair; eyes of a bluish grey, lacking lustre, and inclined to droop. They never really sparkled save when he was angry. His features were regular, and he was certainly good-looking, if a clear skin and a proper face constitute good looks; but in his face was no soul, no brightness of in- tellect; nor was it a face that was calculated to inspire confidence at sight. He had been well educated, and, so far as book-learning went, he was a scholar; but of native intellect—of that quality of mind which surmounts all obstacles to clear understanding by an induction of its own— he possessed not a particle. And, further, he was not personally brave, though he could bluster with the loudest He once saw an innocent, unoffend- ing girl in the hands of a brutal ruffian, and he had not the courage to interfere, but turned and sneaked away Bo that he might not be seen; and a boy, younger and smaller than he, and poorly clad, picked up a rock and drove away the cowardly ruffian. Unfortunately—unfortunately for him—Caroline heard of this, for the ragged boy spread the story far and wide,—a thing which he would not have done had not Matthew, at a later date, threatened him roughly and brutally with prosecution for trespass and theft, because he had gone over into the Oxton preserve and picked up a few ripe pears from the ground. Matthew Egerton was the, person, other than Nancy, to speak the name of the boy hero in Caro- line's hearing. She had hoped that her father would speak it, but she had not desired that the loved name should fall from Matthew's lips. "Well," he said, while he was visiting one day at Elmdale—there was a slur in his tone, and con- tempt in his look—for he hated that much-praised boy whom he had never seen—hated him because he was brave, and true, and loyal, and because he knew that everybody else liked him. "Well," he repeated, when he had attracted Caroline's attention, which his first utterance had not done—" I see that some of those fellows over in France have been writing up for the Gazette about the youngster that your father—" "Perhaps you mean over in Belgium," suggested the girl, with disgust in her look. "Well, over there somewhere, anyhow. Say, did you read the stuff?" Caroline felt in that moment that she ought to have had claws. She was never more indignant; never before had she felt herself so insulted. Mat- thew knew how she honoured and esteemed tht " youngster " to whom he had alluded; but in a moment more—before she had made a fool of her- self—the cooler thought came to her that the coward was trying to provoke her. His every look and tone showed that he wanted to see her angry ; he would punish for her thinking well-and nobly of Percival Gordon. It required no powerful effort to put back the fierce wrath he had provoked, but she was equal to the emergency. He observed her silence, and mistook its cause. "I spoke of your old-time hero of the brigands' cavern,' he added. "Did you see the correspon- dence in the Gazette?" "Yes," she replied with outward calmness. "I saw it and read it; and knowing Percival Gordon as I do, I VMS not at all surprised." "Perhaps you believed it all ? " said the youth, sneeringly. "Perhaps you did not?" retorted the girl, with peculiar emphasis upon the last words. "Most certainly I did not," he responded, with a provoking toss of the head. "And I should not have supposed you would," Caroline answered, looking him clearly and search- ingly in the eye. She started to speak further, and stopped and caught her breath. Presently, with an expression of countenance made up of pity and disgust, she went on: "1 will not speak as it was upon my tongue to speak. I had meant to taunt you with being a coward—born a coward—but I will leave you to judge yourself after your own instincts. But this will say: Were Percival Gordon here at this element, boy as he is, you would no more dare to speak to him an insulting word than you would dare to face the Bengal tiger in his native jungle." "Ho 1 ho! Upon my soul!" the youth exclaimed, trying. to laugh, "you are a whole-hearted champion. I should really—" "Beware, sir 1 " interrupted the proud-spirited girl, her feelings now stirred to their utmost depths. "Do not push me farther, I beg and implore. If you do," she continued, advancing a step nearer, and raising her finger towards his face, "I may be tempted to ask you where you will find the maiden with cause at heart to bless you for your heroism in defending her in the hour of danger. 0 1 how cowardly! how mean and contemptible! to stab a reputation of a fatherless and motherless bey behind his back, into whose frank and manly face you would not dare to look uncivilly. There —enough. Let me go, and do not, ever again, try to provoke me 1" And with this the proud girl turned and swept from the apartment—going more like a tragedy queen than like a miss of only a dozen years. Had Matthew Egerton possessed sense and reason, he woeld hay seen what a grand and noble wife

that girl would make for the man who could truly appreciate her, how pure and loyal she would bel and how true to the man whom she loved aria honoured. But sense and reason were not this, so he only saw a vixen who had struck him a smart- ing blow, and he was very angry, and swore that he would be revenged. But we may say here, he was never able to find means for the revenge he had sworn. Time passed on, and as Caroline grew older and older, she continued to grow beyond his moral and mental reach. He could not strike her as he did his valet, and his shafts of ill-natured irony did not wound her. He hated her because he knew she disliked him; the only creature in all the world for whose love he cared, and )et he hated her. But he bided his time. By and by she must be his wife, and then—ab, then,—he could train her to his will. And time passed on—more months and more years—until had dawned the year. eighteen hun- dred and twenty three. With the opening of the bright springtime of that year Lady Caroline saw the twentieth anniversary of her birthday. And Matthew Egerton was twenty-six, and very near, he thought, to the grand event of his life. The earl of Oxton had three times cheated the doc- tors, three times taken new lease of life, when they had consigned him to his death. But there could be no further lease. He was dying now, and he knew it: and his expectant heir tried to conceal his satis- faction. . And not more than a score of miles away another earl lay dying—Joseph Maxwell, Earl of W enham. He feared not death, but he strove mightily against it until he could see his son. He only asked that he might breathe his last in the arms of his brave and gallant boy. And his wish was to be granted. That wish the dying earl expressed to the lord of Elinciale, Richard Archer, and he spoke of it in the hearing of Matthew Egerton, whereat that young man was tempted to sneer. He had heard so much in praise of Col. Harry Maxwell that he hated him; and he told Caroline that he cared not to see him. _ _ _
Ah I little dreamed he, as he carelessly spoke, what the corning of that same Harry Maxwcll— General of Brigade—was to bring to his (nip.
(To be continued.)
HOBBES HITS THE NAIL ON THE READ.

TnE armies of things are the counters of wise men, but the money of fools." So says Philosopher Hobbes. He is quite right; and of all the sorts of slavery tha men are subject to, the slavery of mere words is the one from which we are slowest to break away. For example: Mrs. Eliza Chandler, of Natton, near Tewkesbury, says that her mother (Mrs. Sarah Kear) never knew what it was to be well for forty years. She was troubled with flatulency, had a sense of great weight at the chest after eating, with a stuffy, choking feeling, and marked difficulty in breathing; in fact, she seemed at times as if fighting for her breath, as a person would struggle against another who was trying to throttle him. From this point Mrs. Chandler says: "My mother got so weak she could scarcely crawl about the house, and for ) ears I had to attend upon her constantly. She could do no house-work, not even sweep her own room. For seven years she had had a bed in the sitting-room, being unable to climb the stairs. She got very little sleep on account of the sense of suffocation before spoken of. She always felt easiest when reclining in an arm-chair. Dur- ing some of her bad attacks I used to think every breath would be her last. Indeed, her sufferings were so great, she was always wishing she was dead. She was under
the doctor's care for many years, and was blistered and poulticed times without number.

"The doctor said her co:nplaint was asthma and debility,but he was puzzled at her breathing always being easier after getting up the phlegm. "In November, 1878, she had a very bad attack, and I had given up all hopes of her recovery, when one day Mr. Merritt,the insurance agent, called and told me what great benefit his mother had derived from taking Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and persuaded mother to try it.

I sent to the stores at Cheltenham, and got a bottle, and to my surprise and delight,after taking that single bottle, she found relief, and by persevering with the Syrup she got quite strong, and has never ailed anything since, Although eighty-one years of age, she can do any kind of house work, and feels better in every way than when she was thirty. She is constantly working in the garden evenadigging potatoes, and has an appetite like a boy in from the plough. She tells every one that Seigel's Syrup has saved her life after forty years' suffering, and wishes every one to know of the medicine." Such are the leading facts of Mrs. Chandler's story, and nothing could be more obviously sincere and truth- ful. Now the remedy which cured Mrs. Bear is not recommended for lung disease;; this the public well know. Then how account for its results in this case? Easily enough. Asthma, although it affects the breath- ing, is sot a lung disease at all ; it is a nervous disorder resulting from a poison in the blood, the same poison which under other conditions produces gout and rheu- matism. The source of this poison is the stomach, bowels, and liver when stupefied and deadened by chronic indigestion and dyspepsia. In other words asthma is a sympton of indigesti6n and dyspepsia ; it may or may not be the leading symptom, in this case it was. Let the reader learn this lesson, and it is sure to prove a lamp to his feet sooner or later. What was it Hobbes said about names? Oh, yes; "names are the money of fools." Perhaps that's put- ting it a trifle strong,- but this much is certain—viz., that asthma, rheumatism, gout, liver complaist, kidney trouble, and fifty more are names only. "Words, words," as Hamlet says. They mislead doctors and patients, and have done so time out of mind. If we could abolish them all, and call:the pains and dangers they stand for by the comprehensive term of indigestion and dyspepsia, we should get down to what miners call hard pan, for then we should resort to Mother Seigel's Curative ;Syrup at the very outset, and try no more foolish and useless experiments.

Mr. Gladstone, writing to a correspondent, says Mr. Osborne Morgan's scheme for a Welsh National Council, sitting in the Principality, with legislative and adminis- trative powers, is without doubt a matter of much in- terest; but he thinks it would not be advantageous to Wales to give an opinion upon it until it has reached greater maturity. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. THE NEWFOUNDLAND BILL.—The Earl Of KIMBERLEY moved a resolution to the effect that in view of the assur- ances recently made by the Newfoundland delegates, it was not desirable to go into committee on the Fisheries Bill until a reasonable time had been given to the New- foundland authorities to legislate in the matter. After a few remarks by Lord FERSCHELL and other noble lords, the Marquis of SALISBURY. said what the colonists wanted was not a temporary delay, but for the bill to be drooped altogether. The motion was lost by a majority of 83 votes, and the bill eventually passed through its committee stare. The liollse adjourned at ten minutes oast seven. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

The Speaker took the Chair at three o'clock. THE MANIPUR EXPEDITION.—SiT J. GORST. replying to a question, said the papers relating to the Manipur ex- pedition would include not only the instructions which were given to Mr. Quinton, but the correspondence which had taken place betaceen this country and the Indian Government.

TECHNICAL EDLICATION.—Sir W. HART DYKE informed Mr. IT. H. Fowler that a number of County Councils and county boriaughs had decided to apply the whole of the contribution from the beer and spirit duties to the pur- poses of technical education. FREE EDUCATION.—Mr. GOsCHEN, in answer to ques- tions as to the purposes of the Government for the ap-. plication of the Scotch sum under the free education scheme, said he was hot prepared to make disclosures with reference to Scotland until he had made those with reference to England and Ireland. THE LAND PILL.—The House again went into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Bill, renewing the debate on Mr. J. Morley'a amendment to omit section 1 of clause 5, relating to aid in case of exceptional agricultural calamity from the purchaser's insurance and reserve fund. Mr. BaLroun opposed the amendment, which. after a lengthy discussion, was rejected by a majority of 70 votes. Mr. Sexton's amendment, to except from the insurance scheme holdings in congested districts and those under £25 annual value, was rejected; as was another moved by the same hon. gentliman, providing that during alternate years of the first nine years the annuity should be £4 Bs. per cent. The House adjourned at 12.15. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TITESDAY. _ _

The Lora Chancellor took his seat on the wool sack at -a quarter past four. 113ILIS ADVANCED. - The Savings Banks Rill passed through Committee.—The Registration of Electors Act Amendment Bill was read a third time and passed.—The Statute Law Revision Bill passed through Committee. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS--TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock.

• PRIVATE BustwEss. The Loro.s' amendments to the Lancashire County Council Bill were considered and agreed to. THE SCOTCH EDUCATION GRANT.—Mr. GOSCHEN, reply- ing to questions, said the amount which would be granted to Scotland for educational purposAs would be £200,000. AGED MARRIED PRUPERS.—Answering Mr. Elliott Lees Mr. 111rirniE said instructions had been sent to Boards of Guardians that married couples in workhouses who were over 60 years of age were not compelled to live apart. BEER AND EDUCATION.—Sir W. HART DYKE informed Mr. 0. V. Morgan that the contributions from the beer and spirit duties to technical education towards the re- duction of local rates had only been applied by two counties and one county borough. TriaMenem:rum or MEMBERS —A Bill enabling mem- bers of Parliament to resign their seats was introduced by Sir H. James, and read a first time. Inrsn LAND BILL.—The House then resumed considera- tion of the Irish Land Purchase Bill in Committee, when Mr. Sextou's amendment to clause 5, reducing the amount of the purchase annuity from 80 to 76 per cent, of the annual value in certain cases, was negatived. Several other amendments submitted by Irish members were also rejected, in discussing some of which Mr. T. Healy and Mr. Story were called to order for irrelevancy. -The House adjourned at 12.20. HOUSE OF -COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-pat twelve o'clock.

Pntvivry. Rms.—The Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway Bill and the Local Government (Ire- land) Provisional Order (No. 1) Bill were read a third time. INFL'URnA IN GAOL.—Mr. BALFOUR, in reply to Mr. T. lealv, said the Prisons Board reported that Mr. John Cullinane was still seriously ill in Tullamore Gaol from Influenza, and could not be moved. Other inmates of the prison, including warders wore suffering from the disease, and there were many cases in the town. ASCENSION DAY SITTINGS.—Mr. W. H. SMITH moved that committees should not sit to-day, being Ascension Lay, till two o'clock. Mr. PICTON did not think that an occasion like that ought to pass without comment. The motion was characterised by a kind of pious arrogance. (Hear, boa,.) lie protestod against the motion, and should certainly divide the house against it. Sir W. LAWSON said perhaps the First Lord of the Treasury would state whether he intended to propose that the House should adjourn over the whole day for the Derby. Mr. W. JOHNSTON regretted that there should be any op- position to the recognition of the sublime rites of Chris- tianity. Mr. A. ELLIOT expressed the opinion that a man was none the less a good Christian because he did the work that was before him. The house divided, and the numbers were :--For the motion 110, against 32,majority for 78. IRISH LAND PURCHASE BILL, &C.-Then, at twenty-five minutes ts one o'clock, the house went again into Com- mittee on the Purchase of Land and Congested Districts (Ireland) Bill, and proceeded with the consideration of the fifth clause. Progress was reported, and the Labourers Cottage Gardens Bill was read a second time. and the Reformatory and Industrial School Children Bill Passed through Committee.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three. CAPTAIN VERNEY'S CASE. The Speaker intimated receipt of a letter from Mr. Justice Smith, stating that Captain Verney had been sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment. Mr. GOSCHEN stated that on Tuesday the House would be invited by the Government to take this letter into consideration. MR. SMITH'S PROMOTION. On the motion of Sir WILLIAM WALROND it was decided that the Speaker Should issue a warrant to make out a writ for the Strand Division, Mr. %V. H. Smith Having accepted the office of Constable of Dover Castle and Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports.

QUESTIONS.—Mr. BALFOUR supplied Mr. W. T. Russell With figures as to proceedings in Ireland under the Crimea Act. Other questions had reference to half- timers, the Education Act in Northhamp -onshire,alleged sweating in the baking trade, and the engagement of Zanzibar porters by Captain Stairs fora now expedition. Lord George Hamilton informed Colonel Hill that there was no intention to deprive the Navy of the assistance of the Naval Artillery Volunteers. It was proposed to gradu- ally convert them into Marine Artillery. Mr. Stanhope informed Sir George Campbell that preparations were be- ing made to replace the police with troops at certain posts within the colony of British Bechuanaland because they might be required to resist the trekkers. Mr. MACLEAN and Mr. SUMMERS asked a series of questions relative to Lord Salisbury's attitude in regard to the Berlin Labour Conference and child labour, and Sir J. YEauusson de- clared that the Government had acted consistently. Mr. Gosennw informed Mr. Cunninghame Graham that it would he impossible to allow the Eight Hours (Mines) Bill to he read a second time and referred to the select ' Committee on Railways. Mr. Sydney Stern took the oath and his seat for Stowmarket. hum LAND BILL.—The House again went into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Bill. On Mr. Balfour introduc- ing an amendment which he said was intended to relieve the ratep3yers and to prevent evictions through wide- spread calamity, Mr. LABOUCREIRE said if he ondeavoured to understand an amendment which was not on the paper he should lose the last glimmer of intelligence remaining to him, and under these circumstances he should retire from the Committee. Thus PASSED.—The „Cotramissioners for Oaths Act, 1889, Amendment Bill was read a third time and passed. The Reformatory and Industrial Schools Children Bill Was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at ten minutes past twelve o'clock.
