WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of thiEt,Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening, when there were present the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Aldermen Harri- son, Wright, Chandley, Sutton, Burgess ; Councillors W. Pierpoint, Shaw Green, Monks, Voisey, Walker, Greenall, Jenkins, Hepherd, Greening, F. A. Roberts, Blackhurst, R. T. Fairclough, Bolton, Flood, Muir, Hill, Heaton, Browne, Dixon, Garner, Beaman, Cannel], Hutchinson, H. Roberts; Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Dr. Goruall (medical officer), and T. Longdin (borough surveyor). It should be mentioned that Alderman Platt and Councillor Fleming were prevented from attending by the death of near relatives. fIIE FREEDOM OF THE BOROUGH FOR RETIRING

div.head: ALDERMEN.
div.p: ALDERMEN.

Prior to the ordinary meeting a special meeting of the Council was held to consider the question of conferring the honorary freedom of the borough upon. Mr. Joseph Davies and "Mr. John Crosfield, who had resigned their positions as Aldermen. The MAYOR said he had two resolutions to submit, and he proposed to submit them separately. He moved "That Joseph Davies, Esq., J. P., be and he is hereby ad- mitted an honorary freeman of this borough, in recogni- tion of valuable and eminent services rendered by him to the borough." That resolution was, the Mayor said, unanimously passed at the General Purposes Committee meeting. They considered Alderman Davies had been such a valuable member of the Town Council for many years,and had done so much eminent work for the town, that it was believed the Council would willingly- accept the resolution. He hoped it would be passed unani- mously. Alderman CHANDLEY seconded the motion, and said he regarded Alderman Davies's departure from Warrington as a most serious and unfortunate loss to the Town Coun- cil. He did not think there was a man in Warrington who had dope done so much for the Corporation as Mr. Davies had done. And it was not only in that Council that they had learned to appreciate him' for in Com- mittee his ready and matured judgment was always equal to an emergency. He had had at all times a single eye to the welfare of the borough, and his frequent ex- pression would be remembered by many present, "Is it for the welfare of the borough 2" (Hear, hear.) Alderman WRIGHT said that, as a member of the Pav- ing and Sewerage Committee, he deeply regretted Mr. Davies's resignation. Whenever any trouble had arisen, lie always seemed to have with him that " bottle of oil," to which Alderman Holmes referred at the previous meet- ing of the Town Council. The younger members of the Council could ill afford to lose such a man,and he trusted the older members would remain with them as long as they were able to do so. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Houfis said he was exceedingly glad they were going to confer the honorary freedom of the borough upon Alderman Davies. It was a compliment he well deserved. Alderman Davies had worked hard n the Council and in the town, and had dene everything be possibly could at all times for the benefit of the inhabit- ants of theborough. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SUTTON did not think there could be two opinions as to the unfortunate loss the Council had sus- tained by the resignation of Alderman Davies. Councillor Mum said he was enticed to become a mem- ber of the Paving and Sewerage Committee because he was told that it had a merry chairman, and that the Committee was a comfortable one. He was also told that he should get a good dinner once a year. (Laughter.) He thought the honour it was proposed to confer upon Alderman Davies was quite deserved. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS thougkt the honour they were about to confer on Alderman Davies had been eminently earned.not only in that Council but in ether departments of the borough. As they had commenced the work of conferring the freedom of the borough upon gentlemen who had distinguished themselves he hoped they would not be wanting in treating others who had equally cm- served it in the same way. pear, hear.) The motion was then carried unanimously. The MAYOR then moved "That John Crosfield, Esq., J.P., be and he is hereby admitted an honorary freeman of the borough in recognition of valuable and eminent services rendered by him to the borough." (Applause.) Mr. Crosfield had been equally unanimously nominated by the General Purposes Committee, and would no doubt be accepted by the Council quite as readily as Alderman Davies. Mr. Crosfield had been a member of the Town Council for about 17 years, and during the whole of that time had done his best for the town. (Hear, hear. Dur- ing his mayoralty he was very liberal, and had erected several works which would be remembered and handed down to posterity to show his great generosity. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Gue.matr, seconded the motion. Councillor BOLTON, in supporting it, said he con- sidered the honour well deserved. They had an excel- lent institution in Museum-st.—the School of Art—and it was Mr. Crosfield's generosity that had brought it to its present state. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then submitted and also unani- mously agreed to. The MAYOR said he should be pleased if a small Com- mittee was appointed to decide how the .freedom of the borough should be presented. Alderman SUTTON proposed the selection of Aldermen Chandley. Burgess, and Holmes and the Mayor. Alderman WRIGHT seconded the motion, which was carried. The MAYOR: The Committee will report to the General Purposes Committee, who will bring the matter forward at the next meeting of the Council.

TWO .VACANCIES IN THE COUNCIL. The Mayor re-iead Alderman Davies's letter, and de- clared the aldermancy vacant. He also read a letter from Councillor Taylor, resigning his seat, and declared his seat also vacant. The Mayor next read a letter from Mrs. Litton, thanking him and the Council for the heart- felt sympathy they conveyed to her on account of the death of Major Litton.

div.head: POLICE.
div.p: THE POLICE.

?he Watch Committee's minutes contained the fol- lowing :—That P.C. John Turner be awarded the Merit Badge, and an increase of pay of is. per week for good conduct and meritorious acts done in the execution of his duty. P.C. Richard Singleton having given notice of his intention to retire on life pension after 31 years' service, it was resolved that he should be allowed a life pension equal to two-thirds of his annual pay. The minutes were adopted on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman HARRISON. FINANCE.--THE VALUE OF LONGFORD MANURE.

In the Finance Commmittee's minutes was given an amended total estimate of expenditure on improvement rate account for the year commencing March, 1891, amounting to a total of £26,992 ss. The assets deducted by the Committee were as follows : Uncollected rates, £2B; accounts owing for manure, £750 is. lid.; value of manure in stock at depots, £1,465 ; estimated Value of manure to be concentrated during the year, £1,600; consideration for use of Hospital, £104; probable receipts for market rents, tolls, hire stalls, and adjusting and stamping weights and measures, £3,600; amount due from Lancashire County Council for the repair of Wilderspool Causeway to October 1890, £446 10s. ; amount falling due during the year for do., £349; value of material in stock for the construction of private streets, to be repaid by owners of the property, £530; total assets, £8,872 lls. 11d. The assets deducted from the £26,992 54., leaves a total estimated expenditure of £18,119 13s. I.d, against £14,921 16s. Bd. last year. The Committee had also passed the following resolution :—Mat the Finance Com- mittee be authorized to make an Improvement Rate for the year commencing 26th March, 1891, at 3s. in the pound, to be collected by two half-yearly instalments, which is estimated to produce about £18,612. Alderman HorztEs prbposed the adoption. Councillor SHAW GREEN seconded, and pointed out that the amount of uncollected rates mentioned in the minutes had been reduced to £3 25., and he thought that the fact that a total of £7,613 had been collected within £3 2s. showed clearly that the collector was doing his duty thoroughly. Councillor PIERPOINT remarked that the estimated value of the manure, £1,600, was a very serious reduc- tion from the estimate of the previous year, and asked at what value per ton they had estimated the make for the corning year. Alderman Elkitiusori asked if the whole of the £750 alleged to be owing for manure would be available or whether part of it would consist of bad debts. Alderman HOLMES said as far as was known the ac- count of £750 set down was all recoverable Alderman SUTTON said the value of the manure men- tioned in the minutes was the correct estimate, as given by Mr. Chorley, of the value of manure in stock. Councillor 15IERPOINT : No, that is another thing. It is the make forth° ensuing year. Alderman Serrox said that was the estimated value according to Mr. Chorley's information and knowledge. Any member of the Council could get any further in- formation from Mr. Chorley or by attending the Finance Committee. Councillor BOLTON asked whether the estimate of £1,600 put upon the manure by the Finance Committee was the same value as the Sanitary Committee had put upon it. He understood that the latter's valuation was considerably more, and bethought it was only fair to the town that they should know whether both were of the same opinion, or if not why there was a difference. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS did not think Alderman Sutton had answered Councillor Pierpoint satisfactorily. To be told that this was the value estimated by Mr. Cheney raised one's credulity somewhat, because he did not know that Mr. Chorley knew about the value of manure. If the Corporation had a practical guarantee from the Sanitary Committee that this amount was correct he could have unierstood it, but the Council could not throw the responsibility on the Borough Trea- surer, and he for one objected to any servant of the Cor- poration being saddled with the blame of members of the Council. Alderman BURGESS replied that the Sanitary Commit- tee had nothing whatever to do with the figures before the Council. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS asked if the figures were such as the Sanitary Committee were prepared to substantiate. Alderman BURGESS : The Sanitary Committee have

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 9, 1891
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 9, 1891

not approved of them and they think—and I speak it out too—that the ratepayers are having a slight injustice done to them. Councillor F. A. Rowswrs : Hear, hear. We have get what we want. Councillor MUIR, in justice to the borough treasurer, had to say that the Committees he was connected with had generally given him their estimates ; he-did not think any officer made estimates for the Committee. Councillor SHAW-GREEN thought he could put some thing tangible before the Council which would enable them to determine whether the £1,600 put down was an .unreasonable sum. £6OO had been brought forward as owing for manure last year. £1.510 had been received during this year for the manure sold,and there was £750 owinz Now, if you deducted £6OO from £1,510 with the £750 added thereto that would leave £1,660. They had a right, therefore, to assume that what was made last year might be made this—whether it would improve oi decrease in value they were not prepared to say. Councillor JENKINS asked how £1,465 was arrived at. Councillor Dixon: No answer. A Councillor : And you will not get any. The minutes were adopted. NEW HOUSES. &C. The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee recommended that the plans of the following buildings, &c., be approved: Seven houses at Conies Corner for Mr. John Appleton; four honses in Ellesmere-st., for Mr. George Hand; two houses in Green-st., for Mr. Thomas Williams i • gymnasium in Palmyra Square, for the War- rington Gymnasium Committee; four houses in Arpley- sc., for Mr. William Silcock. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Alderman SUTTON seconded by Councillor 13ovrox
TEE -SANITARY _COMMITTER

_ This Committee recommended that the order given to Messrs. W. Smith and Sons, for two sanitary tumbler carts be countermanded, and that the order be given to Messrs. Wadsworth and Son at the price of £56. The Committee resolved that 1,000 copies of the annual re- port of the Medical Officer of Health should be printed and circulated among the ratepayers. Alderman BURGESS moved and Alderman SUTTON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor JENKINS requested that his motion might be taken now instead of at the fag end of the meeting when there was usually a disinclination to thoroughly discuss subjects which were really important in them- selves.
The MAYOR said that was a matter that he would leave to the Council to determine: _

Alderman BURGESS had no objection to the course proposed. Councillor PIERPOINT thought the ordinary business should first be disposed of. Alderman BUTTON expressed the same view. Councillor BOLTON moved that none of the money for Longford'depots be paid until the Council were fur- nished with the information as to how the calculation as to the return on manure had been arrived at. (A Voice: Vote.) He was only doing so to put the matter in order, not that he intended to carry it through, but he•thought they ought to be satisfied as to whether there had been a clerical error or otherwise. Councillor DIxoN seconded. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS appealed to them consider- ing the difficulties of the Sanitary Committee to allow them time to try to investigate the matter to the core before pressing it on the Council. After a murmur by Councillor Dixon as to matters being delayed month after month, the motion was with- drawn.
The minutes were then adopted. PAVING AND SEWBRAGE COMMITTETt

Resolution. that Fountain-st. be paved. The Gas Com- mittee having intimated their willingness that this Com- mittee should have the charge of the boilers at the Gas Works, during the summer months. Resolution, that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to take over and work the engine awl boilers at the Gas Works, for five months from the Ist May next, and that he report at the end of the first month as to whether the boilers are suffi- cient for the joint purposes of this and the Sanitary Committee and that he also state the number of hours worked, and the comparative cost to each department. Alderman WIUGHT proposed the adoption of the minutes. Councillor HUTCHINSON seconded.

Councillor PIEnpoiNT asked whether the object of the recommendation as to taking possession of the boilers at the Gas Works was to enable the Committee to work the sewage at Latchford regularly, and if so, whether the necessity for bricking the culvert on private property could be done away with. Councillor DIXON asked when Fennell-st. was going to be paved, . _ - -

Councillor BROWNE : What has been done about How- ley brook ? Alderman WRIGHT replied to Councillor Pierpoint's first question in the. affirmative. The culverting of the brook in Lat.:Hord -was, he was informed, an absolute necessity, but it would not be necessary to make so large a culvert. The Howley brook was being progressed with as fast as possible, pending arrangements with the ad- joining landowners for an outlet. Fennell-st. would be done as soon as the Committee could afford it. At pre- sent they could not. _ _ . . . .
CounCillor DixoN : That is the old tale. The minutes were adopted. THE SCHOOLS.

From the report of the Inspector to the School Attend- ance Committee it appeared that 38 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 34 cases for 77 children. That 41 cases had been taken before the magistrates, and fines inflicted in 34 cases, one boy sent to an industrial school, two orders made, two adjournel, one boy ordared to the Workhouse and one dismissed. 36 cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. The average attendance at the Public Elementary Schools, during the month of March, wal 7,982, corresponding period last year 7,573. increase, 389. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Councillor SHAW GRHEN, seconded by Councillor Muni.

I was authorised to order a coke-barrow to cost 30s. and a ladder to cost 15s. ; that the wages of W. T. Cranlc be raised to 18s. 6d. a week ; the Librarian was authorised to purchase additional copies of popular books to a cost of £25; that the lending department be prepared for opening free by the 4th August. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Councillor 11. ROBERTS, seconded by Councillor PIERPOINT.

Councillor R. T. PAIRCLOIIGH said that now the greatest bathing place in the borough, Howley brook— (laughter)—was likely to be done away with, he thought they ought to have a free bathing place for boys, and he suggested that a very suitable place was some land below the cemetery, as they could get water from Pad- gate brook at a little expense. The MAYOR said that had been already before the Council on the suggestion of Councillor Jenkins. Councillor HEATON said that he was of opinion that Warrington baths were as good as those of many places he had visited. He was rather doubtful whether, even if they had better baths, there would be much improve. ment in the number of those who made use of them. He was afraid they had a lot of people in Warrington who did not like to be washed. (Laughter.) Councillor E. GREENALL spoke in favour of a lurkish bath being provided. Councillor HEATON added that he was afraid the plan that had been drawn out would not be completed for less than £5,000. Councillor HEPLMAN asked if the Baths Committee had made any alterations in the discharge of waste water in the shower baths. The MAYOR said that was provided for in the new plans. He could not quite agree with Councillor Heaton as to the cost of the alterations. Mr. Longdin must be their guide in that matter. He also differed from Coun- cillor Heaton as to the baths of other towns, for in every place they have visited the baths were very much in ad- vance of those of Warrington. The baths at Warring- ton were wretched and a disgrace to the town. (No. no and hear, hear.) There could be no doubt of that. They were dirty in the extreme and the walls were filthy. As for only two per cent. of the population going to them, it was a wonder to him that anyone went to tho place. (Hear, hear.) If they had good baths he had every rea- son to believe that they should have a good per centage of the population using them. He aiso thought it would be well for the Committee to provide a Turkish bath if possible. Couocillor DIXON was amazed that so little was said about the increase of rates, although there was only one borough that had higher rates than Warrington. Councillor PIERPOINT thought that a judicious expendi- ture on baths would have the effect in the long run of saving the rates of this borough considered from a health point of view. It was all very well to be economical, but there were times in which a little judicious expenditure is perhaps well timed. He sympathised with the diffi- culty of the Committee in having a chairman who rather tried to throw cold water upon the scheme. Alderman Chandley spoke about promises being made to constitu- encies, but if some of the aldermen had to gosbofore the constituencies they would be just as prone to give promises as any common councillor. (Hear, hear, and laughter...) The minutes were then adopted with the "alteration suggested by Councillor Roberts. THE MARKETS.
_ The minutes of the Markets Committee, the substance of which we gave last week, were adopted on the motion of Councillor GREENALL seconded by Councillor BLACK- HURST.

div.head: MUSEUM AND LIBRARY
div.p: THE MUSEUM AND LIBRARY

The minutes of the Museum, Library and Arts Com- mittee contained the following :—Return for the month of March : Visitors to the Museum 3,254, decrease 23 per cent, compared with March, 18)3 ; nooks is;ue-1 in read- ing-room 2,309, decrease 9 per cent. ; books issued in lending department 1,759, decrease 1 per cent. Report of the following gifts, for which the thanks of the Com- mittee were ordered to be sent to the donors : A bramb- ling from the Town Hall Committee; hammer-stone found as Irlam from Mr. J. S. Sherratt ; fossil shells, from the Ship Canal Cutting (12 species) ; Pholas candida from Hilbre from the Field Club ; " School law of Cali- fornia," and other pamphlets (4) from Mr. H. Whitham: "Present to youths and young men," by .E. Shorthouse from the Author ; " Linguistic Essays," third series,and "low I spent my holidays," from Mr. R. • W. Guest. An estimate of the income and expenditure of the Com- mittee for 1891-2 was submitted and approved. Resolu- tions : That Messrs. S. E. and 11. Johnson's tender for new blinds, &c., at a cost of £2 17s. 3d., be accepted; that the temler of Messrs. Hesketh and Son, for painting &c., to cost not exceeding £3B, be accepted ; the Curator

div.head: CEMETERY.
div.p: THE CEMETERY.

From the report of the registrar to the Cemetery Com- mittee it appeared that the interments during the past four weeks were :—Adults-65; minor, 50; stillborn and premature, 9; corresponding period last year, adults, 49, miners, 55; stillborn and premature, 14. The receipts for the past four weeks were R 77 us. 4d., corresponding period last year, £7l ss. Alderman HARRISON moved the adoption, remarking that the health of the town was satisfactory, and that the mortality among young children was not so great as before.
Councillor HtrranNsorz seconded,and the minutes were adopted. THE NEW BATHS TO COST £3,500.

From the report of the Bathkeeper it appeared that the income from the baths for the past four weeks was £7 13s. 6d. ; corresponding period last year, £6 55. 2d. The Committee had passed the following resolutions That the tender of Messrs Williams and Clay for the wall tiling required to be done in the east entrance to the Town Hall at £l9 10s. be accepted; that the plan now produced for alterations at the baths be approved, and that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to prepare esti- mates of the cost.

Alderman CHANDLEY proposed the adoption of the minutes. At this stage, he said, he forbore offaring any 'opinion as to the merits or demerits of the plan or of the advisibility of altering the baths. The plan had been before the Committee, and had been well con- sidered, and it was thought advisable to make them. The accommodation would be very ample. The only question that would appear to the Council to be worthy of consideration now was that of cost. He was informed by the Borough Surveyor that the approximate cost would be about £3,500. He daresay a great many in the Council were pledged in their addresses to their con- stituents to do something with the baths; and it was a very easy thing at election times to promise this, that, and the other, and to :fulfil the promises if there was plenty of money to do it with. The question was whether it was advisable to spend £3,500 in altering the baths. It was a great boon to have a good bath, but the bathers in this borough did not number more than 2 per cent, of the population ; and the Corporation must bear in mind that there were other works to be done. It was likely- that the widening of Bridge-st. would be brought for- ward by the Street Improvement Committee and the alteration of ' the Town Hall would very likely be brought forward by the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee. Then the Watch Committee had had notice that the Inspector of Police considered the police cells , were inadequate, and this being the third time he had .notified this it was likely that the authorities would pre- sently insist upon something being done. He (Alder- man Chandly) was simply 'throwing out these hints to show that there was money to be spent in all directions and there was this before the Council for their con- sideration.

Councillor Bovrox seconded. He mentioned that the plans already exhibited showed only a portion of the scheme. It was intended to provide Turkish baths and other things. (A chorus of hear, hear.) The land could be so laid out that the buildings could be ex- tended to meet future requirements and it was only a question of means. Councillor JENKINS while appreciating, the remarks of Alderman Chandley as to the necessity of economy thought if money could be expended in as economical a way as possible to bring the bath system of the town to something approaching that of other towns in our imme- diate neighbourhood, it would be an immense benefit to the population. He considered that Turkish baths might conveniently be provided overhead. Every effort would be made to find money to carry out the scheme, which would meet what he thought a very great need in War- rington. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS thought the resolution per se committed the Council to the approval of the scheme without knowing the cost, though he was very much in favour of having good and adequate baths in the town. He thought especially' considering that additional extensions were now talked about, that the Corporation should have a more complete scheme and some esti- mate before them ere they approved of the plans. Alderman CHANDLEY explained that it had not been thought' worth while giving the borough surveyor a great deal of trouble in order to have estimates prepared until they know whether the Council were disposed to spend the money. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS appreciated this argument, but said the wording of the resolution did not say this.

Alderman SUTTON differed from Councillor Roberts, considering that the resolution committed the Council to nothing, as the plans and the estimate of cost would have to be confirmed before,the scheme Ruld be carried, so that the Council would still have toNlecide upon the matter.

Councillor H. ROIIHRTS suggested that the word" re- ceived" be substituted in the resolution for the word "approved." That would leave the entire matter for the Council to consider and discuss When the estimates were prepared. He must, however, express his intense surprise at the manner in which those minutes in re- gard to the proposition for extending the baths had teen put before the Council by Alderman Chandley. If ever anything was "claimed with faint praise" the question of new baths had been treated in that manner most effectually. (Hear, hear.) All the members who were elected last November, without exception, were pledged to the extension and improvement of the bath accom- modation. (Hear, hear.) Councillor 11EPHERD : Except me, Mr. Roberts. Councillor ROBERTS, continuing, said there might be a solitary exception and the solitary exception only proved the rule. .They all knew that in every community there were some who were laggards and behind the others. (Hear hear, and laughter.) But besides those who were elected in November a majority of the Council had ex- pressed themselves in favour of better bath accommoda- tion. In addition to that the Corporation obtained powers in their Improvement Act last year for the bor- rowing of a capital sum, and,lherefore, to come there and remind them that there were other things in pros- peet with a view of keeping back those necessary alter- ations and improvements was hardly fair. The reason why only two per cent. of the population made use of the baths was that the baths were not fit to be made use of. (Hear, hear.) He thoughtit would be a crying shame if that matter were put off any longer than necessary, and he rejoiced that they had got to the point at which theßaths Committee had submitted a plan, and he hoped they would go forward with a determination to remove , the odium which attached to the Committee and War- I rington in regard to bath accommodation. He also spoke , in favour of a Turkish bath forming part of the scheme, I and concluded by moving the alteration of the minute referred to.

div.head: GAS.
div.p: THE GAS.

The Gas Committee reported that the average power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to. 18.83 candles at both works. The minutes were adopted on the motion of* Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Councillor FAIRCLOUGII. THE NAVIGATION OF THE RIVER. A SERIOUS OUTLOOK.

The minutes of the Rivers Committee contained a letter from the Board cf Trade in which were set forth the conditions on which the Corporation of Liverpool had been allowed to lay a temporary pipe-line across the Mersey, and also the resolution of the Committee thereon which we gave last week. Councillor FAIRCLOUGA in moving the adoption of the minntes said he considired that the Liverpool Corporation had woefully mismanaged the putting of the pipes under- neath the river. He did not think that they should have put the pipes under there at all. It was the worst place between Warrington and Llverp,ol, and was well known by all the watermen to he the worst place. (Hear, hear.) When boats, leaving Warrington Bridge with the tidal wave, reached the spot where the pipes were laid, it would be a question of touch and go whether they got over them or not. Again there was no condition as to seeing that the pipes would be out again. He thought that probably 101000 or 15,000 tons of traffic in the year would now be diverted from the river. Councillor HEATON seconded the motion that the minutes be adopted. Alderman Sorrow said that he should have been glad if the rivers committee had succeeded in getting what they wanted, but he did not think that, after all, they had much to regret when they came to consider the Conditions lised upon by the Board of Trade. The con- ditions entered on• the ntinutes appeared to afford suffi- cient protection to the corporation of Warrington and those whose vessels navigated the river. Councillor BOLTON thought the Board of Trade had done all that they could for Liverpool and nothing for Warrington. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that the rivers Committee of the Warrington Corporation had been simply" chucked , overboard entirely" by the Board of Trade, and every request made by LiVerpool had been agreed to. Many of the craft on the river belonged to comparatively poor men and the new arrangements would simply bar these men out entirely if there were any risks,because in order to get compensation they would have the Corporation of Liverpool to fight. (Rear, hear.) In answer to Councillor Flood, the TowN CLERK said the decision of the Board of Trade was final. The minutes of the Committee were adopted. THE FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE. The minutes of this Committee were approved. THE PROPOSED DOCKS.

The most important items in the minutes of this Com- mittee were given in our columns last week. With re- gard to the resolution " That the Manchester Ship Canal Company be requested to insert in the Bill now before Parliament a clause providing for the construction of the docks at Warrington before the 6tWAugust, 1895, that being the limit of time allowed by the original Act," Councillor FAIRCLOUGH pointed out that the only way ships would have of getting out of the canal into the river would be through the docks. _ .
The minutes were approved on the motion, of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman Surrox.
TRE AMENDED IMPROVEMENT RATE.

Alderman Hotatas moved :—" That the estimate for an improvement rate as recommended by the Finance Com- mittee be confirmed, and that the Finance Committee do make an improvement rate accordingly at three shillings in the pound, to be collected by two half-yearly instal- ments, and be authorized to affix the common seal of the borough thereto." The motion was seconded by Councillor GREEN, and carried.
THE DEPOTS QUESTION. A. LONG SPEECH BY ALDERMAN BURGESS.
Councillor JENKINS moved the following resolution, of which he had given notice :—"That a Special Committee

of this Council be appointed to inquire into and report upon the working of the intercepting depots, and also.to inquire into the working of the Longford depot, and for these purposes to take such evidence and to call in scientific, technical, or other assistance, and that the co-operation of the Sanitary Committee be invited with a view of making such inquiries exhaustive and complete. and that the Council do forthwith proceed to the appoint- ment of such Committee." He (Councillor Jenkins) did not think it necessary to make a long speech. The facts of the recent developments at Longford were so well known that it was not necessary for him to go through the whole of the reasons why it seemed to him necessary that a dispassionate committee should be appointed for the purpose of making the inquiry he suggested. He was tiorne out in that view by pu!4lic opinion and by the expression on all sides of the public Press, which, ha ventured to think, were the exponents of public opinion in this borough. Without any dissentient voice, the Press was of opinion that such an inquiry as he sug- gested should be made. He had written to Alderman Burgess, making suggestions, but of course the Council was in no way bound by that. Alderman Burgess had not thought fit to adopt his motion,and it therefore came before the Council in its integrity to adopt or cast aside as they thought fit. • Councillor DIXON seconded the proposal, and severely criticised the character of the machinery at Longford, and also the way in which it was used. Councillor BOLTON did not know whether to vote for the motion or not. He should like to ask—had there been mismanagement at Longford? or, were things going on there as well as they would go on ? The Council were entitled to some information in these re,pects. If they could appoint a special Committee with special informa- tion, and who could sit as judges on the Committee al- ready in existence, then let the Council be appointed. It was information the Council wanted, and which they ought to have. He did not see what scientific and tech- nical evidence could do. They had had repeated com- plaints about a nuisance at the intercepting depots. At times, he was satisfied there was a nuisance, and the ratepayers ought to be satisfied that the Committee were doing what they were expected to do. They had been led to believe that they were going to receive enormous profits from the manufacture of manure at Longford, but had they receiypd those profits? If they were manu- facturing at a loss tift ought not to manufacture any longer, if they could tet rid of the material in any other way. They had been led into a trap, but by whom or when they could not tql. There should be some answer as to why 200 tons of manure were missing, and why the rases were increased. They were trustees of the rate- payers' money and they ought to have the information he alluded to or retire altogether. With regard to the ap- pointment of Mr. Tunstall to try to find out about the loss of the 200 tons of manure he was told that the Sani- tary Committee possessed no information as to the ap- pointment, and he wanted to know who employed Mr. Tunstall and where the resolution was that made the ap- pointment. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Surrox said he gave credit to Councillor 'Jenkins for an honest desire to bring about such a reform fof Sanitary matters as he believed would be beneficial to the Sanitary Committee and the town of Warrington,but at the same time he was decidedly of opinion that Mr. Jenkins was taking the wrong course in order to accom- plish his purpose. He was not surprised that Councillor Bolton should say he was in a dilemma with regard to the resolution. With all due deference to Councillor Dixon's superior knowledge of machinery and sanitary matters,and all other matters,he (Alderman Sutton) could not support that resolution

Councillor PiEneotivr : (Laughter.) Alaerman Surrox said the Sanitary Committee believed, and, after all the experience ttrihct h, they were quite as much eatitlesd to an opinion on the subject as any one else, that the present system of deal- ing with the excreta refuse was the best system known anywhere. (Oh, oh, and hear. hear.) The resolution was a reflection on the Sanitary Committee,and,if passed, would he regarded by that body as nothing more than a vote of want of confidence. The Sanitary Committee were satisfied with what they had done. (Oh, oh.) He repeated that they were satisfied, and not only that but others who had come over to Warrington to inspect the depots and examined the system adopted, were perfectly satisfied that it was the best in existence. Instead of pas sing such a resolution as that of Councillor Jenkins it would be far better for any member of the Council who wished to take the matter up and investigate for himself. If he wanted any assistance the Sanitary Com- mittee would grant him lL the information and help they could.
It was not expected

Councillor GREENALL : They did not some time ago. Alderman Surrow said if there was any member of the COuncil who could suggest to the Sanitary Committee anything. that would be of benefit or advantage the Com- mittee would willingly accept it. Councillor JHNICINS : That is p .ecisely what I sug- gest. Councillor (IREENAtt said he should support the resolu- tion. It showed that the Committee had a weak case when one of its members had to talk such a pack of nonsense. (Laughter.) Alderman Haßßisonsaid his opinion was that if they passed the resolution the great difficulty would be in getting anyone to work it. He did not know where they would find anyone possessing the peculiar quali- fications necessary in order to make an effective and ex- haustive enquiry, or who would have the time at his disposal to do so. At the same time, he did not see why the Sanitary Committee should regard the motion o Councillor Jenkins as a vote of censure; he would have thought the Committee would have been glad, after what had been said of them, of an inquiry, because they must know whether they had striven intelligently and honestly to do their duty. He felt satisfied they had en- ' deavoured by every legitimate means in, their power to improve the sanitary c,ordition of Warrington. There was another matter for which he must hold Alderman Burgess reponsible. Alderman Burgess was of a very sanguine disposition, and ever since he commenced he had been too prone to hold out hopes which nobody but himself thought would be realised. He had drawn rosy pictures of the great profits that would accrue, while it would have been better if he had gone in the contrary direction, and told them that he could promise them no profit but that if he couldklispose of the town's refuse at any cost almost it would be a great achievement. ' (Hear, hear.) It was not a thing out of which they ought to expect to make any profit. It was not a question of profit at all, and do not let them delude themselves into the belief that any- body could make profit out of it. (Hear, hear.) There was not a Corporation in England or out of it who could make a profit. That must necessarily be an expensive matter for them, just as the cemetery was. Notwith- standing what some people considered the excessive charges at the cemetery they incurred the very serious loss of £7OO or £BOO a year, and they must regard the work of the Sanitary ..ommitteF in the same light as they did that of the Cemetery Committee. It was a work es- tablished entirely for the purpose of making the town healthy, and do not let them be: misled by the idea of making profit. (Hear, hear.) He sympathised with Alderman Burgess and the Sanitary Committee, although he should have no hesitation in supporting the resolution, as it would relieve the Committee of a good deal of odium which he thought undeservedly attached to them. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS was glad of having that opportu- nity of defending himself, akhe did not go through the newspapers to defend himself. He never attempted to defend himself, except in that Council Chamber. He should endeavour before lie sat down to convince the reasonable portion of that Council that a strange error had crept in. To use the words of Alderman Harrison, the talk of "profit" was quite' t new thing to him. They had never talked about making profit, though they had talked of making money. And they had made money, and he should show them before he sat down that the rates of the borough would this year have been about 3d.in the £ more if they were not earning money through the instrumentality of an article which had no value in I it. With regard to the letter Councillor Jenkins had ! written to him, he took the instractions of the Commit- tee as to the course that should be taken, and they were going upon it then. He might say that he thought the acuteness of Councillor Jenkins might have shown him that the present Sanitary Committee was called into existence only in November last. It had no existence before then, and it had no responsibility fOr anything thet had taken place before it came into existence. For a committee of that Council was a new creation in November, and it started with a clean sheet. Every act of the Committee up to the 28th of October, 1890. had,he believed, received the confirmation of the Council. More than that ; two out of ten on the Committee only be- came members of the Council on the Ist November last, and they surely would not appoint a committee to in- vestigate what these two gentlemen had been doing since they became members of the Committee. Two members had not been on the Committe above a year, and two more had not been on much more than two years. Councillor BoLTON : We will exonerate all these six. Alderman BURGESS thought that all the other members shottld be exonerated and let the whole onus rest upon himself. He thought that was what was intended, and he was prepared to take it. The resolution that was proposed implied that tne Sanitary Committee were either incapable or were guilty of wilful negligence in the discharge of the important duties they had under- taken.

Councillor JF.NKINS submitted that Alderman Burgess had no right to impute to him any such motives as a desireto charge any Committee Of that Council with criminal negligence. Alderman BURGESS said it was implied. Councillor Jenkins wished their accusers to sit in judgment on them. As to the scientific and technical evidence he daresay there was nobody in that room who knew so much of the value of technical evidence as Councillor Jenkins. He knen very well he could buy it a price, and that if he (Alderman Burgess) had more money to give he could out-buy Councillor Jenkins. (Laughter , and hear, hear.) Scientific and technical evidence was a most abominable thing and the man who had the long- est purse got the greatest quantity of it. He might as well state that the Sanitary Committee would consider that proposal, if carried by the Council, to convey to them that they had not the confidence of the Council. They felt that they would be unworthy of a position in

the C6uncil, much less on the Sanitary Committee, whrek was the finest Committee in the Council—(laughter)—. if they accepted the vote of the Council as proposed to be carried by Councillor Jenkins. If the Council accepted the proposal the Committee should at the same time ex- pect to be superseded in the work that had been given them to do. He wished the Council to judge of the work of the Sanitary Committee in all its hearings. The Longford and intercepting depots were only a small part of the work. Councillor JENKINS submitted that Alderman Burgess I was going entirely outside the terms of the motion. I Alderman BURGESS said he should ask the Council to allow him to show that the depots were only a small pot.. don of the Committee's work. Councillor JENKINS said he had impugned the Sanitary Committee solely on tke information conveyed by Alder- man Burgess himself on the laches which had taken place. Alderman Burgess came and complained of the loss of 200 tons of manure. Alderman BURGESS: That was at the last meeting of the Council. Councillor JENKINS: You have reported to the borough treasurer that in consequence of a serious diminution or loss in the stock of manure at Longford depot, you were obliged to admit that the amount to be carried to the credit of the Longford depot working was wrong and that the sum of from £BOO to £l,OOO would have to come off the estimates, The information was furnished by you. Alderman BURGESS : When? Councillor JENKINS : I don't know when. Alderman BURGESS said a great deal depended upon that, as Councillor Jenkins had formalated that resolu- tion three months ago. The MAYOR said the argument was becoming too per- sonal. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that Councillor Jenkins had had an opportunity of stating his case, but he had failed entirely to do so. Councillor PIERPOINT pointed out that Councillor Jen- kins had risen for the purpose of taking exception to Alderman Burgess travelling outside the terms of his motion. He should also like to remind the Council that a few years ago they had a discussion on Sanitary matfers, and Alderman Burgess then orolonged his remarks so long that a quorum could not be maintained. He did not want that to happen that night. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS was proceeding to speak of sanitary matters in a general way when objection was again raised. Alderman Surrox : They complain that they get in- sufficient information, and when tliut information is given they object to it. Alderman BURGESS said there were five departments of sanitary work. The hospital department— Councillor DIXON: There is no question of the hospi- tal ; we don't want to ramble all over the town. Some discussion then took place as to .the limits of Alderman Burgess's discourse, and eventually it was put to the Council whether they would hear him at large on sanitary matters, or that he should confine himself to the motion. Seven voted in favour of an exhaustive discus- sion and 11 against. The MAYOR : Then, I must ask you Alderman Burgess to confine yourself to the resolution. Alderman HARRISON : Which means cut it short. (Laughter.) Alderman BURGESS said that all he would say on that pcint was that the town was in a healthy condition as a Jesuit of the Sanitary Committee's work, and the strength of the people of the town to do all labour was considerably increased by the work of the Sanitary Coin- mittee. Speaking of the depots he argued that there was no nuisance at these depots, but if the Council required the erection of chimneys at the intercepting depots to make them more salubrious they would be erected,. though ho thought MO would be a waste of pane k mewl.. He maintained that the Sanitary Committee I not only promoted the health of the borough but were a, 'source of income to the Corporation, The money that hail been paid into Mr. Chorley's exchequer last year was £1,465 3s. sd. and every shilling recelved for the sale of manure made them a shilling better off. The alderman then went onto refer to the old system of night-soil !noval and several members left the room in the cow S 3 of these remarks. Councillor JENKINS said that with a v'ew to sav;ng time and preventing the worthy alderman 11.tcoming too exhausted he would withdraw his motion. Alderman SUTTON (to Alderman Burgess) : You have talked them out. The MAYOR said the motion could not be withdrawn without the consent of the seconder who had left the room. Alderman BURGESS said he could assure them that the bet and funniest part was to come. (Laughter.) After some further remarks during which members still con- tinued to leave the chamber, Alderman Burgess sat down. Councillor CANNELL said that Alderman Burgess had simply tried to talk away the time. The Sanitary, Com- mittee, he contended, was not above suspicion. The ratepayers were dissatisfied with it, and there ought to be an inquiry. If such a matter as the loss of 200 tone of manure were to come before the registrar in bankruptcy thy would have had to know something about it. Alderman HotatEs thought that the passing of the re- solution would be a vote of censure on the Committee and he could not vote for that. - Councillor PIERPOINT said he could not for the life of him see that the motion could be construed into a vote of censure. The motion was then submitted to the Council, the voting being as under For. Against. Councillors Pierpoint The Mayor „ Hutchinson Alderman Holmes „ Monks „ Burgess \„ Jenkins I ~ Sutton „ Hilt I Councillors Walker „ Bolton „ Hepherd „ Cannell Flood Greening 99 Beaman Falrelough H. Roberts —ll It was accordingly declared lost.

Councillor Dixoie's motion," That the members of the Sanitary he required forthwith to resign," was not sub- mitted, Mr. Dixon having left the room while Alderman Burgess was speaking. This was all the business.

div.head: STOWMARKET ELECTION.
div.p: STOWMARKET ELECTION.
LIBERAL VICTORY.

Polling took place on Tuesday for the Stowmarket division of Suffolk. in place of the late member, Mr. E. Greene, Conservative. The candidates were Mr. E. W. Greene, son of the late member, Conservative, and Mr. Sidney Stern, Liberal. Polling commenced briskly at eight o'clock. Party colours were freely displayed at Bury St. Edmunds, and the Conservatives seemed. better furnished with vehicles. The weather was beautifully fine. There were thirty-six polling stations scattered over 110 parishes, some booths doing duty for as many as six parishes. Many of the electors in the rural districts lived seven or eight miles from their polling stations. The result of Tuesday's polling was declared at Bury St. Edmunds, on Wednesday afternoon, as follows : Mr. S. Stern (L) Mr. W. G. Greene (C) 4,132
Majority ,
The constituency in 1885 returned a Liberal, and in 1888 (on a smaller poll) a Conservative. The figures were :- 1885. _ _ _
Mr. F. T. Cobb°ld (L) Sir T. Thornhill (C)
Majority 1886.
Mr. E. Greene (C) Mr. E. N. Buxton (GL)
Majority

THE SCENE AFTER THE ELECTION. Immediately after the declaration of the poll there was a scene of great excitement in the streets, Mr. Stern's large majority being greater than was expected. The crowds which thronged the Market-place and ad- joining streets cheered loudly and accompanied their newly-eloeted member to the Angel Hotel, from the steps of which Mr. Stern addressed some 2.000 people, the crowds leaving their stalls in the streets, where the weekly market was in full swing. Mr. Stern said that the Liberal party had that day won their greatest vic- tory since Spalding, while it had sent a cheering mess- age to the "Grand Old Man," and was only the fore- runner of another such victory in Harborough. The Conservative candidate subsequently addressed his supporters at the Conservative Club, and after a ". while the excitement in the streets died away. THE IRISH NATIONAL FEDERATION. At a meeting of the Irish National Federation held on , Wednesday, in Dublin, the secretary, Mr. D. Sheehy, M.P., announced that the receipts during the last fort- night amounted to £1,362. Mr. Murphy, M.P., who presided, referred with satisfaction to the result of the Stowmarket election, as an evidence that, in face of the efforts of Mr. Parnell to damage the Efbme Rule cause by denouncing the priesthood, English Liberals stiil held the determination to do justice to Ireland. A resolution was passed thanking the electors of the Stowmarket division for returning a Liberal member.
PRESENTATION TO-MR. O'BRIEN, li.P.

The" Daily News "states that iirt before Mr. Patrick O'Brien was sent to prison a subsription was got up, witft theintention of presenting him with a money testimonial. Sire Mr. O'Brien has declared himself in favour of Mr. rivll, there has been a meeting cf the Committee, where there was some talk of returning the money to the subscribers. This was, however, negatived, and the money will be handed over to Mr. O'Brien, together with an intimation that it will be no use his offering himself fr re-election in North Monaghan.

MR. SAMUEL PLIMSOLL is not at A Timely present a member of the House Warnino% of Commons; but he is always doing good work bearing on legislation. Instead of being the member for a particular borough, he may be said to be everybody's member. He has rendered immense service to seamen in protecting them from rapacious shipowners; and just now he is directing attention, in the "Nineteenth Century," to the harm which is done to the community, and especially to the labouring classes, by the estab- lishment of what are known as "Trusts." It is in America that the Trust system has suddenly and enormously developed, with the result that the promoters are acquiring vast sums of money which have never been legitimately earned. In England the two rrincipal combinations have been amongst the owners of salt mines and the manufacturers of alkali. The usual plea at lithe formation of. a Trust is that,by operating on a large scale,economY in working can be effected, while prices will not be materially altered. This is what was said when the salt combination was being formed; but what has been the result? "The effect," Mr. PLIMSOLL says, "of the combination among the owners of salt mines has resulted in an increase of price, so far as e can ascertain, of 75 per cent. (ss. to Bs. 9d.)" This means that the scheming capita- lists have established a monopoly, and, like all monopolists, they are disposed to fill their pockets at the expense of the public. If the price of salt people e had been increased 25 per cent. through a rise in wages,lete wouldr being have avemeant thate nefi t a large bu greatly b case the increase is three times 25 per cent., and the plunder—for we cannot call it anything t nut mi nb °Li psf else—goes into the hands of a few who are well off

div.p: to begin with. We cite this as an instance of what we may expect if Trusts become as common in this country as they are in the United States. . The evil growth has been singularly rapid. Trusts in America have for the most part sprubg into exist- ence within the past three years ; and at the pre- sent moment it is estimated that" these corpora- tions include no less than Two Thousand Million Dollars, or considerably more than two-thirds of the manufacturing capital of the United States." Our American correspondent, Mr. WHITHAM, has raised his voice against these grasping combina- tions ; but it will be a surprise to people in this country to learn that their influence has become' almost overpowering, Mr. PLIMSOLL gives a list of 15 Trusts which are plundering the public on the average to the tune of over 50 per cent! This means that unscrupulous capitalists are grind- ing the faces of the poor, whilst they themselve are becoming enormously rich as partners in System pf wholesale robbery. Can we wonder ir view of these facts that the cry of discontent growing louder and louder amongst the workers o the United States? They have a right to cr3 aloud, and they will be justified in doing something more if steps be not taken to check or put an end to these organisations of rapacity and rascality. What is the use of teeming inventions ; of improved and speeded machinery; and of those twin-giants, Steam and Electricity, being made to do a world of labour, if the mass of the people are to re main in the position of slaves, while bloated plutocrats ride rough-shod over them I Mr. Pumsorz, looking ahead, would save this country from the vampires that are sucking the life-blood of the United States; and his suggestion is that there should be a Royal Committee to inquire int-i the subject. Steps, he urges, should be taken for" reporting to Parliament in time for some tentative Act restraining the formation of these Trusts in Englang for a year at least, to be passed in this session of Parliament." And we quite agree with him; it is better than waiting until the vampire has fastened itself upon us.

SIR Robert PEEL, who was twice Peel' The Prime Minister of England, was Statesman, unquestionably the greatest States- man that the Tory party have produced. He was great because he was open-minded and liberal in his aYrapathies. He was a Reformer of the conserva- tive type ; and it Was because he was too much of a Iteforiner for the Tories that they ultimately broke from and deserted him. Mr. GLADSTONE commenced hie official career under PEEL, in 1835, as a junior Lord of the Treasury; and it is a matter of corn- nn observation that he never speaks of his former chief except in terms of the highest re- gard. Those who wish to study the character of Statesman who left such a distinct mark. upon Xiglish history cannot do better than procure the brief biography from the pen of Mr. J. R.' uitsPIELD. It is published by Messrs. Macmil- .Thian and Co., as the last of their series of "Twelve nglish Statesmen." Singular as it may seem to "Ile, it is to the lasting credit of Sir Robert PEEL that his name is associated with three notable sur- renders in matters of policy—surrenders which Were by no means agreeable at the time to the Tory party, but which successively proved of in- calculable benefit to the nation. The first change . related to the currency question. Sir ROBERT was , Chairman of the Committee appointed_ to inquire into the merits or demerits of " soft, " money. He bad been trained in the belief that paper money was a blessing to the country ; but he came out of the inquiry convinced of the error of his views ; and,acting on his conviction he initiated legislative changes which resulted in the Bank of England resuming cash payments in May, 1821. He was reproached for his conversion by the agriculturists, who could not see an inch beyond their noses; and he was reproached again in 1829 for being 1 wise enough to perceive that the country must either accept Catholic Emancipation or prepare for revolution. The measures then adopted do ' ll°t seem at the present day to have been observes "they liberal; but, as Mr. TIIURSFIELD were probably the best that could be extorted at the time from an obstinate Sovereign a reluctant legislature, a hostile church, • 1t1,.11n a hesitating people." It is characteristic of 1:1e, that he did not take credit to himself in the .2.l,tter. Indeed, in his speech, on the second 'cling of the Catholic Relief Bill, he said—" The Z`edit belongs to others not to me," and went on Illention Canning, Fox, Grattan, and Plunket. t'ilew different is this frankness and honesty to •a),(3, Conduct of statesmen of the Beaconsfield m te—'f Salisbury type, who oppose everything of ,a je °reaing tendency, and pretend, when resistance 13% 118e1ese, that such measures have always 4: a part of their policy. Lord SALISBURY is t° commit himself to Free Education; but he, like NEL, admit that he has been over by the arguments of the Liberals? till: shall see. PEEL'S greatest conversion was oni question of the corn laws; and here again he tribute to those who had won him over—to the unadorned eloquence," as he termed it, of 4:31„.4.,,n1) COBDEN, .and the splendid advocacy of I.ORT. His surrender on the question of tsf tllab of the corn laws was the noblest act his life; but so incapable were the Tories of 14/Preeiating the greatest 'of their leader that the It 3' reviled' him mid drove him from office, Lord oNsiusza), then Mr. DISRAELI, exerting him- to the utmost in the art of vilification. In the 4Peech announcing his resignation, PEEL replied his malicious aceusers in dignified and touching ."erms. He said:

til shall surrender power severely censured by ers who, from no interested motive, adhere to tie Principle of protection, considering the main- of it to be essential to the welfare and in- of the country.; I shall leave a name ex- itbie‘ted by every monopolist who, from less to honour- eo,Motives, clamours for protection because it t'auces to ilif4 own individual benefit; but it may Nvittat I shall leave a name sometimes remembered Ivbo"xprestions of goodwill in the abodes 9f those brea, lot it is to labour and to earn their daily 441 r with the sweat of their brow, when they ant recruit their exhausted strength with !ibund- and untaxed food, the sweeter because it is no leavenbd with a sense of injustice." t o Plitt. was right and •thE4 the Tories were t‘nrig le known to every man and woman who fc,4aY provided with "abundant and untaxed tweh, Attempts have been made during the past or 017'3' Years to return to Protection in one form vvPther ; but the nation refuses to .be hood- as. (e Tecl, and will have no more of the bread which aysened with a sense of injustice."

tiirki • ng RE THE is a "plentiful lack" o ill at buty. moral courage in the world, and lack . there was no little evidence of the the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday. hue-ri,e,, was a large attendance, and the principal izin.-81;-88 was the consideration of a motion for an, forlcithq 4intii the Intercepting Depots a.nd-the Long- haa I,l:mare-Works. That such an inquiry is needed 37et, "een repeatedly demonstrated. For several 6lizirs there have been strong complaints,during the fl 111/(3r tinle,of the nuisance caused by the depots,

and member after member of the Council, not excepting the vice-chairman of the Sanitary Com- mittee, has admitted the existence of the nuisance Then as to Longford—its huge expenditure and unsatisfactory results have been the theme of fre- quent discussion; but there has been no such start- ling revelation previously as the double deficit this year amounting in all to no, less than £1,600. Concentrated manure is the only article manufac- tured, but the manager of the works and the Sani- tary Committee were in such ignorance as to what was being done that they put cloim their stock-in- hand at 500 tons, when, on being tested, it was no more that 300. Added to that, the machinery has been stopped for several weeks while material in stock was being got ready for the market ! That there is something seriously wrong is obvious, and that an independent inquiry is needed is equally obvious; but when the motion for an inquiry was , put to the vote, out of 30 members who attencle d a the meeting, 7 only voted for it. It is true that 11 a only Voted against it, and of this eleven DO few er, LS than seven are members of the Sanitary Com- & mittee. Of the twelve of whom there iss y no record, the majority had, we believe, left 4 the Council Chamber before a division was 3 taken, although sour of them had given pledges t to their constituents on this very question: In- I deed of the two Liberal members of the Council , who voted for an inquiry--Councillor PIERPOINT and Councillor MONKS-it is due to say that neither of them represents a ward in which a depot is situated,and it is therefore all the more creditable to them that they have shown the courage of their convictions. Alderman PLATT and Councillor FLEMING, who have both in the past expressed themselves strongly as to the depots, were absent from the meeting, but their absence was unhappily due to the recent loss of near relatives. rt is those who attended the meeting and failed to vote who are to blame, thus leaving it to the Sanitary Committee to defeat the motion for an -inquiry by voting in effect for themselves. What could be more unsatisfactory-, for instance, than the conduct of Councillor DIXON in seconding Councilor JENKINS' motion,and then leaving the Chamber be- fore the vote was taken ? It is true that Alderman Burgess repeated the farce of talking against time; but surely,when the comfort and perhaps the Hies of the inhabitants are at stake, it is not too much to require that even those who are disgusted with such tactics shall stay the farce out, however long it may last. As the matter stands, .nothing is settled, and everything is unsettled. No explana- tion is given of the blunder in stock amounting to over £BOO ;or of mismanagement which results in machinery being idle for weeks at a time when it should have been in full swigig. The warm weather is approaching; the nuisance of the depots will in all likelihood show itself as of old,and residents in the neighbourhood are to he allowed to sicken and die, so far as any help goes which might proceed from an inquiry. Fortunately, there is a power outside the Council ; it 'is the power of public opinion,and we shall be much mistaken if it does not exert it- self in protesting against the indifference and id- action of the Council.

Mr. Whitham's numerous friends in Warrington will be glad to hear that, according to a private letter recently received, his health has very much improved. He has been enabled to resume work, and he regards his prospects as much better than they have been for some time back.

, It is interesting to note how the names of per- sons are the means of originating new words. Who hasn't heard a thousand times of " boycott ? " Blucher and Wellington gavt their names to differ- ent classes of boots. The great Sir Robert Peel organised the police force of Ireland, and hence the words " Bobby " and " Peeler" as titles of the man-in-blue which are in force to the present day. j

It transpired, at the inquest, that the Warrington boat lad who was drowned in the canal the other day was unable to swim. So many lives have been lost in this way that it has become a question whether a person should be allowed to work on a canal, or river, who has not learned to ,swim. The qualification is not a difficult one to acquire, and is more important in these cases than any standard of education.

There.is good authority for the saying that the old order changes and gives place to the new; but at Newton there is a difficulty about the "new Order." The Order.has reference t4;:the new system of electing Commissioners, and it is as yet uncer- tain whether it will receive the royal assent in time to govern the next elections. The Clerk is having an eye to the matter, and in so far as he can he is trying to induce the Local Government Board to "hurry up."

It will not be the fault of the Liberal party if Free Education does not become the law of the land this year. If the Government introduce a narrow bill, the Liberals will, of course, try to make it a wide bill. Referring to the matter, on Monday, the Rector of Warrington said that when the grant of public money came, there would sure to be a cry for representation and con- trol." And quite right, too ; those who pay the piper should have a say as to the tune.

The Parnellites are at a discount abroad as well as at home. The mission to the United States is a complete failure. The New York correspondent of the "Daily News" says:—" They had small audiences everywhere, and collected scarcely more money than was necessary to defray travelling ex- pipses. The newspapers paid little attention to them, and the general public none whatever." Mr. Parnell has loftily ignored the divorce proceed- ings; but can he ignore an empty cash-box?

It is as Ave stated the other day: the married woman can decline to live with her husband, after the manner of Mrs. Jackson, but she cannot com- pel the despised and rejected man to contribute to her maintenance. A Mrs. Purcell, of Bromley, (Kent) tried it on the other day; but she got no encouragement. The magistrates told her that as she had decided to leave her husband she must take the consequences. Moral: Let married women who haven't a living of their own cling to the living in their husbands.

This is Mow mercenary view to take of the holy estate of matrimony; but since the Jackson episode took the town by storm the low and mercenary has ,been in the air. It has been in the air before. There is a story told of a poor woman whose hus- ;band was drowned in a swollen stream. She saw ;the corpse float past her; and her instant exclama- tion was, "Eli! my living! my living. Aw've lost I my living."

; The "Daily News" thus pokes fun at the pro- limotion:of Mr. W. H. Smith to the post of Lord Warden of tho Cinque Ports :—One is reminded of the story of the brilliant and witty Irish barris- ter who did not gut on, and the heavy judge who 'did get on, and who rebuked him one day for. his ;levity. "My lord," said the unsnceessful, "the laws of nature have been reversed in our ease—my levity has kept me down here, and you; gravity has floateil you up.there."

General Booth has opened a match factory as one feature. of his "Darkest England" scheme. The factory is in Ekackney, and was formally ppened on Monday. He proposes to give the 'workers about 60 per cent. more than other firms usually pay, and if he can make ends meet, after that, he will be a benefactor to his species, while his success will be a revelation as to the large margin of profit in the match trade. SUCCESSES OF A LOCAL LAW STUDENT. Mr. George William Allen son of the late clerk to Widnes Local Board has just passed the final examination of the Incorporated Law Society and is now qualified to practice as a solicitor. Out of 166 examined 79 passed. SPRING. FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt.

TROTSFER OF LICENSES Al' RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magis- trates granted the transfer of the following licenses : The Prospect Inn,Weston,to William Owen ; The Grapes Inn, Halton, to Mrs. Field, from her late husband ; The Navigation Inn, Canal-st., from Thomas Jbnes to John James Linton; The Norton Arms, Halton, from the late Edward Badley, to George E. Turley; The Travellers' Rest, Runcorn Hill, from William Owen to Wm. John- son; Brunswick Vaults, Brunswick-st., from Win. Ains- worth to Geolge Sole.

Captain, the linnouraWe C. G. Lem, her Majesty's Inspector of Conshibulary, held the annual inspection of the Runcorn Division of Police on Tuesday afternoon. There were on parade Suptu Large, Inspector Bowyer, Sergeants Woolley, Gosling;Dutton, Booth, and Costello and 22 constables. Three constables were en duty and three sick. The Inspector examined the clothing and accoutrements of the men, who were afterwards put througn a number ef evolutions by Supt. Large. He then visited the cell, the court room and the offices' and expressed himself highly pleased with the great irriprove- ments effected by the structural alteration of the build- ing and the general cleanliness of the place. The books were also examined and- found neatly and accurately kept. The Inspector was accompanied by Colonel Hamersly, the Chief Constable. THE THEFT OF A HORSE AND GIG AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage, „yrank William Lightfont, of Runcorn, was charged with having stolen a, herke and trap and various other articles, the property of Josh. Griffiths, farmer, Manor House Farm, Hale. While Mr. Griffiths was in the Conservative Club on Thursday night, he left the prisoner in charge of his horse and gig,but when he came ' out of the building the horse and trap had disappeared. Information was given to the police, who communicated with other districts, and on Friday morning it was as- certained that the prisoner had :put up at toe stables of Mr. Hamer, Bootle. Supertendent Xoblett informed Mr. Gossage that a short time ago the'prisoner was in an im- becile ward at Wigan, and as some doubts were now en- tertained of his sanity, two medical gentlemen had been called in to see him. They were,of opinion that he was not accountable for his actions. The prisoner,who made a rambling, incoherent statement, was committed tothe asylum.

Captain Verney is one of tbe big fish who have failed to break through the net of the Criminal Law Amendment Act ; and he deservedly receives sentence of a year's imprisorment. As he could not resign and could not be offered the "Chiltern Hundreds," steps will be taken, on Tuesday, to effect his expulsion as a member of the House of Commons. Sir Henry James is bringing in a bill to permit of resignation in an ordinary way; but the change is hardly worth making. When the iniquity of M.P.s is disclosed, it is a question whether the way out for them should be made easy.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday George Warren,of St. Helens,was sentenced to penal servi- tude for seven years for‘ a murderous assault on his wife. The man seems to have been lacking men- tally, but, as the judge remarked, a long imprison- ment, with regular work and regular living, might help him to recover his mental equilibrium. There is a tendency in some quarters to refer to all crime as a species of insanity; but even if that view be admitted the duty still rests upon society to keep mischief-makers, sane or insane, under control.

Mr. Luke Fildes as an artist seems to go from strength to strength, and from victory to victory. A London correspondent, referring to the opening oi the Academy, on Monday, says:—" All day long a very large number of visitors crowded round the pictures and the fashionable element was well represented even from the very first. There is no longer any doubt that Mr. Luke Fildes's splendid picture of the Doctor,' will be a popular favourite. The crowd which- collected round it yesterday remained dense and sympathetic from first to last."

The Statham farmer who committed suicide, on Tuesday, seems to have been unnecessarily de- pressed about the Ship Canal shares which he held. Nothing has happened to suggest that the under- taking will not in the end be successful. There is every prospect of the money being obtained ,to ' complete the work ; and,once completed,the shares will rise in value. Meantime tlie hardest thing to bear by people who have invested most of their savings in Canal Shares is the suspension of the payment of interest. But this, under the cirownstances, would §eeni tg be inevitable.

----- The Liberal Victory at Stowmaricet has thrown the Tories upon their beam-ends. They were be- ginning to hope that the turn of things was in their faVour,and speculate upon an appetil to thecountry in general, when—disgusting spectacle !—a Liberal takes possession of a Tory seat; a Tory majority of 543 in 1886 is converted into a Liberal majority of 214 in 1891. The" Standard's" comment is that the electors decline to accept the bribe of Free Educa- tion, and sees in the result evidence of "Conserva- tive reaction." This is good, very good. Oh that the "reaction " would continue here, there, and every where

And it is continuing. Yesterday the result was declared of the South Dorset by-election. In 1886, the Tory candidate was returned with a majority of 991. A Tory is again returned, but this time the majority is one of 40 only. The Liberal gain as between one election and the other is 951 votes, in South Dorset ; and 757 at Stowmarket. It will do. The more the merrier of this kind of "Conservative reaction." Keep it up, and England will be a happy land at the next General Election.

From a communication to the Warrington Magistrates, which has been received from the Home Secretary, it appears that the practice of imposing costs along with fines of 55., or under 55., is contrary to law. It is only in special, cases that this is allowable. Alderman Sutton commented freely on the Home Secretary's letter at the War- rington Police Court on Thursday; and most people will agree with him that costs become a hardship when they are heavier than the fine, and are the means sometimes of people being sent to gaol who would otherwise be in a position to pay the fine alone. Having had this hint from the Home Office, the justices at Warrington and else- where should see to it that their justice for the future is not injustice.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

A sitting of this Court was held on Tuesday, by his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes. 58 original plaints and 12 judgment summonses were dealt with, but there was no case of public interest. NEW RATE FOR WIDNES.

On the application of Mr. J. Goff. the assistant over- seer, the Widnes magistrates on Thursday sanctioned the levying of a poor-rate of 2s. in tiot £ estimated to realize £13,878 14s. 6d. DEATH OF MRS. JOHN HAZLEHURST.

Yesterday morning, Mrs. Sarah Hazlehurst, of Roche House; High-st. Runcorn, widow of the late Mr. John Hazlehurst, died at the age of 84 years. She Was one of the oldest survivors of an old Runcorn family. _ DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORNIAN.

On Thursday afternoon the mortal remains of Mr. William Houghton, of Shaw-st., Runcorn, were interred 4 'at the Cemetery, in the presence of many fellow-work- men and friends. The deceased had been an employe of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company for 47 years, and amongst those who followed him to his last resting- place were the following comrades :—Messrs. J. Crank, D. Bisbrown, Thomas Buckley, J. Siletoe, James France, T. Moores, S. Booth, and W. A.brains. Before the fune- ral procession left the house the friends sang "Safe in the arms of Jesus." Mr. George Marshall conducted the funeral service, and delivered a brief and appropriate address.

WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, WIDNES. , With the object of reducing the debt of this chapel, a bazaar was held in Lacey-st., schoolroom, on Thursday afternoon. There was only a moderate attendance at the opening ceremony, which was performed by Mr. J. Edwards, of Liverpool. The Rev. D. Davies, the pastor, explained that originally the debt on the chapel was £560, but by means of a bazaar and a grant from the Congregational Union the amount had been reduced to £260. (Applause.) They wanted to be free from the debt in order that they might exercise their energies in other directions.—Mr. Edwards, in declaring the bazaar open. spoke of the importance of a small chapeL, be- ing free from encumbrance, becauss it was as much as they could do to mee ordinary church expenses. Allud- ing to Mr. Davies's labours in connection with the church, Mr. Edwards said Mr. Davies was honoured and re- spected not only by the members of the congregation but by the ministers of all denominations in Widnes and elsewhere. (Applause) A vote of thanks having been accorded to Mr. Edwards, the ladies commenced the sale of their wares. The stalls had been tastefully ar- I ranged, and were presided over as fellows :—Refresh- ment stall, Mesdames E. Edwards J. Owen, M. Edwards, and Wvmant, Miss Haekney and Miss Maggie Edwards; No. 1 stall, Mesdames W. Williams, C. Owen, Hackney, and Miss C. Hughes; No. 2, Miss L. Owen, Mrs. U. Thomas, and Miss Thomas; No. 3, Mesdames Thomas and Bevan and Miss Morgan.
