ALLEGED SWPATINIa A'r WIMPS. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. E. A. Stapleton Bretherton, IT/avid John Brookes, tailor and outfitter, Victoria-road, brought an action under the Employers' and Workmen's Act, to recover £1 Os. 11d. from Frances Jones for breach of contract. Mr. T. J. Peters appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. .1. W. Knowles defended. The plaintiff said the defendant had been in his employ about six years, and she was engaged on an agreement to give a week's` notice on.either side. The defendant made seven or eight pairs of trousers a week. The profit on a Pair of trousers was between 2s. and 2s. 6d. It was the custom of the trade to give and take a week's notice.—Cross-examined by Mr. Knowles, plain- tiff said it was not a fact that he employed tailoresses on what was known as thesweating system. • They had not to find their own basting cotton, machine thread, and oil. They might have to find the wax. The girls earned between 4s. 6d. and 9s. per week, and had earned as much as eleven shillings a week.— rhe defendant, who said she sitt s 20 years of age, denied that there was any agreement to give a week's notice. In the winter time she earned between 4s. 6d. and 10s. a week. It was oftener 4s. 6d.,0r ss. a week, and out of this she was to find her own basting cotton, wax, machine thread, needles, and oil. They had also to find the soap and brushes to clean out the room.—ln reply to Mr. Peters, she said she left without giving notice because it was not the custom to do So. Mr. Brookes dismissed girls at a minute's notice.—Mrs. Jones and Nora Kenyon(formerly in the employ of Mr. Brookes) confirmed the defendant's statement,and the magistrates dismissed the case on the ground that the plaintiff did not prove that it was the custom of the trade to give a week's notice. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. HUTTON'S Warrington.—Advt. • DEATH AND FUNERAL OF A RUNCORN CONTRACTOR. Our readers will learn with regret of the death of Mr. James Wilson' contractor, of Greenway Meadows, which took place at his residence on Monday. About seven years ago, while engaged in erecting a large chemical works in Widnes, he was attacked by a disease, which all the medical skill available could not eradicate, and eventually caused his death. A short time ago he was thrown out of his trap when driving from itocksavage, and this shock,acting on a weak constitution,accelerated his end. Born in Runcorn, in 1824, Mr. IVilson was left fatherless at an early age, and in consequence he had an uphill battlets tight to attain the position in life which he occupied. His early struggles had deeply imbued him with sympathy for others similarly circumstanced, and nothing gave him greater pleasure than training, helping, and encouraging a poor fatherless lad, and many trades- men who stand to-day in the front rank owe much to his kindness. In 1847 he became closely connected with the development of chemical apparatus and plant at Widnes, being associated with Mr. Deakin and Mr. Hutchinson, and 'he was considered a most practical and reliable authority upon heating and smelting. As a contractor ha had carried out many important works of various descriptions, and it may be mentioned that he erected bit. the Bridgewater Trustees sheds and warehouses at Runcorn and the general offices in Percival-lane, and also large warehousesand offices at Duke'a Dock Liverpool. He had also erected chemical works in the South of France. In religious affairs he took a deep and active interest. He was an adherent of the Primitive Methodist Connexion, and he had held a position of honour and trust in that body. Since the year 1848 he had been a lay preacher, and in fulfilling this office he had travelled some thousands of miles and preached hundreds of ser- mons. In all matters of dispute he was on the side of mercy and forbearance, and his demise will be widely lamented. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Thursidav afterno,m. In front of the hearse walked a large-number of the members of the Primitive Methodist Chapel and other gentlemen, headed by the Rev. C. Finch and the Rev. H. Davenport. Follewing were the members of the local branch of the Society of brick- layers and the workmen of Messrs. Wilson and Sons. Service was held in Greenway-road Chapel and after- wards at the Cemetery,the ministers mentioned officiat- ing. There were many indications of the respect and esteem in which the deceased was held, and the windows en route of the procession were darkened.

CADISHEAD CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL. The anniversary sermons of tile Congregational Sunday school were preached on Sunday in the above chapel. The Rev. J. Crewe, pastor, preached both morning and evening. In the afternoon Mr. F. Fearuley, Ship Canal Mission Hall, conducted the service. The collection for the day amounted to a little over £l2. Thomas Evans, a labourer, of Ellesmere-st., Run- corn, fell down dead in his house on Sunday morn- ing, and as the doctor gave his opinion that death was due to heart disease the coroner did not deem it necessary to hold an inquest. Evans's wile bad only died on the previous evening, and the two bodies were interred together at the cemetery on Wednes- day. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. a. W. RAILWAY BLOCK NEAR WARRINGTON: A serious.rail way block occurred at Acton Bridge, near Warrington, on Wednesday night, owing to some waggons getting off the lines. The London mail due to pass about five o'clock was over two hours late next morning, and many other trains were more or less delayed,specials having to be put on in sOrne cases to keep the advertised connec- tions. Fortunately no further mishap occurred. as.ssixrrrEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Add.
HEAVY PENALTY FOR SECRET DRINKING AT ST.

HELENS. At the St. .Flelens Town Hall, on Vriday, Peter Clare, a working-man, residing in Vernon-st., Parr, was charged with selling drink without a license. A fine of £lO and costs was inflicted, or. in default of ,payment 28 days' imprisonment. 4vidence was given that two constables .entered the house in plain Clothes and purchased drink. A sergeant afterwards followed them,and found a number of-other men in- side of the house, some of whom had been supplied with and were drinking liquor. HELENS COUNTY Cou*Cru The Eobbouse return, presento last month to the House of Commons, giving details of the last complete year's financial working of the Local Government Bill, shows how that measure has oper- ated for the County Council district of St. Helens. " THE DISHONEST ST. HELENS POSTMAN.

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, Edward Ellard, aged 31, pleaded guilty to having, on the 23rd February, at St. Helene, then being employed in the Postoffice, stolen a post letter containing a postal order for the payment of 20s. Mr. Hardy prosecuted and Mr. P. Swift defended. It was stateLby the prosecuting counsel that prisoner had stolerfTwelve orders which had been entrusted to him during four months, their value being £6 Bs. —Mr. Swift said that prisoner had previously held , a good character. He married early in life—in fact, when he was only receiving 14s. a week. His family and responsibilities increased more rapidly, than did his wages.—His Lordship said that many a man was honest on less wages than the prisoner received. He saw no excuse for the crime. Pri- soner must go to jail for 18 months with hard labour. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire:---GIPXA.ND. Warrington. —Advt. THE ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER AT ST. HELENS. On Monday, at Liverpool Assizes, George Warren (27), labourer, was charged with having, on the 20th March, at Eccleston,' feloniously wounded his wife, Esther Warren, with intent to murder her. Mr. T. Swift, who prosecuted, &lin that prisoner had been married to prosecutrix over three years. Their manned life had been an unhappy one. On one occasion prisoner had been in, in asylum, and after coming out he lived apart from his wife. On the 20th March he met her. in the street, spoke to her, and ultimately followed her into a house. They quarrelled, and prisoner picking up an iron poker' struck his wife repeatedly about the head with it. Eleven wounds were inflicted, and the woman was in a clangorous condition for some time. When charged, prisoner said, "I don't care what, you do to me ; you may hang me to-morrow." The jury found him guilty, and his Lordship, in passing a sentence of seven years' penal servitude, said that he entirely agteed with the verdict. If men would beat their wives within an inch of their lives those men must take the consequences. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. de W. DUTTON'S. sankey-st., Warrington.—"ldet. SPI/11/OVEI ntECHAA.I'S PILLS. in the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice yesterday week, before Mr. Justin Vaughan Williams, the case of Beecham v. Fisher came on for hearing.—Mr. Kennedy, Q.C., for the plaintiff, explained that this, action was brought substantially for an injunction to prevent the sale by the defendant, a chemist at Preston, of certain pills which were not manufactured by the plaintiff, although sold as his. The case for the defendant was that certain persons went to his er2ablishment, and asked for small quantities of Beecham's pills, in pennyworths, and persons who asked for pennyworths had it explained to them that the pills sold to them were the defendant's anti- bilious pills, and not Beecliam's.—At the conclu- sion of the evidence, his Lordship came to the conclusion that the plaintiff had proved his case, and granted an injunction with costs. In the Queens Bench Division; on Saturday, Mr. Eve, for the plaintiff,mentioned the case of Beecham v. Clue. The learned counsel said this was an action on the part of Mr. Beecham, of St. Helens, to re- strain the defendant, a chemist and druggist, of Portsea, from selling pills as Beecham's pills which were not of the plaintiff's manufacture. The de- fendant had agreed to an injunction, and also to pay a certain amount of damages for costs; and he asked his lordship to make an order accordingly. Mr. Justice Vaughan Williams granted the injunc- tion asked for. SPRING Fesmoss 'now Showing at J. & W. Durrox'a Sankey-st., Warrington.—.Advt. SUDDEN DEATH AT NEWTON. On Monday evening a man named David Sandi- man, who resided in High-st., Newton, died in a most sudden manner. Sandiman was an engineer, and was employed by Colonel McCorquodale to look after and take charge of his yacht. For the last 10 months he has been on the yacht, which has been hired by a lady at Beaumaris, and only returned home to Newton a fortnight ago. During the time he was not on the yacht, he was engaged in the printing works foundry doing odd jobs. On Mon- day he was at his work in the foubdry as usual, and apparently in gool health. Ile left work at six o'clock and ate a hearty tea, after which he set about erecting a shed'over the boiler in the back yard, to be utilised as a wash house. For the pur- pose, he borrowed a step ladder from Mrs. Hibbert of the Blue Bell Hotel. When on the top of the 'ladder, he said to his wife "Eliza, I feel giddy," and his wife told him to come down. He descended the ladder, and when he reached the second step from the bottom, he fell, and his wife and son dragged him into the kitchen. His wife then sent for Mr. Hibbert, but he not being in, a young man named Charles Birkbead, went into the house, and found the deceased lying on the floor, with his head on his wife's knee. Mrs. Hibbert came in almost immedi- ately, and they gave the deceased brandy, but it did not • revise him, and after sighing two or three times he expired. Dr. Harold Watkins who had been sent for came in shortly afterwards, and adminis- tered morphia, but without effect and he then prolounced life to be extinct. The Coroner was communicated with, but on being assured by Dr. Watkins that death was due to disease of the heart, he did not think an inquest necessary.—Deceased leaves a widow and eight children.

Mr. Lea said some days ago, a married woman ap- plied to Mr. Ward, the relieving officer of Runcorn, for relief to her husband, who was dangerously ill. Mr. Ward wauld notinrint her any relief, and he put her out of the • office by main force. Her husband died on the Saturday following. He should like to know whether Mr. Ward had any power to put anyone out by main force.—The Clerk : He ought not to treat anyone in that way.- --Mr. Ward was called into the room, and said the woman— Mrs. O'Malley—asked for a medical order. He gave her the order, visited he man, and the next thing he heard was that the man was dead.—Mr.Lea : Did not she apply for him at the beginning of last week.—Mr. Ward: 29th April, and I gave her the medical order.—Mr. Stokes : Did she ask for any assistance.—Mr. Ward : Nothing whatever.—Mr. Lea.said Mr. Imison, a member of the Board of Commissioners, recommended thewoman to go to him, and Dr. Gastaldi visited thecase. The woman told him that Mr. Ward put her out of the office by main force and her arm was black with the mark of flis hand. —Mr. Ward : I never was round the partition, and when I gave her the order through the pigeon hole she thanked. me.—Mr. Lea : The woman herself told me, and I shall inquire further into it.—ln reply to Mr. Taylor, Mr. Ward repeated that the woman merely asked for a medi- cal order. If he died where he stood he.never touched the woman. It was a great untruth.—Mr. Lightburn :'You deny it entirely.—.N.lr. Ward : I do, sir.—Mr. Lightburn suggested to Mr. Lea that it would be as well in future if he would investigate such complaints himself before he brought them before the Board. It would simplify the matter very much.—Mr. Taylor said he could assure the Board that if he brought all cases reported to him he might keep the Board occupied the whole of the sitting. He personally inquired into each case, heard both sides I ascertained the full facts, And acted accordingly. If members would do that it would save this kind of dis- pute and trouble. The Chairman : Mr. Lea will know better in future.—Mr. Lea remarked that he would. There was no other business eof public interest

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY ' AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided and there were present Messrs. C. Reynolds, J.P. (ex-officio), Knowles, J. Weir, J. }holey, Lewis Edwards, Brandreth, Parr, Pickering, Stokes, P. Hall, J. Hall, E. Aaron, J. Ashton (clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer.)

THR AUTHORITY AND THE SHIP CANAL co. The Clerk read a letter from Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, solicitors, Runcorn, stating that they had re- ceived a letter from the solicitors, of the Ship Canal Co., and asking whether they (Messrs. Linaker) would be justified in instructing their agents to move for the dis- solution of the injunction at once, or had they better wait until the agreement were signed. They understood from Messrs. Grundy that the Authority's part would be sealed at the Directors' meeting on Friday. The letter from Messrs. Grundy,Kershaw, and Co. referred to, was as follows : "It was a great inconvenience to the Corn- pany that the agreement was not sealed last Tuesday. They thought that after the way the Company had settled the question of costs, the Authority might have made arrangements for an earlier sealing."—The Clerk said he had replied to Messrs. Linaker that he saw no reason why they should not take steps for the dissolu- tion of the injunction. He produced the agreement for sealing and at the request of several members it was read.—Mr. Weir asked whether Grange Mill water would be.preserved or not,and the Clerk replied that this agree-. ment only dealt with sewers, and that was a watercourse —Mr. Knowles said it was for the landlord to look after such a watercourse.—lr. Parr said he was of opinion that if this sewerage work was slurred over or not satis- factorily carried out, it would be a most expensive item to the Board.—The Chairman said Mr. Wells was em- ployed to see that the work was carried out in a thorough andefficient manner.—Mr. Parr: And is there anyone to look after Mr. Walls. (Laughter.)—Mr. Aaron pointed out that the work done by the company in Runcorn had been of the most excellent character, and the Board need have no fear that the sewers of the Authority would be improperly dealt with.—The seal of the Board was agreed to.

A HOTBED OF DISEASE. he Medical officer reported a case of typhoid fever at a house in Mersey View, at the back of Wood's Row, Halton-road, Helton. He had inspected the premises and was of opinion that the disease had been caused by the defective sanitary arrangements, which appeared still to be the rule for this class of houses. He made a house to house inspection both of Mersey View and Wood's Row, and found privies and ashpits full and overflowing, the open space in the rear ot Wood's row was flooded' with running and stagnant sewage, which was escaping from blocked inlets in Wood's Row; scarcely a back yard was free from pools of stagnant sewage, numbers of grids were blocked, the sewage escaping into neighbour's yards and in several instances coming up to the back door, or escaping upon the open space in rear of these houses. The defects were too numerous for a detailed n-port, but it waknow time for the Sewerage arrangements for this property to be fully reconsidered and placed upon a foundation of _efficiency which should be able to prevent the recurring nuisances to which the existing system was continually giving origin. In its present condition, he had no hesitation in con- , donning it as a nuisance, dangerous and injurious to health, and calling for an immediate abatement. Two , cases of typhoid fever had also occurred at the Keepers cottage at Stonehills, off Halton-road, Halton. He found no sanitary defects on the premises but the only water supply to the house was from pools and ditches and from the casual mercies of a defective rain supply. Anim- proved water supply was urgently called for to this property but the means of obtaining it would require to be carefully considered. During last year ,Sanitary defects on property in Red-lane, Bridge-road,Stock- ton Heath, gave rise to diptheria and typhoid fever ; now diptheria and erysipelas had occurred in two villas, known as Ivy Villas. The property had recently changed owners and sewerage arrangements were being carried out which under the circumstances he would recommend should be placed under the supervision of the Inspector of nuisances as the workmen were on the premises.—Inspector Farrington said the nuisances at Wood's-row and Mersey View, were the result of Jerry building. The whole of the property required re-arrang- ing and the Authority would be brought in to bear a portion of the costs. He reported dpon this property ten years ago but it was then considered to be a nuisance —Oil the motion of Mr. Stokes? the Inspector was in- structed to issue notices for the immediate abatement of the nuisances.

THE FIRE BRIGADE. * The Canal Boats and General Purposes Committee re- commended that ten additional street hydrants be pro- vided, the surveyor and the fire brigade superintendent to fix the situations of the same. That the following fire brigade appliances be purchased :-200 yards hose, 8 in- stantaneous couplings for new hose, 11 instantaneous couplings for hose in use, altering 5 double-stand pipes, altering 5 branc:i pipes, &c. The gross cost would be £56 175.6d.—1n moving the adoption of the IBBIIItES.Mr. Hankinson said this expenditure was necessary, in order to put the fire brigade in a state of efficiency and in a position to act with despatch in a case of emergency.. fact, in order to put the brigade in a thoroughly good condition;doublp the amount ought to be spent, but the Committee had decided to defer further dealing with the matter until next year, and Mr. Wright would do with- out certain things.—Mr.Lightburn sec,mded the motion, and suggested that an occasional test should be made to ascertain the time occupied by the brigade in arriving at the scene of a fire. The minutes Were passed, and the Committee were asked to deal with Mr. Lightburn's sug- gestion.

WATERLOO BRIDGE. Waterloo Bridge Committee recommended that Messrs. Morrison and Sons' tender for lowerin,, the girder railing, &c., of Waterloo Bridge, for £9 10s., 'be accepted.—Mr. Pritchard moved the Passing of the minutes, and said this alteration would effect a decided improvement in the appearanceof the bridge. The bridge had been built according to the places; and it was no fault cf the con- tractor.—Passed.—On the motion of Mr. Pritchard, it was also decided that the tender of Messrs. W. Farrell and Son, for pulling down the ccttage and building the re- taining wall be accepted. The tenderof Messrs. Dunbar, Kelly, and Company, of 3s. lid, per square yard, for tke composition pavement of the footways of the bridge, was accepted.

Accounts amounting to £353 6s. 9d. on general fund; loan account £6l 6s. 9cr. ; district fund £7 Ss. 3d. and library fund £l7 103. 'Od. The treasurer's balances were as follows : General fund £428 6s. 3d. ; unspent loan £1,082 Os. 5d.; district fund £8 12s. 2d. ; sinking fond £487; and library fund £3 14s. 6d.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Imison.

IMPORTANT TO BUILDERS. Mr. Humphreys moved the appointment of a Com- mittee to revise the building bye Jaws and to make such a byelaw ducler the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 189 b, as may he deemed advisable; such Committee to report to the Board.—Mr.Light burn seconded the motion, which was carried without discussion.—ü0 making the selection of the Committee, Mr. Imison asked how ft was that the model bye-laws had not been adopted by the Board.—The Surveyor said they were too stringent and would be ruinous to the builders.—Mr. Lightburn said in towns where the model bye-laws were adopted they were responsible for 20 per cent. of the cost of building property. That was the experience of Wiclnes.—Mr. Fisher said if they wanted to deter anyone coming into town and to stop building operations, they would take the right course by adopting the model bye-laws. If they wanted the t.iwn prosperous, and building to go on, they had better let well alone. It wculd be a waste of ' time to appoint a Committee—The Chairman. But it has been decided to appoint a Committee.—The Law Clerk in reply to a question by Mr. Fisher,said the Local Govern- ment Board had never passed byela xs that did not in- clude model byelaws but they did not say they would not. —Mr. Pritchard said the present byelaws were antiqu- ated, and it was necessary for a committee to reconsider them, and make them consistent with the present Acts of Parliament, especially that of last year. They were under no necessity to adopt byelaws of too arbitrary a character.—lt was decided that the committee consist of the chairmen of the standing Committees and Messrs. Wiswall, Timmins, White, and Humphreys.

At the Liverpool Spring Assizes, on Tuesday, be. fore Mr. Justice Grantham, Mugh Hyland (33), fire- man, was indicted for having,a Widnes, on the 28th March, maliciously- wounded Timothy Burns, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. Prisoner denied that he had used any sharp weapon, prefei-, ring his fists when he .wanted to fight. Prisoner was found guilty. His Lordship, in passing sen- tence, said 1-)ie would, in consideration of his previous good character, sentence prisoner only to six months' imprisonment, and be hoped this Ivould be a lesson to him not to use the knife again, or he would get a severer sentence.
I7NOORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at ...e Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. S. Taylor pre- sided and there were present Messrs. J. Pritchard, H. J. Grice, IL White, J. W. Lightburn, W. Fisher, Timmins, E. Imison, W. Hankinson, F. Wiswall, E. W. Humphreys, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor.) MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The Medical Officer of health reported that the num. ber of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 39. Three were inquest cases, and of the remaining 36 deaths 11 were due to bronchitis,4 to whooping cough 4 to mesenteric disease, 4to phthisis, 2 to inflammation of the lungs, 2 to kidney disease, 2 to cancer, 2 to typhoid fever, 2 to convulsions, and one each to malformation of tile mouth and softening of the brain. Computing the population at 20,000,it would show an average death rate of 231 for the 12 months, but, exclusive of the inquest j cases, the death rate would be 21.8. He had reason to be- lieve that at the last census the population of the Autho- rity's sanitary District was found to be about 19-829. Since then a further increase bad taken place by the im- portation of additional labour.—The Surveyor said there were 31 deaths in the corresponding month last year. HIGHWAY AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this Committee, which were passed on the motion of Mr. Fisher, seconded by Mr. Grice, con- tained the following recommepdat ions :—That the tender of Messrs. Henry Heys & Co., for edgings at is. 9d., and channel 3 at is. Bd., less ai per cent, discount, be ac- cepted. That the tender of Messrs. Thomas Catterall & Co., Liverpool, for the sewering, excavating, and bottom- ing of about 270 lineal yards of the upper portion of Victoria-road, be accepted. That the following plans be • approved: Mr. Richard Morris, for the erection of a villa residence in Weston-road. Mr. William Thomason, amended phtn showing additional wash-house and bath- room to house in Stanley-st. (plan approved August 7th, 1890). Manchester Ship Canal Co., villa residence to be erected at the corner of Heath-rd. and Victoria-rd. Mr. Daniel Dutton, for the erection of two cottages in Cam- bridge-st.
SPRING
PREPARATIONS.

AT THIS SEASON OF THE YEAR the human body stands in special need of being strengthened and renovated, and the impurities which have accumulated in the blood during the trials and hardships of the past winter, re- moved. The ideal Spring Medicine is one which would purify the blood, strengthen the nerves, give tone to the system, banish any germs of disease which may have settled in any organ, and enable the system to derive the full benefit of the reviving influence of spring.

TRANSFERS OF LICENSES. At the Borough Police Court on Monday, the Bench agreed to the temporary transfer of the license of the Norton Arms, Wilderspool Causeway, Latchford, from Joseph Taylor to John Sampson. At the same Court on Tuesday the license of Mr. Derbyshire for the Boar's Head, public-house, Town Hill, was temporarily trans- ferred to Mr. Charles Monk. BREAKING INTO MRS. MONKS'S PREMISES. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday morning, George Wicks was charged with feloniously breaking into and entering the warehouse of Mrs. Elizabeth Monks, Arpley, some time between 1 p.m. and 4.50 p.m. on Saturday. Evidence was given by P.C. Dean, P.C. 6, Mr. Monks, and a witness named Leslie. and from their testimony it appeared that Mr. Monks had left the lock of the warehouse intact about one o'clock, and between four and five o'clock had found him in the warehouse, the lock having been newly forced. Mr. Monks had had two valuable pigeons stolen the previous day. He was sent to prison for 14 days. THE R.S.P.C.A. MEN ON THE ALERT.—CIIARGES OF CRUELTY TO HORSES. At the Bortmgh Police Court, yesterday, Peter Casey was charged with cruelly treating a horse by working it while in an unfit state, on the 25th of April; and Ben- jamin Grimshaw (owner) was charged with aiding and abetting the same.—Mr. Jenkins appeared for the defen- dants, and pleaded guilty on their bet.alf. Inspectors Dowby and Wilson, R.S.P.C.A., proved the case,and said the horse was suffering from an enlargement of the pas- tern and inflammation of the foot, and had much pain. It was being worked on stones for which it was not fit, though it was fit for soft ground.—Mr. Jenkins said the horse was being worked for the first time on stones.— 'The defendants were ordered to pay the costs.—Patrick Potter was charged with working a horse while in an un- fit state on the 16th ult., and Ralph Poole, the owner was charged with aiding and abetting the offence.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defendants.—lnspectors Dowty and Wilson deposed that the animal had contracted ten- don and an overshot fetlock.—Mr. Taylor, veterinary surgeon, deposed that the horse was unfit for work on hard ground.—Mr. Hewitt, veterinary surgeon gave contrary evidence. It was more a case of unsightly gait, he said, than of real pain.—Mr. Pilkington having given evidence in the defendant's favour, Alderman Harrison the Chairman) remarked that it was an old saying that scientific evidence was perhaps the most unsatisfactory and doubtful of all, and commented on the contrariety of the experts' evidence' but considered there was more hesitation in Hewitt's than in Taylor's evidence.—Patten was ordered to pay costs, 3s. 6d., and Poole was fined 10s. and the veterinary surgeon's fee, £1 us. 6d. in all. —James Wilkinson was similarly charged,the date of his offence being the 25th ult. Similar evidence was given, and Mr. Browne said the horse was just below, and asked the Bench to go down and examine it for them- selves, and let the veterinary surgeons on both sides accompany them. Alderman Sutton accordingly went down with them to view the animal; but on their return, the Bench fined the defendant 108. and costs and the veterinery surgeon's fee, £1 Bs. 6d.—James Drink- water, was charged with cruelly-illtreating a mare by working it in unfit state on the 27th ult. The defen- dant begged the Bench to be lenient with him as he had had a great deal of trouble through a child dying at Enutsford. He was fined 10s. and costs, 19s. in all. CHARGE OV BRUTAL WIFE ASSAULT. At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, William Richardson, aged 28, paper hanger, residing in Naylor- st., was charged under a warrant with assaulting and beating his wife Alice Richardson, aged 23, on the 11th of April. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the complainant and Mr. A. Browne for the defendant. Mr. Davies said there was a Royal Humane Society for the protection of animals, but he thought their worships if he proved his c.aee.would agree with him that there ought to be another society for the prosecutien of brute animals,and he should call the defendant one of these. Prosecutrix was a most respectable woman having been a servant both at Canon Dodd's at Stretton, and at the vicarage at Latchford. She fled to her father's, Mr. Ashurst's, at Hill Cliff, on the 12th inst., and he was so upset by her account of the manner in which she had been abused that he took to his bed, and died on the following Tuesday. The defendant, it could be shown, had attempted to murder her with a knife.—The complainant said on the night of the 11th ult, her husband came in about 10 o'clock, drunk. She was nursing the baby at nearly 12 o'clock, and without cause, thumped her on the ear,and knocked her to the floor, and said "Lie there and die,and if a drop of water would save you, I would not get it for you." Herears bled in consequence of the blows. He went to bed some hours later, and she stayed downstairs, having no sleep. He came down at half-past six in the morning, and thumped her on thearm and kicked her on the leg. She walked that morning to Mr. Ashbronk's her father's, at Hill Cliffe, through the rain, her ear bleeding all the way. She wheeled the child in the bassinette before her. Dr. Argo attended her that night. —By Mr. Browne : The whole trouble between them bad not been through her mother. He had quarrelled with the mother. She had sent a message to him making advances, although she had since applied' for a warrant. —Elizabeth Leicester, residing next door to Mr. Asbrook's, said she had known the complainant to come there twice for her husband. On the night of the 12th her ears were inflamed and witness saw a black bruise on her leg.—Dr. Argo deposed to finding the complainant suffering from bronchitis and pleurisy. It was a risky thing for her to walk to her father's in her condition which he thought she had endured more than three days. Her corning home through the wet would account for her condition. Mr. Browne maintained that the whole object of the proceedings was because Mrs. Ashbrook being lonely she wanted her daughter to live with her and have an allowance made her.—The defend- ant in reply to the Bench said he was willing to have her back. She was all right when the mother did not come. —The complainant, said she dare not live with him.— The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months, in two sureties of £lO and his own recognizances of £lO, and ordered to pay the costs, 195., or to be imprisoned for a month.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb) and Alderman Harrison. PITCH AND Toss.—Samuel Browne, for playing at pitch and toss in Halifax-st., on Sunday afternoon,was fined ss. including costs ; in default 7 days imprison- ment. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.--Patrick Burke, puddler, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-St., on Saturday nlght, was 6ned Bs. including costs.—Agnes Cloynes,of Dial-st., and her husband, Thos. Cloynes, who did not appear, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dial-st., at 11.50, on Saturday night.—P.C.'s Amson and Hollingworth proved the case. They requested the defendants to go home and they refused to do so, upon which the officers took them home; but ten minutes after Faw them out in the street again,creatimr, a disturbance. —Mrs. Cloynes said she had been ill-used in her mother's house, and produced a handful of hair which she said had been dragged out of her head.—The Mayor: No doubt there v as a family love scene amongst you. What about the drunkenness.—Mrs. Cloynes : They put me uut into the street.—The two defendants were fined 55.

each, being allowed till Saturday when the husband re- turn from Ellesmere Port, to pay. THE CIIRLEYS AGAlN.—Martin Curley, labourer, of Stanley-st., Wm. Curley, and Bridget Curley, their mother, were summoned on a charge of being disorderly and fighting in the street named. Bridget was the only defendant who appeared, and the Chief Constable now asked to be allowed to withdraw the case against her and for warrants for the apprehension of the two men. The charge arose out of a case which came on at the court the previous Friday, with which the parties were con- nected. Mr. Hunt's applications were acceded to. ARMY DESERTION. —Llewellyn Jones, fireman, of Liver- pool, was charged with deserting H.M.'s garrison of artillery while stationed at Malta, in Nov., 1890, and was sent to Strangeways gaol to await an escort. FIGHTING .—Michael Preston, labourer, rank-st., and Martin Burke were charged with fighting at Town Hill, on April 28th.—A Constable deposed that he saw Burke stripped for fighting; and Preston had been taken into a house to be washed, having had a fight with Burke. Witness saw Preston when he came out.—Burke said he was in a public-house where Preston was going to thrash an old man, and said to him "I would not hit an old man," upon which Preston caught him (Burke) right nude r the nose with his head.—Preston' a much smaller man than Burke, said the latter pulled his shoes off and ran after him. He was a big bully who got his living by boxing, and bullied people who would not pay for beer for him. Preston denied striking him.—The Mayor: My experience of little men is that they have always got too much tongue, and annoy other people.—Burke said Pteston seized him by the neck, and took his shirt off to fight. He was.one of a gang of about six who went about biting and thumping people.—Preston: Them are your own games. I reckon, and you come and put them on to me.—The defendants were bound over to keep the peace, and ordered to pay the costs, 7s. each. VAGRANCY.—James Dyson, who said he came from Ulverston, was charged with having been found sleeping in the hay and straw shed of Joseph Ashton, Bridge Inn, this morning. He was dismissed. CHIMNEYS ON FlRE.—George Shaw. labourer, Latch- ford, Christopher Strong, Jonathan Taylor, and Ellen Warburton were each fined Is. for having their chimneys on fire. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. J. Guest (chairman) and E.

_ DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Kilgarry and Thomas Healy, were charged with being drunk and disorderly, in Mersey-street the previous night, and Kilgarry was charged with assaulting P.C. Hollingworth. On P.C. Unsworth getting held of Kilgarry the latter threw him down. Both fell to the ground and while there, Kilgarry tried to kick Unsworth. Kilgarry was fined 10s. and costs and Healy ss. and costs. SCIIOOI, CASES.—At the instance of Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, the following persons were dealt with on the charge of not sending their children to school regularly :—Peter Cain; pensioner, Tanner's-lane, in whose case Mr. Riley pressed that the defendant's stepson might be sent to the ship Clio. The defendant said if he sent the boy there everybody would cry shame on him; and he would like the Bench to give the lad another chance. The Chairman: You seem to have no control over him, and we shall grant an order for the boy to be sent to the ship Clio.—Peter Carey, forgeman, Dallam- lane and Hubert Clarke, shopkeeper, Church-street, 2s. dd. including costs each.—Michael Connor, forgeman, Oliver-street, ss. including costs, was informed by the Chairman that if he came up again his son would pro- bably be sent to the Clio.—Patrick Corfield, labourer, Ashton-street, 2s. 6d. including costs.—Wm. Deakinson, slater, Silver-streer, order made for attendance and a fine of 2s. 6d. imposed. William Duubobbin, rope spinner, Bridge-street, 2s, 6d. Patrick Heastry, indiarubber maker, Mersey-street, 2s. 6d. George Jaundrill, forge- man, Winwick-road, ss. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Fairclough. _ . .

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Frank Ayres, drunk and disorderly in Wellington-st.,the previous day. A female witness deposed that she was burying her husband in the cemetery, and the defendant who had married her daughter, was drunk there and used very had language. He was fined 10s. and costs.—Michael Dow,22nd appear- ance, was charged with being drunk and disofderly and using indecent language near the iron bridge at Arpley, on Thursday night. A constable and a female witness proved the case, the latter stating that he had run after her threatening her life. He was fined 10s. and costs. ASSAULTING HIS DAUGHT'ER.—Jas. Hogan was charged with assaulting his daughter Elizabeth Hogan OR the 4th ult. The complainant and her mother made state- ments from which it appeared the assault was that he had when drunk, thrown a mug full of suds over her because she did not get up early enough, and she having been advised by a medical man not to get up soon, she being delicate. The mother gave a very bad account of his behaviourgenerally to her and her daugh- ter.—The defendant said his daughter was going to get married, and she and her mother were always getting up disturtances with him to drive him away, so that the daughter might bring her husband to live there.— Mrs. Hogan said she should like a separation with main- tenance from him, and told the Bench she would be con- tent with 7s. ed. a week. WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Picktnert and Mr. John White. _ .

RIDING BY RAIL WIT A TICKET.—John Driver was charged with riding the previous evening on the London and North-Western Railway, from Manchester to Earlestown without a ticket ; also with assaulting Alfred Thorpe, a fellow passenger. It appeared that he had travelled by express, and on reaching Earlestown would produce no ticket, and would give no name or address. He had only 6d. in. his pocket ; and had a bot- tle of whisky with him which he kept supping.—Alfred Thorpe said he travelled in the same carriage as the pri- soner, there being no one else in it. Driver said although he had only just coma out of jail that morning he would fight any two policemen that could be brought against him. He got very excited, and used very bad language and" cracked" his fists on the seat. He asked the com- plainant if he would light, and he replied that he was not in alighting humour. After a while the prisoner said if witness would not he would force him or cut wit- ness's throat. Driver then took his coat off ; and wit- ness pulled the communication cord; the train was stopped.. The guard locked the prisoner in the carriage, while witness got into the nest one. At Earlestown the guard handed Driver over to the stationmaster.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, but expressed great contrition, and promised to takethe pledge. He was fined 40s. and costs on each charge, in default a months' imprisonment in each case. DRUNK AND DISOIMERLY.—AIfred Twiney, drunk and disorderly at Rixton, on the /Bth inst., and Catherine Melia, drunk and disorderly on the same date were each fined 55., including costs.—John Rothwell, drunk and disorderly, at Burtonwood, on the 11th inst., was fined 55., including costs. BICYCLING WITHOUT LAMPS.—Joseph Goldstinne and Max Cowen were summoned for bicycling in Warrington- road, Penketh, on the night of the 26th of April, without having lamps. Cowen did not appear, but was repre- sented by another bicyclist who said Cowen was suffer- ing from Russian influenza, and that he had been with him on the occasion in question, and rode before the defendants to lead the way to the Central Station, as they wanted to catch the train; and he had his lamp lighted. They rode in Indian file. The defendants were each fined is. and costs. BREACHES OF THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ANIMALS ACT.— James Drinkwater and Charles Whitfield were charged with removing pigs from the railway station at Penketh, without a pass,in contraventionof the above-named Act. They had been removed into the road, and then to Drinkwater's house. Drinksvater's only defence was ignorance that he was breaking the law, and that there was no notice put up in the station to enlighten him. Whitfield was discharged and Drinkwater was fined the costs, 6s. 6d.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazlellurst. Poott RATE.—The magistrates signed a poor rate of is. 3d. in the £ for the township of Sutton. A WOMEN'S QUARREL—Elizabeth Sweetman, and Mary Rawlinson, were summoned for having on the 25th April assaulted Ann Surrell. There was a cross-sum- mons charging Surrell with having assaulted Sweetman and Rawlinson. Sweetman further charged Surrell with using threats. The women live in Cartwright-st., and the evidence showed it was a neighbours' quarrel. Mr. Lake represented Surrell. The three women were each bound over to keep the peace for six months. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon John Sefton Ball, Jane Ball, Stephen James Grant, and -Charles Johnson. Jchn Preston was fined £1 including costs. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. James Handley and Dr. Steele. George Lloyd, a well-dressed man from Manchester, was fined 40s. and costs for being drunk while in charge of a horse and trap. The prisoner had been thrown out of his trap at Sutton Weaver, and the horse ran away, being secured at Halton, by P.C. Fryer.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage. DRUNKENNEss.—John Starkey, Marsh-st., Thomas Griffin, Moss Bank, Prtrick Breen,Catherine-st., and Jno. Murphy, Wellington-st., were each fined ss. and costs for being drnnk on the highway at Widnes.—Patrick Leon- ard, no fixed residence,for a like offencewas fined 7s. 6d. and costs, or in default of pa 3 ment 10 days. BEIEACII OF THE PEACE.—Michael Myler, Catherine-st., was charged with creating a breach of the peace at Wid- nes on the 3rd inst., and he was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months,or go to goal for seven days.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 0, 1891.
THE VERNEY SCANDAL.
PLEA OF GUILTY. CONVICTION AND SENTENCE.

At the Central Criminal Court, London on Wednes- day, Captain Tdmund Hope Verney, on bail, was charged before Mr. Jastice Smith with conspiracy and with divers offences aga, inst the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment A•ct. Mr. Poland, Q.C.,Mr. Matthews, and Mr. Horace Avery appeared to prosecute, and the prisoner was defended by Sir Charles Russell, Q.C., and Mr. Besley. The court was crowded. The clerk having read out the indictments to the pri- soner.

Captain Verney answered—My lord, I plead guilty to these indictments with the) exception of the first three, and to those I plead not guilty. Mr. Poland, in opening the case, said the prisoner had pleaded guilty to the fourth count, which charged him with having solicited and incited Madame Rouillier to procure Nellie Maud Baskett for unlawful purposes. The fifth count charged the same offence only with reference to a woman not known ; the sixth with conspiring with Rouillier to procure Miss Baskett, and the remaining counts with offences with the same purpose in view. Ile did not think it necessary to proceed upon the other counts. With regard to the third. both in effect and in law there was a difficulty, because undoubtedly the evid- ence did not go to show that he endeavoured to procure the woman for the purpose of becoming an immoral character. On the first two counts also there were technical difficulties, but the prisoner bad, in fact, pleaded guilty to ths substance of the charge. He would .briefly remind his lordship of the facts of the case,and would mention that in Novem- ber last Madame Rouillier was sentenced to four months' imprisonment in connection with thesame case. She was recommended to mercy by the jury, as they believed she had been the tool of Wilson, and had acted under his influenee. There was no doubt Captain Verney was Wilson, and that he had been concerned with Rouillier as far back as 1884. Mr. Poland then referred to the facts of what he termed a most painful case, and recapi- tulated the main points of the story told at Bow-street Police Court a few days since. In conclusion, he said the sole idea of the prose3ution was to get at the truth of this matter.

Sir Charles Russell said that he had to perform as painful a duty as any he had to discharge in the course of a long professional life. He would address a few words on behalf of the prisoner, whom he, in common with many hundreds of people in this country, had knows and honoured up to the time of the very sad disclosures in this case. But he had pleaded guilty to thesubstance of the charge in this indictment— that he had availed himself of another with a view to procuring persons for his own object. It was true that under the name of Wilson he had sheltered himself, per- haps apart altogether from any idea of his own safety, but for the sake of preventing a slur being cast upon his name, or bringing anguish upon his family. When, however, it waspublicly announced that he was identi- fied with the person Wilson, he took the course which at least was manly and straightforward. He was abroad at the time, but within three days after he heard from. his friends he telegraphed to the Speaker of the House of Commons that he intended to return to this country. He now confessed the fault he had committed,. and was prepared to bear the pen- alty. it was true the prisoner conspired with Rouillier to procure Miss Baskett (who was now in her 20th year), and to get her to France. Altimigh his design was his own selfish gratification yet when he found she was a woman of virtue;, it stood confessed that he was guilty of no untoward act. In the deposi- tions certain statements were attributed to Rouiller in her conversations with Miss Baskett, and undoubtedly the woman was endeavour- ing to undermine the virtue of the girl, but there was no suggestion that any language of that kind was ever addrossed by Ctptaln Verney to Miss Baskett. Re served in the Crimean war and in the Indian mutiny, and he had medals and special recommendations for his gallantry in that service: On three occasions at sea he risked his own life to save that of his fellow-man. That was the man who was to be dealt with in the course of justice. He had now to look te the future to redeem the faults of the past. Mr. Justice Smith, addressing the prisoner, said—You have pleaded guilty to certain counts in the indictment, which charges that you in the month of September last, in conjunction with ,a WOlllan named Rouillier, conspired to procure for your, own base and wicked purpose a girl about 19 years of age.. Fortunately for the girl, enticed • and decoyed as she was by the woman Renner to leave this country and go to Paris,. she, by her own sound sense and virtue, was enabled toescape that ruin which you had sought to accomplish, Lhave read, and re-read the despositions, but it has been impossible to do so with- out coming to • the conclusion that this was not the only case in which ypu have been implicated in the same way. That,. however, we have not got to investigate now. No doubt you are now keenly alive to the position in which you stand, and the disastrous results which, will necessarily and obvi- ously fall upon a man in yourposition. I have listened to what your learned counsel has stated on your behalf, that you did not commit any act of indecency to this girl, but I cannot shut my eyes to the fact that it was her own strong sense of duty which prevented you carry- ing out that which you contemplated. I have only now to pass sentence upon you, and. the sentence is that you be imprisoned for twelve calendar months. The prisoner, on hearing the sentence, bowed to the learned judge, and was then conducted to the cells below the dock. There was no demonstration in court.

The journey of the Lancashire Eleven ta Oldham in search of " talent" on Saturday was says the "Man- chester Guardian " " altogether without good result. For reasons.which are hard to discover, the supply of "colts" in thia country has for many years been alto- gether unequal to the demand ; and throughout the length and breadth of a region which is given over to cricket on Saturday afternoons we cannot discover one single candidate whose form could justifiy his inclusion in the county team. The Oldham coilts batted and bowled badly, and their fielding was wry poor. T:ie most that can be hoped is that they may derive some benefit. from the example that was set them in all depart- ments of the game."

Mr. R. Bates, of Stockport, who has scored very well of late against good bowling, promises to be a great acquisition for Cheshire. Mold was a great sufferer at his hands at al Trafford on Wednesday, when the. amateur carried out his bat for 108 ;: but the fast bowler- was considerably hampered by having to bowl with a+ wet ball.

div.p: CYCLING

What a magnificent collection oF prizes the Du Croses must have won on the Ball's Bridge track alone! These Irish riders are a wonderful family; at every Duerin meeting they seem to divide all the good thing, whilst on this side the Channel they can wore than hold their -own against the very flower of English cycledom. Arthur Du ,Cros won the mile championship of Ireland, whilst his brother Harvey was second. Arthur was also second to Kilkelly, the Dublin university crack, in what was rather ridiculously called the mile championship of thz. world; whilst here again Harvey was close behind. The time, however, was ridiculous, 3roin. 26 4-55ec., and sufficiently indicates the wretched crawl and the desperate burst. G. Du Cros won the five miles handicap rather easily from M. J. Harte and Ackland, both local riders; whilst Wardley, of Curragh, was the successful rider in the mile bicycle handicap.

div.head: LABOUR AGITATION.
div.p: THE LABOUR AGITATION.
LOSS OF LIFE IN FRANCE.

The riot on May-day at Faurmies, in the north of France, was more serious than at first reported. During the attack of the mob on the Town Hall a soldier was dangerously wounded in the head by stone. The Riot Act was then read, and the soldiers ordered to fire. Nine persons—a woman, two men, two young girls,three lads, and a child—were killed,, and twenty persons were wounded. In Belgium strikes have been begun, and the villages round Liege are in a state of seige. Some fur- ther conflicts have occurred in Spain. THE LONDON DEMONSTRATION. The Demonstration organised by the London Trades Council and the Legal Eight Hours Day Committee, to demand legiSlation for a working day of eight hot7s, took place on Sunday, in Hyde Park, a.processton having previously been formed tin the Thames Embankment. There were twelve platforms. Mr. C. Graham, M.P., Mr. John Burns, Mr. Tom Mann, and Mr. Ben Tillett were the principal spealn3rs, and resolutions in accord- ance with the object of the gathering were passed. The demonstration, the second of its kind, proved very suc- cessful, being much larger and much better organised than that of last year.

div.p: BREAKING A. OONSTABLE'S LEG AT RUNCAN.

A yoaing man named Joseph Ankers was brought before Dlr. Chas. Reynolds and Major Hazlehurst at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Mbnday to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly, of assaulting P.C. Proctor, and also of assaulting P.C. Dickinson. Mr. R:. D. Maddock (Messrs. julliffe and Maddock), appeared for the prisoner. Sufficient evidence to justify a remand was given and went to show that at midnight on Saturday thotwo constables heard a dis- turbance in VicaD.street. nay proceeded there and fouralthe prisoner in a statoof drunkenness and using bad language. Hl3 father informed the constables that he had been badly kicked and‘abused by him, and the constables ordered; him to go away quietly. Instead of doing so he ran at. Dickinson and knocked him down. He th&u, ran at Proctor with his head down, and, clasping the constable's kaees, lifted him up and threw him overt lii.Oiead. Proctor cried out-that his leg was broken, and inoeponse to Dickinson's call, for aid, Mr. Coventry and Hlsrding came upon the scene. The prisoner was secured and taken to tile police station. eroctor had his leg bandaged and, was carried home on the ambulance aarriage.—Mr. Bankes, assistant to Dr. Robinson, said 'Ale lower mil of the fibula of the left leg was ,broken, and it would be, quite two months before Proctor would)ne able to walk.—The Bench decided to remind the p:isoner for a week,and Mr. Maddock applied :for bail to be allowed.—Superintendent Large strongly opposed the application, and said the prisoner had been a wanderer allover the country, and had been a wither. He had thrown Proctor in the Lancashire style °fewest- ling. Bail was refused.

CORON-W7ON OF Tlll4 Ma* QUICEN.—The Committee of the Galborne Maytime festivities have nc reason to complain of the weather this year. For once.in a while the sun favoured thecelebrati-n, and as a consequence Saturday's proceedings were a great success. Special trains bringing hundreds of visitors, cams from War- ringt" St. Helens, Earlestown, and Wigan. The child- ren assembled at two o'clock at the Recreation Ground,. where they were marshalled:for the general parade. Up. wards of 1,002 children took part in the procession, and , very pretty did they look in their dresses of divers ea-. ours. The central figure in the show was tiny Miss' Tither, a little lady of eleven summers % on whom fell the I care of tbs. kingdom for one day may. She bore her' lkonours and discharged her duties with all the dignity befitting her exalted office. Next, in favour•witb.the crowd were tha May-pole dancers, and Colonel Tbomp- son's sturdy young soldiers. On the return of the pre- cession to the Recreation Ground, the ceremony of cor- onation was gone through, following with the May-pole dancers—who had been trained by Mr. John I",earden— the Bohemian dancers,andthe miniature Volunteers enter- tained the spectators by some pretty performances. Sub- sequently, the three local bands engaged—Golborne, Ashton, and Haydock—played for public dancing until dusk. Mr. E. Last was chairman of the Committee of Management and Mr. Joseph Sankey filled the import- ant office of serretary, Mr. E. Lash acted AS master of the ceremonies.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

IMPORTANT MEETISG OF SLIAREHOLDETIS CROWDED ATTENDANCE. An extraordinary meeting of the shareholders of the Manchester Ship (Jana) Company was held in the Gentlemen's Concert Hall,Manchester, on Mon- day, for the purpose of considering the provisions of the Bill now before Parliament to enable the Company to raise additional loan capital for the completion of the undertakiog, and authorizing the Manchester Corporation to lend money to the Company, and to extend the time for the completion of the Canal. There was the largest attendance of shareholders ever seen in the Concert Hall, the building being crowded. Lord Egerton of Tattoo, the Chairman of the Com- pany, presided, and, in, opening the meeting, briefly stated its object. They had conferred, he said, with the Mayor and Corporation of Manchester, who had received them with great cordiality, and had, with the rate- payers and property ownere„ he believed, unanimously agreed to promote a Bill in Parliament for a total sum of £3,000,000, which was considerably more than the Directors of the Company had asked for, but the Cor- poration had done that in orderto have the whole scheme completed, without haying additional works which might have been left over to be delayed. Salford had gener- ously come forward to assist, but found it to be too late this Session to promote a Bill in Parliament, and he hoped that the Bill of the Manchester Corporation would not be delayed by any action that it might have been thought desirable to take to get a.clause inserted in the 'Bill in the interests of Salford. With regard to some of the clauses in the Manchester Bill relating to the re- payment of the loan, the Company might not be in corn- pleteacconi, but their objection was only as to. matters of detail. He did not think that any action would be taken by the House of Commons on the motion which was to. be proposed by Mr. P. Stanhope to convert the Cant into a public trust. He moved a resolution sanctioning the promotion of the Bill now before Parlia- ment. Sir J. LEE seconded the motion. The directors, he saicl,had enough of money to go on with the construction of the Canal until June. The last call, would produce £49o,oooand they had thelB9o debentures with which to bring in £330,000. These debentures-wculd take pre- cedence of the money provided for in the Bill the share- holders were now asked to approve. They would be first- class security, and could be obtained from the secretary of the company in the usual way. As they were aware, the supervision of the completion of the works had come under a Committee of the Board, and he had pleasure in telling the meeting that the engineer's estimate on, the Ist January Ist had not been exceeded within the last two months,.and the Committee hoped to be able to con- struct the works within the estimates. He had also to inform the shareholders that the expenditure upon the Canal was not likely to exceed the amount which the chief engineer had stated to be necessary. (Hear, hear.) He asked themeeting to support the motion before them, , for he felt that not only would the company, be enabled , to pay off the money provided by the Corporation in a. few years, but should be able to realise the promise that had been made to the shaareholders originall, and also by the Consultative Committee three and a.half year,- ago. (Applause.) Mr. Horsfall said he considered the chairman's-state- ment most satisfactory. What he wished to asktwas that in the event of,Mi. Stanhope's motion before the House of Commons with regard to the Canal being converted into a public trust being successful what would the effect be upon directors of the Canal. The Chairman said Mr. Stanhope had not the slightest idea that his motion would be carried,, nor had he (the chairman). He, therefore, did not think it worth while. to consider what the changes might be if it were carried. (Hear. hear.) Mr. Stanhope had told him that he was not hostile to the Bill, but was, on the contrary,.a sup- porter of the Ship Canal, and would not do anything to imperil the Bill: He had, however, a few views on the subject that he wish to liberat€ in the House. (Applause and laughter.)' Mr. J. B. Fdden said Salford had taken a very large interest in the Canal. It was the only borough that went to Parliament and asked to take up £2.00, in shares. Was the chairman in a position to state why the Board did not approach Salford in conjunction, with Manchester to contribute some portion of the money?" Mr. J. C. Lee said he was afraid he was the culprit. (Laughter.) Seeing the difficulty the directors were in he went to the-Mayor of Manohester and Sir J. J: Har- wood for their advice, who called together a few of the principal members of the Corporation and communicated with them in a fefw hoors. (Applause.) The result was that they agreed to bring the matter before the Council. It had never struck him as being desirable to apply to any other Corporation. It seemed to be a one-Corporation job, and if they had applied to Salford, Oldham, or,War- rington as well, they might have landed themselves in a quandary, and they thought it better to deal with onlly one Corporation, and. if any of the Corporations amnia Manchester wished to join in the guarantee they might do so by applying to the Manchester Corporation. Sal- ford, unfortunately, did not apply until the Bill was drafted 'and before Parliament, but the directors ot' the Canal had no idea of casting any slight upon Ealford. They did not think of it. (Applause.) The resolution was then put and carried unanimously,. followed by cheers. ' ' MR. STANHOPE'S MOTION. In connection with the motion which Mr. P. Stanhope has given notiee.of his intention to move on the, second reading of the Ship Cana/ Bill, it is stated the hon...mem- her holds that it it improper to give municipal guarantees to limited liability companies • and that, if the Man- chester Ship Canal is completed by municipal assistance it ought to vest wholly in some public authority, in the manner of most of our great harbour boards at •?resent controlled by commissioners, such as those of the 'Tyne, Mersey, and Clyde. Mr. STANHOPE explains that his motion is not brought forward in a sense hostile.- to the Manchester Ship Canal, but with the object of placing that undertaking upon a sure and solid footing, mad one justifiel in the public interest.

div.p: THE 'PRINCE OF WALES'S DEETS,

"Atlas" in the" World" writes :—I am informed that the severe financial pressure, which, as many are aware, has been for some time past weighing heavily- on the Prince of Wales, and: which has caused the depression in his manner and aspect that has been so generally observed, is now in at fair way to be mitigated, and that, althoughit is improbable that resources will; be forth- coming wholly to liquidate the obligations which have gradually accumulated around his Royal Highness, there will be averted the necessity, which until quite recently has been seriously apprehended, of an application to Par- liament on behalf of the Prince. It has been arranged, I believe, that the Queen will contribute a large sum from her accumulations—a subsidy amounting to several' hun- dred thousand pounds, the administration of.? which, in the satisfaction of certain classes of the obligationsof the heir,apparent,wi lit be in the hands of unoffidialliquidators nominated by her Majesty. Other measures- are under consideration, said among the stipulations ,to which his Royal Highness has assented is the assignment to the Duke of Clarence and Avondale of an adequate and regular inceme.
A, MAD MOTHER ATTEMPTS TO, DROWN HER CHILD AT ST. HELENS.

On Saturday, at St. Helens Polica-Couxt, before Alderman J. Harrison, Maria Muivilhii wife of Patrick Mulvilhill, 100, Canal Bank,. West, was charged with attempting to murder;ber• child Brid- get, 11 months old, by throwing her into. the canal. —Chief Constable Wood stated that the prisoner and her husbandlhad been married fortabout eight years, and therewere four children. 'Ter the last two or three weeks she had appeared rather strange in her manner, and that morning she asked I;.er husband to throw the four children into the faun'. He refused,and she then asked him to go for Father, Walmsley. He left the house for that purpose, but Patrick Hyland, a labourer„residing next door, was .asksd to watch her. He did so, and after she had stood at the door with the child B2idget in her arms for some, time, she walked rapidly across the street and dsliberately threw the chUti into the-canal, which is opposite to the property. The water was a a considerable depth, and was very diy. Hylandtran and seized the woman and tried to pull her back. She struggled as if aiziousto throw herself into the water,but he succeeded in getting her back inta the housa. At that time Hyland's son sames, 16 years oZ age, cam,3 on the scene, and jumped iato the water. Ilexes- cued, the child just as shit-was sinkix--; for the second time, and not her to the side, In6artaation was given,to Sergeant Bunter, who apprehendpd the prisoner._ At the peliee station she was chrerged with attempting to murder her child, and in reply she saioll"• I never did." After a pause she added" I threw it it% this morning."—Patrick Ryland was called to give evidence, and the prisoner was remanded.—After her retrieval from the court Dr. Carney, assistant to the borough medical officer, ex- amined her and certilled that she was insane Alderman ,Jr. Harrison, J.P., thereupon, signed an ordez tor her re- moval to Rainhill Asylum.

TEE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON ON
FREE EDUCATION.

On Monday evening the monthly meeting in connection with the Church of England Temper- ance Society was held in the large room of the National Schools, Church-st. There was a fair attendance, and the chair was occupied by the Rev. P. W. Willis, rector. The Chairman took advantage of the oocasion to refer to free education, a subject 1:).! great interest at the present moment. The measure was not, in his opinion, introduced by those who were 1110 st friendly to religion and the Church. Rather the °Proosite. Further, it had not been demanded by the 'ç Pie. On the contrary, so tar as he knew, the respect- aola hardworking artisan was perfectly satisfied to pay the school fees of his children. Again, the name had !come before them in a rather disingenuous way. It had ?lrst come before them as" assisted" education, and now It was to be entirely free, which led them to view it suspicion. Further, the people would, in the !!Iture, have to pay in some manner. It might be true Flat the landlord paid the rates and taxes, yet when the landlord fett the burden of the rates and taxes, he would .taise the rent. The good side was this. It would save !hat waste of time which was now taken up en Monday Tnrnings in receiving children's pence, and prevent all mat friction which often occurred between the school- tlaater and the parents. But, continued the Rector, they :"11.at be on their guard, and remember that another at- nleic would be sure to follow, and when the grantof public t•°neY name there would sure to be a cry for representa- Inn and control. I:,he Rev. E. J. HAM afterwards addressed the meeting, flu !poke of the evils arising from the use of strong drink, 421 d introduced appropriate anecdotes in support of his it_nntention. He asked them to do all in their power to tui) the society which was doing so much good work in "at locality Sacred songs and solos followed, after Which the meeting terminated.

, At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Grantham, Thomas Farrell (28), labourer, I°4B indicted for having at Warrington, on the 21st ADM robbed James Cunningham, and stolen from hie person the sum of 255., using personal violence at the time of the robbery.—Mr. Collingwood Hope Prosecuted, stating that the prosecutor was a farm labourer, and came to' Warrington. He visited the Iligher Angel Hotel, public-house, where he met the Prisoner. At that time prosecutor had 255. in his posses- • which was tied up in a sort of fob made by fasten- ing a string across part of the shirt, inside of which was Placed the purse and money. Prisoner attacked the Prosecutor, who is an old man of very hirsute appearance, cut out the piece in his shirt where the money was, and tOt away, On being apprehended the piece cut out of the B,lprt was found in one of prisoner's pockets,and the police ?tecovered afterwards a considerable portion of the money her. Prisoner, coal-place of the prisoner's house under some dm- _ r. Prisoner, who was found guilty, made a strong 4,13 peal for another chance, saying that lie was on the T"ge of consumption, and that he would reform. His :.ordship said prisoner had asked for another chance,and ; (Isymuld get one. The chance would be penal servitude, 1 "'eh, according to the experience of those who man-1 tgled the affairs of the Discharged Prisoners' Aid Society, I then of the greatest philanthropy, afforded the best I • .nce of reform for a prisoner who was repeatedly con- and showed no signs of amendment.—The Pri- or tre,r Oh, my lord, give me one more chance. He said if there was one English 'Port that came under the name of athletic that he • 14,nould like to excel in it was that of swimming. here Was always about the news of :an expert 4Wirotner saving a life a sort of charm; and on the ontrary there was an uncomfortable thrill on read- ellg that some one bad been killed on the cricket or iootball field. He was not one of those who would WoUld stop athletic games because a life was lost 1,..1.01V and again, and so long as vicious or foul play wete kept from these games they never would in. his °Pinion either be short of an athlete to compete or a man lock on. In Warrington they could boast of excel- lent cricket, bowling and lawn tennis grounds, and of a L°otball field almost second to none; and very shortly ‘oev hoped to be able to boast of a fine gymnasium :thich would be one of the best in the provinces.
