div.head: STOCKTON HEATH YOUTHS.
div.p: THE STOCKTON HEATH YOUTHS.

• Sir,—That report, in your last impression, of the com- plaint of Mr. Whitley to the Daresbury Magistrates, as to the disgraceful' conduct of youths, at Stockton Heath, 'was not a pleasant piece of reading. It seems to lend confirmation to the startling assertion made recently by a clerical authority that morals are lower in rural than In urban districts. These young barbarians who hang about street corners nd pollute the atmosphere with their vile and disgusting colloquialisms, besiles exposing street passengers to the necessity of running the gauntlet of their gross insults, are social plagues of the most ob- noxious type, and, so far as the law admits, ought to be dealt with as such. It is a strange anomaly that these social pests, who make life unbearable to some of the inhabit- ants of Stockton Heath, can be dealt with only by being kept moving on by the police, because they commit their offences in a country district, whereas in a borough such deiinquents could be condignly punished. But this inconsistency in our law is only of a piece with much more that is anomalous in our capricious and fantastic legislation. Mr. Whitley complains to the magistrates, And he perhaps makes matters worse by doing so, for the practical outcome of his complaint is really what amounts to a proclamation that these juvenile black- guards of Stockton Heath are free to continue their e,out- rageous misbehaviour, provided that they move on when the police requests them to do so. But is it quite true that persons cannot be proceeded against for the use of foul language in the streets of rural districts? It strikes me that I have seen plenty of instances to the con- trary in your reports of the county petty sessions. But, in default of other means,l devoutly trust that the police of Stockton Heath will use to the utmost their powers 'by moving on these juvenile street pests, and stamp out an intolerable nuisance.—Yours truly,
DECENCY.
IN VERITABLE VERITAS.

Sir,—l know not whether " Veritas" be in his first or second childhood; whether it be his parents or guardians who are responsible for allowing him thus to rush un- revised into print. He "still regards" himself as in the right and myself as being the author of this luminous idea. Now if this had been my idea, how are we to regard this sentence which may be found in my reply to Veritas and combating this notion? "I should have thought it to have been within tne mental scope of even a Veritas to have grasped the idea that even Newton and Herschel might very well remain uninfluenced by the undiscovered." Now it is evident that " Veritas " might • as well class Newton with Aristotle as being uninfluenced by evolution in their judgment upon matters theologi- cal. The anachronism is evident in both cases. As to Herschel, will" Veritas "allow me to point out to him that it is one thing for a man to be alive as a contem- porary with a fact and another for him to be alive to the fact. But as to the question of Herschel who discovered his namesake. alias Georgium Sidus, in 1781, being alive when the influences of evolution "were in full sway." "Veritas "must really excuse me if I decline to follow in such leading. But all this is the veriest triflingand quib- bling upon aide issues. Why does not " Veritas "or any of the many other defenders of the faith attack the main ramparts in which I have entrenched myself? Now that Mr. Dignum has "written down" Mr. -Gandy, who has again " shown up" Mr. Dignum, cannot the fatter, after resting from his Patristic labours. get Moses out of the difficulty of pretending to bca historian of the human race from "the beginning" up to his own time, and en- tirely ignoring that greaf and important chapter in which men used flint impl2mento and weapons? And, even worse still, makes metal-working contemporary with the life of the first man! What PalDiaS says of Polycarp, or Mosheim of 1-ntli,pales before the immensity of the issues involved in the determination of this question. Upon , the answer to this depends the acceptance or rejection of Christianity as a revealed religion. Should not those interested in this; question look then to the foundations, rather than. be discussing what, after all, are very much matters of opinion as to the credibility or otherwise of Patristic writers? Will none of these Biblical champions show cause why what I have advanced should not be accepted as the truth ? If they do not, may I not con- clude that they can not P—Very truly yours, JOHN PEERS. May 3rd, 1891.

div.head: APOSTOLIC SUCCESSION, &c.
div.p: APOSTOLIC SUCCESSION, &c.

Sir,—After a lapse of some months, the Vicar of Run- corn has vouchsafed to reply to the question for Scrip- ture for infant baptism. He says in his magazine for this month :—" The baptism of infants is not directly commanded in Scripture ; there is a very great deal in favour of it and nothing against it in Holy Scripture, but there is no distinct command." In last month's magazine, page sixty-three, "It is undoubtedly true,god- fathers and godmothers are not mentioned in Scripture." I would again ask Canon Wood or any of his instructed Churchmen to give chapter and verse favouring infant

baptism from the New Testament. Bishop Burnet wrote "Teaching must go befoie baptism." Bishop J. B.Lightfoot, of Durham,on Colossians 2 c. admits it to be believers. John Wesley's notes says :—" It alludes to the ancient manner of baptising by immersion." Dean Hugh McNeile says:—" The Word of God is silent on in- fant baptism."

I deny the Vicar's quotation "that the bishops of the Church can be traced to Apostolic times—and this suc- cession is the guarantee of the continued historical iden- tity of the Church." There are only two orders in the New Testament; no such an official as a diocesan bishop, but elders or presbyters and deacons. Bishop Ryle says: —"Strictly speaking, there is no such thing as Apostolic succession ; we are the successors of the ministry of Timothy and Titus." Dean Lefroy says :—" It is schis- matical, heretical, unscriptural, and unhistorical ; such Apostolic succession has no place in Christianity." John Wesley says :—" The uninterrupted succession I know to be a fable which no man ever did or can prove." Archbishop Whately wrote :—" There is not a minister in all Christendom who is able to trace up with any ap- proach to certainty his own spiritual pedigree." Am- brose says :—" They do not possess the inheritance who do not possess the faith of Peter." Bishop Jewell says : —" The grace of God is promised to pious souls, and to those who fear God, and is not fixed to bishops' chairs and personal succession." The unanswerable Isaac Bar- row, D.D., said :—" The Apostolic office, as such, was personal and temporary ; and therefore, according to its nature and design, not successive or communicable to others in perpetual descent from them." Oxford Tracts and "Hymns Ancient and Modern "try to bolster up this system to support men (and palaces) from £1,500 to £4,000 a year, and among the means adopted for the purpose, the "touch me not" fiction of an Apostolic Succession has been adopted. But it cannot last for ever. Many of the bishops to-day are aiding the Church of Rome by their teaching and ritual. The storm is gathering fast and may overwhelm them, Frodsham, May 4th, 1891.
ROBERT FOULKES.
LICENSING CASE AT STOCK- PORT. A WARRINGTON APPLICANT.

On Wednesday at the Stockport Borough Police Court, before Mr.,E. Walnasley (in the chair) and other magistrates, the adjourned application for the temporary tran4r of the license of the Bowling Green Inn, Tiviot Dale, was made by Mr. Russell Coppock, solicitor, who stated that he appeared on behalf of Mrs. Hannah Bullock, the applicant, who asked that the license might be temporarily trans- ferred to herself from Mrs. Hodgkinson, the late tenant. The application was made a fortnight ago, and the Chief-constable, on behalf of the police, made certain objections to the tenant and to the transfer being made, and the matter was adjourned so that in the meantime further in- quiries might be made. He (Mr. Coppock) did not appear a fortnight 'ago, but since then be had gone into the matter and had seen the Chief-con- stable, to whom hi- had expitiined the matter,and he (the Chief-constable) was uow willing to withdraw his objections if he (Mr. Coppock) gave an under- taking on behalf of the owners (Messrs. Showell & Sons, Ltd.) and the tenant, that the house should be properly conducted, and that there should be nothing carried on in the way of betting or gamb- ling, and also that on the first complaint of any- thing of that kind by the police the tenant should go out. The objections to Mrs. Bullock a fortnight ago were that she was only a nominal and not the actual tenant, but he thought he had satisfied the Chief-constable that she had bought the in-going from Mrs. Hodgkinson and had paid for it with money obtained from a person in Warrington, and not from her son. Her son was said to be a betting man, and it was said that he was to be the actual tenant, but as a matter of fact he was only going to assist, and the actual and responsible tenant would be Mrs. Bullock, who had invested a large amount of money in the house, and he (Mr, Coppock) had given her such warning on the subject of betting and gaming, that he (Mr. Coppock)could assure the Bench that nothing of that kind would be carried on. The house had always borne the best of characters; it was a good house, and was in a good situation. He thought the warning he had given Mrs. Bullock would be sufficient to make her very careful indeed in the conduct of the business. - He (Mr. Coppock) asked the magistrates to grant a temporary transfer of the license until next trans- fer day, when, if the magistrates made no objection it could be made permanent. In reply to the magistrates, the Chief Constable (Mr. W. H. Jones) said that wl,at Mr. Cappock had said was correct. In view of Mr. Coppock's undertaking he could not carry his opposition further. He had not the slight- est objection to Mrs. Bullock, but to her son. The magistrates at this point retired to consider the matter, and on returning into court ' Mr. Walmsley : The magistrates are quite indisposed to grant the temporary license as deSired, but we shall adjourn the case for a fortnight, and in the meantime the parties interested will be able to brim, it before us in aome other way. We are dealing with the case upon the evidence we have received on oath. - - - -

Mr. Coppock: I could alter that evidence a good deal if you would allow me to give evidence to-day, but hay- ing satisfied the police I did not think it was necessary. Mr. Walmsley : We will give you a fortnight. Mr. Coppock : A great deal of the evidence was incor- rect. It was said that the son had lost his license. He did, but there was an appeal,and the license was granted to hiin on appeal. I did not think it was necessary to 2.0 into that as I had satisfied the police. He held the license four or five months after. Mr. Walmsley : The case is adjourned for a fortnight. Any evidence you can then bring we will hear. Mr. Coppock: I had no idea you wanted evidence. Mr. Walmsley: We don't want evidence ; we are satisfied from the evidence that we have had placed be- fore us on oath that the house is not likely to be conducted under the terms undertaken this morning. Some discussion then took place as to the exact reason why the case was adjourned a fortnight ago. Mr. Gilmore said that the reason of the adjournment was that the owners might get a new tenant.—Mr. Cop- pock: I did not know that was the reason.—Mr. Gil- more : But it was.—Mr. Coppock: I think not.—Mr. Gilmore: I beg your pardon.—Mr. Coppock: You are liable to be mistaken as much as anyone else. Perhaps Mr. Jones will say what he understood was the reason of the adjournment P—Mr. Gilmore: Mr. Jones was not in the magistrates' room at the time it was discussed.—Mr. Jones: I only know that the adjournment was made on my application. I don't know wile.: was done in the magistrates' room.—Mr. Coppock: I think your wor- ships might allow me to call evidence.—The Magistrates' Clem k: Have you got any evidence here ?—Mr. Coppock Yes, but I thought that. on the strength of what had passed between the Chief Constable and myself it was not necessary to call any further evidence. I satis- fied the Chief Constable that Mrs. Bullock would carry on the house herself, and that her son should not be allowed t 3 take any part in the management of the business. The temporary transfer was granted on March 25th last, and when, a little later, she applied for the trans- fer to be made permanent and opposition was raised hy the Chief Constable, she was quite unprepared, and consider that the magistrates adjourned the matter in order that further inquiries might be made and other evidence produceel. I think that the evidence ] given on that day was of very little use. The chief evi- dence given was that by a police officer from Warring- ton, who did not know of his own knowledge a great deal. Mr. Coppock went on to say that.if the license was granted and Mrs. Bullock did not conduct the house in accordance with the wishes of the Chief-constable, or if it was known to be frequented by betting men, or betting was known to be carried on there, the owners would take care that a fresh tenant would be procured. Messrs. Showell had a very valuable house, and it was their express wish that it should be carried on without the slightest infringement of the Licensing Acts. Mrs. Bullock had put her own savings into the house. She was a very respectable person, and was a widow, and had her own money at stake. She had signed an agree- ment that if anything was laid against the house by the police she would leave it, and Mr. Jones was satisfied with that undertaking. When the temporary transfer was panted her a large amount of money was paid to Mrs. Hodgkinson as an ingoing, and it would be impos- sible for her to sell it again if the license was now refused. It would be said that she was forced to sell, and a difficulty would be felt. He (Mr. Coppock) had Mr. Alfred Piggott, Messrs. Showell's manager, ready to be called to speak as to the agreement signed by Mrs. Bullock, to the effect that if the police found any cause for objection the tenant would have to leave the house instantly. Mrs. Bullock knew that, and had expressed her willingness to do it. He (Mr. Coppock) was sorry for the woman, as she had a large amount of money at stake.

The Chairman: You can continue to sell for a fort- night. Alderman William Leigh: We shall be prepared to hear at the end of that period any evidence Mr. Coppock is ready to call. Mr. Coppock asked for a longer adjournment of the case, as the present adjournment would just terminate in the middle of Whit-week. The next transfer day would be most suitable. The Chairman : When is that?

The Clerk: July 22nd; more than two months. Mr. Gilmore: A new tenant might be got. Mr. Coppeck : Will you allow it till next transfer day, and in the meantime if there is the slightest objection to anything by the police to the tenant, I will undertake that she shall go ? That will give the police an oppor- tunity of seeing whether the conduct of the house is of such a characrer as to cause an objection to be raised. The Chairman We are taking the case as it has been brought before us, and, though we think a fortnight is sufficient for an adjournment, we grant a month.
THF INFLUENZA AT WARRINGTON,

TWO DEATHS. It may now almost be said that influenza has become epidemic in Warrington as in many other towns. On all hands one hears of persons who are suffering from the malady to a greater or lesser extent, and in many instances those who are affected have been incapacitated for work. In one or two cases the attacks have ended fatally. One of the victims is Mr. Henry Newell, of Walker-st., who was taken ill on the Tuesday of last week, and, pneumonia having supervened, his illness ended in his death on Saturday. Mr. Newell, who worked at Dallam Forge, was only 32 years of age, and was a respected member of Wycliffe congregation. He leaves a wife and one child to mourn his sudden and early death. In the case of James T. Leitch, a plumber, of 72, Church-st., who died on Thursday. although influenza is not certiaed as 2, cause of death, it is said that his illness began with that dis- order. Mr. Leitch was also a young man, being only thirty years of age, and his illness was of only about a week's duration.

div.head: BARLESTOWN.
div.p: BARLESTOWN.

There are a large number of cases of influenza in Earlestown, but in some instances it iv not of a very severe form, and so far there have been no fatal results. The medical men are kept very busy, but it is gratifying to note that the disease does not make very rapid progress.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

In Haydock, principally at the Blackbrook end, there have already been one or two deaths traceable to its effects. The medical men at Haydock have their hands pretty full of patients, and are kept unusually busy.
ILLNESS OF MR. SETON-ICARR.
Mr. Setod-Karr, M.P. for St. Helens, •is among the latest of the Parliamentary sufferers from the influenza.
Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., is confined to his room with influenza. The condition of Mr. Craven, M.P., shows further im- provern9nt.

div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB

The annual dinner was held at Riley's Coffee Cafe on Thursday night. A good company assembled, and Mr. P. Speakman C.C., the president, occupied the chair. After justice had been done to the good things provided, the Chairman proposed the toast of "the Queen," and then Mr. Langshaw announced that during the past season the first team had scored 38 goals and 55 tries against their opponents, 12 goals and 17 tries. The second team had played 26 matches, won 20, lost 4, and drawn 2. They had scored 46 goals, 64 tries against 7 goals and 9 tries. (Loud applause.) Mr. Langshaw pro- posed "The health of the President" remark- ing that no gentleman took a more lively interest in the welfare of the club than Mr. Speakman, who was always ready to come amongst them at their social gatherings, witnessed their matches, and was always willing to assist in any- thing they undertook. (Applause.)—The toast was drunk with musical honours, and Mr. Speakman in reply, said since he had taken a deep interest in the club, he had been afforded much sincere plea- sure, and his intefest had been continually on the increase. (Applause.)—ln the different -parts of the country in which he had travelled, he had al- ways heard Runcorn spoken of as one of the lead- ing teams—(applause)—and he felt gratified in having an official connection with them. (Applause.) It was not possible for a man with a large business or a small business to recognise every member of the football Club, when he met him, for although they knew him he did not I-now them personally, and he would ask them if he did not recognise them any- where to always recognise him. (Applause.) If he could be of any personal help to any member of the club in the future, he could assure them that it would be a great pleasure to do so. (Applause.) In conclusion Mr. Speakman, in answer to a writ- ten request, gave an interesting and chatty des- cription of his visit to Palestine.—Mr. Speakman pro- posed the health of the captain of the club and other officials, and Captain Hughes, Mr. Langshaw, Mr. Pownall, Mr. Cawley, and Mr. Faulkner res- ponded. Mr. W. Wright proposed the host and hostess (Mr. and Mrs. Riley), and the proceedings were brought to a conclusion by a vote of thanks to Mr. Speakman for his presence.
THE PROPOSED COTTAGE HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN.

The sub-committee appointed about two months ago to draw up a scheme for establishing a cottage hospital in the town, have just issued their report. They recommend that a hoopital be established, to be called the Runcorn Cottage Hospital, and that such hospital shall be under the control of the sub- scribers, who shall have one vote for each ss. sub- scribed annually, but no subscriber shall have more than 20 votes. It is proposed that Sir Richard Brooke shall be invited to be president of the hospital, and that all subscribers to the hospital of £2 as., or more annually, shall be vice-presidents. The Management Committee is to consist of twelve gentlemen, four to re- tire annually, who shall, however, be eligible for re-election. When any church, chapel, friendly society, or association, or collector shall contribute to the funds of the hospital a sum of £5 ss. Od. or more than £5 ss. Ott. or a sum of 5.9. or more than Ss., the person through whom the payment is made, shall be for the cur- rent year a subscriber in the same manner as if he bad contributed the sum him;elf. All the resident medi- cal men invited by the Committee and giving their ser- vices to the Hospital shall be hon. members of the Com- mittee and possess four votes as ordinary subscribers. The Clergy and ministers of the town shall have access to any patient desiring to see them'at such reasonable times and on such occasions as the Management Corn. mittee shall approve. Each patient shall be attended by his own medical man. A committee of six shall be ap- pointed to obtain donations and subscriptions. In the opinion of the Committee it would be desirable to erect a house capable of containing six or eight beds, to engage a matron and servant and set the Hospital in ' operation at the earliest possible date. The Com- mittee have considered the suitability of various houses, but they are of opinion that no place combines so many obvious advantages as Highfield House, the pro- perty of the Runcorn Gas Company, which is shortly to be vacant. They believe that such a house might be furnished for £l5O, and they estimate the annual expen- diture at from £l5O to £2OO. With respect to the ad- mission of patients the Committee suggest that accidents be admitted at once. Medical or surgical cases (other than accidents) only upon the recommendation of a sub- scriber. Patients to pay not less than 53. a week at the discretion of the Committee of Management. A subscriber to have a recommendation for each ss. The Management Committee is recommended to make special terms with large employers of labour for the admission of accident cases. The report is signed by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, as Chairman of the Committee.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD:
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD:
The monLhly meeting was held on Tuesday night Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present Dr. McDougall, Mr. S. Taylor, and Mr. A. Salkeld with Mr. Moss, clerk.
SCHOOL ATTENDANCS.

The School Attendance Committee reportad that 119 parents had been summoned before them and 102 ap- peared. Fifteen were ordered to be prosecuted before the magistrates. The Clerk read the visitorereparts, from which it appeared that the percentage of attend- ance was 81•3 as against 8311 in the preceding month,and 83 in the corresponding month of last year. The failing off was general throughout the town and was attributed to the prevalence of colds, &c., caused by the inclement weather.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.-SUCCESS OF T.HB EVENING. SCHOOL
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.-SUCCESS OF T.HB EVENING. SCHOOL

The School Management Committee recommended that the salary of R. T. Kenyon, assistant teacher at Green- way-road Boys' School, be advanced to £55 per annum. That a set of calisthenic poles and a set of wooden rings be obtained for use in the physical exercises and drill at Greenway-road School. A letter was read from Mr. J. F. Moulton, drawing attention to the necessity for having a certificated assistant in his school. Consideration was deferred.—The Clerk presented the scheduleof passes at the recent examination at the evening school, from which it appeared that 13 pupils passed in 5 subjects, 20 in 4 subjects, 17 in 3 subjects, 8 in 2 subjects. and 1 in 1 subject. It was decidedto give prizes to all pupils who had passed in four and five subjects.—The minutes were .approved.

div.head: _SERVICE OF POLICE SUMMONSES.
div.p: THE _SERVICE OF POLICE SUMMONSES.

The Clerk of the Peace (Mr. R. Potts) forwarded the following resolution, passed by the Standing Joint Com- mittee—" That the Clerk of the Peace inform the School Attendance authorities in the county, that in the opinion of this Committee it is desirable that the police should discontinue serving summonses under the Education Acts." The members agreed that the work of the atten- dance officers would he considerably impeded, and their influence with parents weakened, if they had to perform this duty,and on the motion of Dr.McDougall, seconded by Mr. Taylor, the following resolution was passed : "That inasmuch as the work of School Board visitors is largely one ot moTal. suasion, necessitating good relations with the parents, it is very undesirable that they should he required to serve Police Court summonses, and this Board respectfully requests the County Council not to make the contemplated change in Runcorn."—The Clerk ix as instructed to forward it to the proper quarter accom- panied by a letter.

div.head: .LY)13,1.
div.p: TiE SUICIDE OF A CHESHIRE. UNDERGRADUATE AT OX- FORD.—Great sympathy is felt and expressed for the parents of Mr. Cecil Langshaw Schwabe who are very highly respected in Lyjnm and neighbourhood. The body was interred yesterday. VESTRY MEKTING.—An extraordinary vestry meeting was held in St. Peter's Church on Thursday evening, Mr. John Devrhurst was elected people's warden in the place of his brother, the late Mr. G. 131 Erewhurst. There were wit many parishioners present. SALE AZ LYMM HALL.—On. Thursday and yesterday there was-a sale of the household furniture, Stc.,at Lymns Hall, consequent upon the tenant, Mr. Wm. Battersby, being about to take up his residence at Cuddington. IVe understand that Mr. Glazebrook, a. Liverpool merchant, will be the next occupant of the Hall. A HORSE STRANGLED.—On Thursday, Mr. John Lake, landlord of the Fleece Inn, purchased a horse in Liver- pool and drove it over to Lymm. On putting it up for the night he incautiously tied a rope round its neck with a running noose. On the followinc, morning the animal, a very valhable one, was found to have been atrangled. COUNTY Porzex •InspEcTi os.—Otr Tuesday her Majesty's Inspector of Constabulary, in company with the Chief Constable of the county (olonel Hamersley), paid a visit of inspection to the Police Stition,. Lyinm. Everything was found • in a highly satisfactory condition. In- deed, the premises are "as- bright as a new pin," and reflect the highest credit on Sergeant Wynne and the officers under his charge.

CARRIAGE ACCIDENT.— On Thursday evening, at Eteatley, a carriage belonging to. Mr. Henry Everton, was returning from the Elation when the pony attached bolted along the lane from the lane from Mr. Oldfield's to the rectory. Mr. Everton and his daughters, who were seated in the conveyance; were thrown out, and though badly shaken were not hurt. The runaway came into collision with a carriage containing Mr. Lyttleton Dewhurst, which it overturned. Mr. Everton's carriage was smashed and the pony injured, . but Mr. Dewhurst's horse and carriage.were practically none the worse for the" turn over." A RUNAWAY HORSE.—On Tuesday a hofse attached to a hansom, hired by a brewer's traveller at Warrington. was left standing outside the Green Dragon Inn, Heat- ley, with no one in charge, and, acting under some im- pulse it bolted in the direction of Heatley Station. The signalman,seeing the runaway coming,opened the gates, and allowtd the charger full scope along Mill-lane. Here it came in contact with a lamp post,. knocking it away, which perfermance swerved the horse and its cab on to the footpath. The horse freed itself, and again got into the middle of the road. It dashed albno. Burford-lane, under the bridge, and ultimately into the hedge near the coal yard. Strange to say not much damage was done to either the horse or conveyance. A BOY DROWNED IN THE CANAL.—OR Monday morning Mr. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest at the Plough Hotel, touching the death of Thomas Wright, nine years of age, who was found in the canal on Monday Morning. Catherine Wright, wife of John Wright, plasterer, who lives on the canal bank at Statham, said the deceased was her son. He left home shortly before nine o'clock on Friday morning to go to school. She had not seen him alive since. He did not come to dinner, and she made enquiries without avail. She then sent for her husband, and he gave informatim to the police. The body was recovered from the canal on Saturday morn- ing, and the mother thought that the boy was hurrying home and, going too near the water,, fell into it. She did not suspect any foul play. Sergeant Wynne said the canal banks were very slippery that day. P.C. Griffith examined the body when taken from the water,but there were no marks upon it, except a slight discolouration on the side. That was all the evidencetand the,jury re- turned a verdict of "Found drowned.'"
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. T. 0, Norris (chairman), Chas. Lister, and W. Long, and Dr. Brabazon

THE DEATH OF' Mn. DEWITURST.—The Chairman said before the business of the Court commenced it was his painful duty to refer to the death of another colleague, Mr. George Ba.kewell Dewhurst, one of the oldest magis- trates of that court. He was very well known to every- one in the district, and had always done his duty faith- fully in his capacity as magistarte. He would be greatly missed both in the village and in the court. The Chair- man then proposed that.a vote of sympathy to the widow and children be sent from the Bench.

FIGHTING.—IsraeI Lee and Ji_lmes Ing/esfield for fight- ing at Lynun on the 10th :nit, were each bound over in the sum of £5 to keep.the peace for six months. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—WiIIiam Price, drunk and disorderly at Thelwall, on the 26th of April, was fined ss. including costs.—John Shaw, at Lymm, nn the 2nd inst., was fined 2s. 6d.—Eunice Aspratt was charged with being drunlcand disorderly at Lymm, on the 4th inst. P,C. Griffiths awl/Drill-sergeant Callaghan proved thc charge. The defendant in a loud and excited manner made certain recriminations against the officer,which the Chairman told her she ought to try to prove against him in court at another time if they were true. She was fined ss. and costs, 14s. 6th in all „ or in default 14 days. USING PROFANE LANGUAGE.—Amos Riley, Ship Canal labourer, 19th apperahrte, was charged with using pro- fane language to P.C. Griffiths on the 4th inst. P.C. Griffiths said Riley and the defendant in the previous case were coming out of the Nag's Head together, and Riley used most foul language to witness. This he repeated to the Bench. Drill-sergeant Callaghan corroborated. Riley said he had been aggravated by Griffiths's conduct to the woman Aspratt, with whom he had lived for four years, though not married to her. He was fined 23. 6d. and costs, 12s. in all : in default 14 days.

div.head: • LYMM LOCAL BOARD.-A LIVELY MEETING.
div.p: • LYMM LOCAL BOARD.-A LIVELY MEETING.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day evening. There were present Messrs. H. Cameron (chairman), R. Dutton, D. Rogers, H. Harrison, J. Holt, F. Swallow, J. Thamasson, R. Whitelegg, T. J. Ridgway (law clerk), W. Mullard (clerk), J. Mort (surveyor), and W. Severs (gas manager.)

THE COUNTY COUNCIL AND THE MAIN ROADS.—The Clerk read a letter from the county surveyor stating that the Main Roads Committee of the County Council were prepared to recommend the Council to pay £254 Bs. 6d. for maintenance of the main roads in the Board's district for the ensuing year, which was £5 less than the sum asked for, nothing being allowed for improvements.—The Clerk was instructed to reply urging the claims of the Board to the full amount claimed for maintenance, and also for an allowance for improvements of the maul roads.
THE ROMEO'S MEN DESIRE MORE N.Y.—An unsigned circular from the Board's men asking for increase of wages was referred to Committee.
TECIINICAL INSTRUCTION.

The Law Clerk read a letter from Mr. Chas. Lister, C.C., desiring to know whether the Board had come to any de- cision as to the course they would take with regard to the adoption of the Technical Instruction Act, and hoping the Board would not lose the opportunity of administering the sum offered by the County Council.—The Clerk re, minded the Board that they had previously declined to adopt the Act. —Mr. Dutton said the Inspector from South Kensington,on his recent visit to the Grammar Schootex- pressed a very strong opinion that the local authority in not adopting the Technical Instruction Act, and claiming the sum which would te allocated for Lymm, and which he estimated at about £lOO per annum, were making a mistake. The Inspector considered that the Grammar School authorities were the body to take up the subject of technical education, and the head master informed him that he would b. willing, to carry on a work in connection with the South Kensington Science and Art Department by bringing his class into the Parochial schools where it would be more in reach of the villagers.—The Law Clerk expressed his regret that the Board had previously de- clined to adopt the Act. The Board, he said, could not

exceed a id. rate, which was not a large thing, but a rate would raise £45 to £5O, and in return for that the Board would get £9O from the County Council. The Board might try to squeezeand economise this year to lay id. rate, and next year do things properly by going in for the Id. rate.—The. Chairman gave notice that at the next meeting he would move the adoption of the Act.
A COMPLAINT AS TO THE BOARD'S GAS.-HEROIC MEASURES THREATENED. - MESSRS. ROGERS AND HOLT EXCHANGE RECRIMINATIONS.

Mr. Bowen appeared before the Board and complained of the quality of the gas supplied in the Market Place, and said his latest gas bill would double that he had paid for the corresponding period last year. He remarked that everybody knew what a poor miserable light they had had these last two years. He considered that the Gas Manager was placed in such a position that he could not give them good gas. Comparative figures were read to. Mr. Bowen toshow him that he had no cause of com- plaint as to price, but he said he did not v ant any; he had had plenty before him. He was not the only victim. Mr. Whitelegge had suffered.—Mr. Whitelegge : I take my part quietly. (Laughter.)—Mr. Bowen : Thank good- ness lam not on the Bcard. I could open my Mouth if I would.—The- Law Clerk r. You will find great sym- pathy.—Mr. Bowen: We shall have to have it recti- fied, or we will do the same as old Cromwell did, have a blow up (Laughter.) The. Chairman: We never read history. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Bowen then wished the Board good evening, and retired. Mr. Rogers said at the last meeting Mr. Holt charged the Board with supplying bad gas to consumers. —Mr. Holt protested against this subject being brought forward without notice.—Mr. Rogers: Did you give any notice when you insulted the Board in that way ?—Mr. Bolt: When it is opening a question you can always do so, but when you are making a charge against me I want to know if it is in order.—The Chairman ruled that Mr. Rogers was in order.—Mr. Rogers then proceened to read a statement to show that during the past 12 months the average illuminating power of the gas had been 18 candles, nine per eent, higher than the Board were com- pelled to furnish. He pronounced the charge of Mr. Holt a false and malicious slander.—Mr. Heft: Have you finished? Mr. Rogers: No, i have net.—Mr. Holt: Go' on then.—Mr. Rogers proceeded to say that Mr. Holt when on the Gas Committee was allowed free control, and he allowed the gas works to drift to the extreme edge of bankruptcy.—Mr. Bolt: That is a lie.—Mr. Rogers: You hear his polite-language, gentlemen.—Mr. Bolt: I cin say nothing else.—Mr. Rogers, continuing, said in the last year of Mr. Holt's connection with the works there was £969 12s. 11d, unaccounted for. If that was not running down .with a vengeance he did not know what was. He left the plant unfit for work, the cash box empty, and a very heavy dent on the work; and since then it had been a work of labour and care and thought to rescue them from the state of ruin into which they had sunk. But the Assessment Committee had now raised their rateable value to an extent which re- presented them to be worth £5.000 ' more than in 1880; and the debt had been reduced by over £2,000. That was the state of things that had prevailed since Mr. Bolt's administration. There was no better-gas supplied to any community within miles.—Mr. Holt thought the charge brought against him was quite uncalled for, be- cause his statement was made before the fa Board and might have been refuted then as well as new; but Mr. Rogers then sat very quiet and never said a word. He had evidently been considering and reading up a whole lot of things which he (Mr. Holt) could not go into now; and he had made deliberate mistaternents. When Mr. Rogers came on that Board £B5O Odd had been paid off the debt in the year, such a thing as- had never been . done before. How did Mr. Rogers make that fit? During the time of his (Mr. Bolt's) connection with the works, though Mr. Rogers said he had-brought them to a state of bankruptcy there had always been a balance at the bank ; but it had not been so since. Mr. Rogers had been connected with them. He went about after the committee had met picking up things, and that was the way he did his business ? Why did he not make his statement in committee instead of now bringing a lot of figures which he could not refute at present, though he knew they were deliberate lies.—Mr. Rogers: That is your bare word: how do you manage to-prove it ?—Mr. Holt defied Mr. Rogers or any other member to prove the truth of his figures.—Mr. Rogers : Prove it.—Mr. Holt : Do you mean to tell me that all the gas- consumers are wrong P—Mr. Rogers : No. I don't say co,. but I say the meters are right.—Mr. Holt : When tlae.gas supplied us was stinking you said it,was good gas. Mr. Severs will tell you that he can't make proper gas as things are.— Mr. Rogers (to the Gas Manager) Have you been falsifying your books ?—Mr. Severs: .11,e4 I have not.— Mr. Bolt: .Then how can you produce good stuff out of ball. You cannot do it.—The Chairman expressed his regret that thisdiscussion had taken place. He thought Mr. Holt had given, perhaps, a strong opinion about the gas. What Mr. Rogers had said affected him (the Chair- man) because he was a member of the Board at the time referred to, and he did not know whether he had not ad- mitted that some of Mr. Bolt's statements were true.— Mr. Bolt: Were the works in a bankrupt state? Had the Committee to borrow money from; anybody P—The Chairman: I would rather not discuss-it.—Mr. Holt said he did want it discussed, and thrashed out —Some fur- ther conversation ensued, in the course of which Mr. Holt re-asserted that the gas was of ' bad quality. The Chairman, however, brought the discussion to a close, and the Board then dispersed.

div.head: DEATH OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF YORK,
div.p: DEATH OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF YORK,

It is with regret that we announce the death on Tues- day morning of the archbishop. of York. After his.re- cent enthrorement, Dr. Magee went to Hull on business connected with his new diocese. He contracted a severe cold while there, but his keen interest in the proceedings of the Infant Life Insurance Committee, of which he was chairman, brought him to London an Wednesday, April 22. Upon his arrival in towrii, the Archbishop went to 11, Suffolk-St., Pall Mall, where-he always staved when in London, and here it was soon found that he was seri- ously indisposed. On theThursdav night he Went to bed and never rose again. On the 24th ult., feeling that he needed considerable attentien,Dr. Maege sent for his man servant, who arrived with- Miss Magee. The symptoms then were in no sense alarming, and remembering the manner in which he ralliedfroin a serious illne.ssin 1883 It was reasonably to be expected that he woulilsoon re- cover. The Archbishop, however, grew worse,, and last Thursday Mrs. Magee came from Bishopthorpe„ where the family were but barely settled. Despite careful nursing and the constant attendance of Sir, Andrew Clarke and Dr. Cassidy,.bronchitis supervened: On Mon- day night Dr. Magee desired the attendance- 4 his old medical man, Dr. Walker,.oi Peterborough, who was tele- graphed for at once. He arrived, but only in time to watch the patient's last moments. In the presence of his wife, daughter, and two Sons, who reside in London, Dr. Magee passed qpietly away at a quarter to four on Tues- day morning. He was conscious to the last. William Connor Mhgee was an admirable, representa- tive of all that is best in the Protestant Church of Ire- land. His grandfather was Archbishop of Dublin in the early part ()Rite century, and his father was curate of the parish,chureh,of Cork. He entered Trinity College, Dublin, at an eerie age as a scholar, and after a distin- guished academical career he graduated in honours in 1842. No otherrahmeus of that University ever attained to the same eminence in the Church of England. For a , short time after his ordination in 1844, he acted as a I curate in Dublin,. but his health fairing he was ordered to the South of Spain, and spent two years at Malaga. On his return in 1848 he became curate (.4 St. Saviour's, Bath, and a Mt% later, having become popular in that city by his preaching, which, thoughevangelical in tone, was remarkable for its vigour andspontaneity, he was appointed first joint and then sole incumbent of the "Octagon Chapel." where he remained six or seven years, until he became minister of Quebec Chapel in 1858, thus carrying his. inilluence into one of the most fashionable districts of London. Flis predecessor at Quebec Chapel' had become Dean of Norwich, and it was thus in accordance with precedent when the Protestant Churchof Irettand recalled its rising star and he became Vicar of Enniskillen and Dean of Cork in 1864. All this time his reputation as a preacher, eloquent, original, witty, and persuasive, was growing, and he had frequently to cross the Irish Channel to be heard at St. Paul's, Westminster Abbey. or Whitehall,or, again by the Queen at Windsor. No one was surprised when, on the death of Dr. Jeune in 1868, Dr. Magee was appointed Bishop of Peterborough—the first instance of a Dublin University man obtaining possession of an English See. In 188% Dr. Magee presided with much ability over the Church Congress at Leicester, and in 1894 he published a volitean of sermons with the general title of The Gospel and the Age," the setae as that pre- fixed to one of his. earliest printed discourses. In the year following hishealth was in a very precarious state, •but he recovered so as to appear, at any rate, much 'r what he had been before, though same of the old vigour was missing, There seemed, however, to be stilla career before him when he was selected by Lord Sails- bury in January this year to succeed Archbishop Thom- son, and he had already won the esteem and admiration of such of the northern clergy as had hitherto known him , only by name when the end so rapidly came. The Archbishop of Canterbury will be unable to offici- ate at the funeral trAday of the late Archbishop of York, owing to the almost simultaneous death of the Archbishop of Canterbury's brother-in-law, Mr. Thomas Hare, at whose funeral his Grace will attend this day (Saturday).

div.head: CRICKET
div.p: CRICKET
Mr. Thornton's Eleven closed yesterday for 203; Cambridge University were at close of play, .107 for 8 wickets.

THE BURLBERT BREACH OF PROMISE CASE,. The Evelyn v. Hurlbert appeal for a new- trial is not likely to be reached before Whitsuntide. Mr. Candy, Q.C., will again represent Miss Evelyn, and the Attorney- General Mr. Hurlbert.

THE CONVENT WILL CASE. In the convent will case—Hampson v. Fig—Justice Butt apd a special jury had set aside Sarah Hampson'S bequest to a Homan Catholic sisterhood on the ground of undue influence. The judgment was now upheld.

DEATH OF EARL POWIS. The death is announced of the Earl of Pciwis, which took place on Thursday evening, at his residence in Lon- don,in his 74th year. The title descends to the nephew of the deceased earl, Mr. George Charles Herbert, ,who was born in 1862.

MR. SMITH TO HAVE A WALK OVER. Mr. W. H. Smith has vacated his seat by accepting the Lard Wardenship of the Cinque Ports, and will have to seek re-election.—It was understood that the Liberal candidate for the Strand Division, in opposition to Mr. Smith,. would be Dr.Guttridge, of Brook-st. but the doc- tor has written to say he will not oppose Mr. Smith's return,

THE POLLING AT HARBOROUGH. The polling commenced yesterday morning .in the Harborough Division, Leicestershire, the candidates being Mr. G. W. Logan, Gladstonian, and Mr. Gerald Hardy, Obnservative. There are nearly• sixty polling stations. Out of 13,000 voters about 3,000 are free- holders, the remainder being mostly labourers and farmers,

MIL GLADSTONE AND THE WREXHAM AND MOLD RAILWAY. Mr. Gladstone gave evidwnce yesterday before the Select Committee against the application of the North- Western Railway Comnany for running powers over the Wrexham and Mold Railway. Ile sontended that this line to Birkenhead independent of the North-Western was necessary.
THE CLITHEROE CASE. A PLAY PROHIBITED.

-- - Yesterday morning, Mr. Reynolds, lessee of Blackburn Theatre Royal, received a communication from the Lord Chamberlain,stating that the provisional licence granted for the performance of a play, entitled "Abduction of a Wife," had been, withdrawn, and that the performance advertised for Saturday was prohibited. The sale of Mr. Jackson's reply to his -vife's vindication has been prohibited by Messrs. Smith and Son at all their rail- way bookstalls. MR. P: STANHOPE, M.P., AND THE SHIP CANAL. A London correspondent,who- yesterday afternoon has had an interview with Mr. Philip Stanhope with resnect to his motiork on the second reading of the Ship Canal Bill, says that the hon. gentleman is not so much op- posed to the Ship Canal undertaking in itself as he is to its control by a private company. What he wants is the control of our waterways by public trusts, "I am in favour of the, municipalisation of canals," he said, " for the reason that private promoters are quite unable by themselves to face tremendous opposition of the railway monopoly."
BANK FAILURE IN AMERICA. NEW; Yba, FitIDAY.— Me Spring Garden National Bank of Philadelphia has closed it doors in consequence of the recent failure of the Keystone National Bank.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at.a quarter-past four. A MAW& INGIMENT.—In reply to Lord Delaware,, Lord 131201v-14r:ow promised to lay on the table a copy of the ad- dress from the Council of the Government of Malta, with reference to, raising a regiment of infantry in Malta. The Duke of-Cambridge spoke highly of thd Malta militia and artillery. FISHERIES Bim—The reports of amendments to the Newfoundland 19sheries.8i11 was read and agreed to. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes past five.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair shortly after three o'clock., Mn: DE COBA.E.S.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHLQUER: I beg to give notice tat on Tuesday a motion will be made for a return of a copy of the warrant of arrest issued.against the hon. member for East Belfast (Mr. De Cobain). Mr. filem,y : Is it intended to give any infor- mation beyond the warrant. I put a question some time ago as to accessories, but could get no information. The CHANCELBOR of the EXCHEQUER: Would the..hon. member repeat his question on a later day, with notice? I am not prepared to answer it now. IRISH LAND, PURCHASE.—The House went into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Purchase Bill. The considera- tion of Mr. T. Hea,ly's amendment to strike out sub- section on, to clause six, which would exclude from the benefits of the, bill all tenants whose holdings.exceed the annual vote of thirty pounds,was resumed.—Mr. Serroa. said the object of the bill was to create as many owners of their holdings as possible. He contended that,if they were to purchase large holdings, at the end of 49 years, they would have about 60,000 small holders in possession of their holdings out of 600,000. Mr. 134.1.- Founopposed theamendment,and after observations from Mr. Sinchkir and Colonel W. Wareing and Mr. M. Healy,. Mr. BALFOL-R suggested that, if the amendment was withdrawn, he was prepared to submit an alternative scheme. Mr. Jourr MORLEY challenged Mr. Balfour-to say whetherbevrould withdraw the sub-section or not,. also whether he would submit his. alternative scheme- so that they might know what they were discussing.. Lord Hartiogton though that if any great number of large holders were excluded,, the dfficulty of working the Bill would be increased. Mr. T: Healy strongly advised the Government, to withdraw the sub-section. After a long discussion, sub- section one was struck out. Cu the second sub-section Mr. BXLFOUR moved an amendment providing that advances might be made under Land Purchase Acts, as amended by this Act.

SEEKING TS FORTUNE ON THE SHIP CANAL.

Patrick Hunt, an Irish labourer on the Ship Canal, was charged at the Runcorn Police Court, with having on 03 30th April feloniously stolen two .£1 Bank of Ireland notes belonging to. Patrick Kelly. Kelly, a young man apparently about 20 years of age. had worked on his father 'S farm in County Galway, up. to a few creeks ago, when he left his native shore to seek his fortune in. England, and the fame of the Ship Can3l having spread even to his native place, he made for Manchester; and there he met twolellow countrymen, the prisoner being one. According to the teile told by Kelly to the magis- trates,. who found, it difficult, to understand his broad eeltic brogue, the- prisoner obtained the Irish motes from him on the understanding that he would get him work at as. per. day and buy him clothes suitable ?or the nork he would be engaged in, and they came on to Runcorn. Kelly alleged that not only had not the prisoner fulfilled his pro- mi.'s°, but he lied chaaged the notes and spent the money in drinking. The prisoner handed up\ to the magistrates an account af•what he had spent for Kelly. He had paid the railway fare friom Man- chester to Vuncorn, had given him ss. to, purchase a scarf, and found himboard and lodging., There was 17s. 6d. due to Kelly, and he would ba glad to hand it over to him As Kelly admitted that the first part of this statement was correct, and as Kelly's evidence was uncorroborated, the case was dismissed on the prisoner undertaking to pay the balanca to him.
